News.title: Doorbell footage shows brazen woman swiping pints of milk at 5am from doorstep
News.content:
Doorbell footage shows brazen woman swiping pints of milk at 5am from doorstep

Doorbell footage from a resident in Bearwood, Birmingham, showed a woman dressed only in underwear walk down her driveway and allegedly grab two bottles of milk

Woman in black underwear caught on doorbell camera snatching milk

Footage shows the bare-faced cheek of a woman who appeared to snatch two bottles of milk from a doorstep wearing just underwear.

‌



A resident from the Bearwood area of Birmingham was surprised to find her milk delivery missing but was even more taken aback when she found out what had happened.

‌



She checked her doorbell footage and allegedly discovered that a woman dressed only in skimpy black underwear and flip flops had made off with the bottles at around 5am in the morning.

‌



The alleged offender could be seen strolling up the driveway, picking up the bottles and walking off calmly before she seemed to show more haste when she got to the main road.

View 2 Images A woman was seen taking two bottles from a doorstep (Image: Birmingham Live)

UK airline issues ‘urgent’ plea as key flights cancelled READ MORE :

UK weather maps turn volcanic red for next 31C heatwave with 19 counties above 30C READ MORE :

The resident took to Facebook to show what had happened and others also reported their milk had gone amiss recently, reported BirminghamLive.

‌



The householder said: "We were very frustrated to see it on our doorbell as have two young children, but you hope it’s someone in such desperate need they resort to stealing.

"Why in her underwear we do not know! Makes us think twice about getting milk delivered as it has happened several times in our area recently."

West Midlands Police confirmed that it received a report of stolen milk at 5.10am on Friday, July 17, and has appealed to the public for information

‌



View 2 Images The woman was caught on doorbell footage (Image: Birmingham Live)

Its statement said: "Anyone with any information is asked to contact 101 or use the Live Chat option on our website quoting crime number 20/328342/26."

Meanwhile, a resident in the Cotteridge area of Birmingham has also complained about milk bottles being stolen from their driveway and he said he had stopped the milk delivery.

‌



The man wrote on Facebook: "Same again this morning. Milk deliveries have been stopped. It’s now being investigated and they have asked for the footage. I’d advise everyone contact their milk companies."

While a person replied: "Might sound and look trivial to some but this is someone's livelihood our tracksuited tea-leaf is impacting.

"No doubt the milk delivery company put a lot of time and effort into developing the round. Only for someone to tear it all up." And a further reply read: "Have you got the video of him walking up to the doorstep? someone may recognise them."

News.title: 'Significant' search launched for man missing at popular lake in Wales
News.content:
'Significant' search launched for man missing at popular lake in Wales

Police helicopter and divers have reportedly been seen at Llyn Geirionydd after a man went missing at the 45-acre lake on the slopes of the Carneddau mountains in Snowdonia

View 2 Images Llyn Geirionydd near Trefriw has been the site of a major search (file photo) (Image: Ian Cooper/North Wales Live)

Police are still searching for a man who went missing at a lake yesterday with police divers and helicopters reportedly joining the hunt.

‌



The alarm was raised on Sunday evening at Llyn Geirionydd, a 45-acre lake nestled on the lower slopes of the Carneddau mountains in Snowdonia, Wales.

‌



The alarm was raised at approximately 7.10pm with emergency services called to the lake. North Wales Police has confirmed that, despite searches conducted throughout the night, the man has yet to be found. His family has been notified.

‌



Search efforts are set to continue at the lake, the force said, with an "increased emergency service presence" amid the ongoing search operation.

Locals reported seeing a helicopter circling the lake at around 8pm. Meanwhile one witness described a "significant emergency response" and another said police divers were at the scene.

‌



View 2 Images The scenic lake has proved very popular with tourists (Image: Ian Cooper/North Wales Live)

The body of a 21-year-old man was recovered from the lake just 11 days ago. Llyn Geirionydd is a popular destination for watersports enthusiasts. The lake draws kayakers to its waters and holds the distinction of being the only lake within Eryri National Park where speedboats are permitted, reports North Wales Live.

North Wales Police is urging members of the public to stay clear of the lake while the search continues. A spokesperson said: "Immediate family have been informed and are being supported.

Article continues below

"We ask members of the public to avoid the area today to allow emergency services to continue their work.

"Anybody who was at the lake yesterday evening who hasn't already spoken to police should contact us."

News.title: Donald Trump vows Iran will 'pay' after killing of US soldiers
News.content:
Donald Trump vows Iran will 'pay' after killing of US soldiers

The US president issued more threats towards the Islamic Republic following the deaths of US troops in Iran

View 3 Images Trump has vowed revenge against Iran for the killing of US service personnel (Image: Getty Images)

Donald Trump has vowed that Iran will pay for the killing of US troops “many times over” following the deaths of three service personnel in recent days.

‌



The president issued the warning after the American military launched a further wave of strikes, sparking retaliatory attacks by Tehran.

‌



The ongoing clashes and the collapse of the interim ceasefire deal have fuelled fears of a return to a full-blown conflict.

‌



US Central Command said two soldiers were killed in Jordan on Friday while defending against Iranian ballistic missile and drone attacks.

It was subsequently announced a service member had died in Iraq during the “controlled detonation” of a downed Iranian drone.

Some 17 US troops have been killed since the start of the war.

‌



Writing on his Truth Social platform, Mr Trump said: “Every time Iran kills an American Soldier they will pay for that killing many times over!”

He added that this “directive” had been passed on to defence secretary Pete Hegseth and top US general Dan Caine as well as other military commanders.

‌



White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has said Mr Trump will attend Dover Air Force Base in Delaware on Tuesday evening for the return of the fallen service personnel.

Iranian authorities have said said at least 50 people have been killed and more than 500 wounded in the latest rounds of US strikes.

Shortly after Mr Trump’s warning, the US defence department posted on X a drawing of a soldier in revolutionary-era battledress carrying a musket, with the message: “We untie the hands of our warfighters to intimidate, demoralise, hunt and kill the enemies of our country. No mercy.”

‌



Meanwhile, Tehran has continued to target shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the US enforce a restored naval blockade of Iranian ports as both sides wrestle for control over the contested Gulf waterway, which is vital to global energy supplies.

View 3 Images This undated image provided by the U.S. Army shows Pvt. Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Carrollton, Texas. (Image: U.S. Army via AP)

The fighting has caused maritime traffic using the channel to plummet, leading to renewed concerns over the impact on economies around the world, including the UK.

‌



The situation in the Middle East and the movement of shipping through the strait was among the topics discussed by newly installed Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the US president in a phone call soon after his arrival in Downing Street.

The strait had been open before the war was launched by the US and Israel on February 28.

In response to the offensive, Tehran effectively closed the waterway to maritime traffic, which disrupted global oil and gas supplies and drove up fuel and food prices.

‌



View 3 Images This undated photo provided by the U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command shows 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan (Image: U.S. Army Space and Missile Defe)

Despite the initial ceasefire deal with the US, known as the memorandum of understanding, Iran continued to exert leverage over the sea route by demanding ships seek permission to transit, raising the threat of future charges and attacking vessels.

Tehran claims it controls the channel, while this is disputed by the US and other countries, which cite international law on freedom of navigation.

Article continues below

US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said the US is still open to negotiating with Iran but that “it has to be real”.

He said: “We’re going to continue to respond. If the door opens to diplomacy — if the guys that want to do something productive for Iran win and take control of that system, or take control of the negotiations — that’ll be a very positive development.”

However, he pointed out currently “that’s not where we are”.

News.title: Wandsworth residents brand structure 'IKEA Bridge' after council's £600,000 paintjob
News.content:
Wandsworth residents brand structure 'IKEA Bridge' after council's £600,000 paintjob

Wandsworth Council said the work on two railway bridges at on East Putney Underground Station cost £600,000, a restoration residents in the southwest London district have blasted

View 2 Images The expensive makeover has sparked backlash (Image: Cllr George Crivelli / SWNS)

Residents have been left outraged after a council spent £600,000 painting a railway bridge.

‌



Wandsworth Council spent the hefty sum repainting two railway bridges at East Putney Tube station in southwest London as part of upgrade works, including “pigeon-proofing” the metalwork. But locals say the new blue and yellow colour scheme resembles IKEA branding - and even HSS Hire.

‌



The paintjob was carried out in March under the borough’s previous administration, before local elections took place in May. Now, residents have branded the new look a “shame”.

‌



Emma, 38, who has lived in the area for eight years, said the colours were “out of character” for Putney, replacing the bridges’ previous muted red paint. She said: “I just think it’s a bit of a shame they’ve gone for this garish colour palette that’s not in keeping with the surrounding area. It’s all just become a bit of a in terms of the IKEA bridge.”

View 2 Images Conservative ward councillor, George Crivelli believes the bridge is too bright (Image: Cllr George Crivelli / SWNS)

Gran refuses to sell patch of garden to save ancient oak from £45,000,000 Hereford Bypass READ MORE :

Dad scoffs record number of fish fingers after making strange vow on The 1% Club READ MORE :

Council officers said the bridges, which are owned by Network Rail and Transport for London, were repainted to a specification recommended by the local authority. They also confirmed the work was not legally required but was considered “capital maintenance”.

‌



Conservative ward councillor and cabinet member for children George Crivelli said: “I think it’s a bit too bright, and not in keeping with the local area. My main concern about it was that, in effect, one councillor has decided the colour scheme on it.

“What I would have liked was that we actually maybe consulted local residents on it.”

While welcoming the repainting work, he added: “I’m very pleased to see the bridge being repainted, and I’m very pleased to see it being cleaned up, but a lot of people think it’s a bit garish, and I have to say I’m inclined to agree on that.

Article continues below

“People call it the IKEA bridge, I’ve heard people say it looks like an IKEA bridge. Perhaps it’s not really in keeping with the East Putney area overall. The only positive thing about those bright colours is that I suppose it will fade over time, won’t it?”

Responding to the backlash last month, a senior transport planner at the council said there were “no plans to revise the design”, adding that the number of negative comments was “relatively few given the very large numbers of local residents and station users.”

A Wandsworth Council spokesperson said: “The cost was £600,000 and the project was completed in May 2026.”

News.title: 'Andy Burnham draws line under Starmer era with Cabinet overhaul - and shocks with Chancellor pick'
News.content:
The clear-out of Keir Starmer's allies was swift and brutal.

Some Westminster wags branded it the "night of the long eyelashes" as Andy Burnham dispensed with the services of a string of top ministers in a clear break with the Starmer era.

Steve Reed, David Lammy, Darren Jones, Peter Kyle, Liz Kendall, Lord Hermer - all close to the former PM - were among those told their time was up.

Rachel Reeves fought hard to stay on as Chancellor but she was too closely tied to the Starmer project, particularly its most totemic failure - the cut to the winter fuel allowance. It is understood that she declined the offer of another big Cabinet job.

‌



Uncertainty over Burnham's pick for Chancellor created a state of hysteria in Westminster. Speculation lurched from initial favourite Ed Miliband to Shabana Mahmood, who was confidently tipped by much of the media in the days running up to Burnham's arrival in Downing Street.

Hope for income tax cut for lower earners as Burnham prepares cost of living blitz READ MORE :

View 2 Images Former Defence Secretary John Healey was named Chancellor in a surprise move (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

But it was John Healey, the ex-Defence Secretary, who was handed control over the nation's purse strings. Mahmood stays on as Home Secretary with a mandate from the PM to deliver her hard-line immigration reforms, while Miliband becomes Britain's top diplomat.

Awkwardly, the pair ended up walking up Downing Street together to learn their fate - but still shared a quick hug.

‌



Healey's appointment as Chancellor was a surprise to many but perhaps it shouldn't have been. The well-liked Labour veteran served in the Treasury under Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, and is seen as a safe pair of hands.

Burnham says he wants to avoid division between Labour's different tribes - despite carrying out a purge of the Starmerites that could set up trouble ahead.

Much of the briefing about the next Chancellor fixated on whether Miliband was too left-wing or whether Mahmood was too right wing. Healey is not aligned to one faction.

The PM's team are clear he wants an experienced and trusted figure in the Treasury to deliver his vision. Healey, a Yorkshire MP, shares his concern about deindustrialisation, the cost of living and backing British industry.

‌



Healey's record as a housing minister, and his commitment to overhauling forces accommodation, while he was at the Ministry of Defence, clearly chimes with Burnham's desire for a council house building boom.

Healey's decision to resign over defence spending will put him under pressure to find cash for the armed forces. But his parting swipe at "Treasury orthodoxy" show he's a safe pick with an edge - one who won't spook the markets but can help to drive through radical reforms.

It is a blow to Miliband, who coveted the job of Chancellor, and played a pivotal role in the new PM's rise to power. For months he was Burnham's most powerful friend in Westminster, and is said to have been the first Cabinet Minister to privately urge Keir Starmer to resign.

But Burnham appears to listened the backlash and handed him another great office of state instead. Whether it is a consolation to Miliband remains to be seen.

‌



He rewarded loyalty elsewhere by appointing key ally Louise Haigh, as First Secretary of State and Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. The former Transport Secretary, who was sacked by Starmer over a historic fraud conviction, is now one of the most powerful people in Government.

Lucy Powell, another ally, becomes Education Secretary - and one of his right-hand women, Anneliese Midgley, was named as Chief Whip.

Angela Rayner is back in Government in her old role, Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government. She fought hard to win back this brief, which is a key priority for Burnham.

The PM kept Pat McFadden at the Department of Work and Pensions, in a sign of his commitment to fixing the welfare system and getting young people into work. He also moved experienced minister Yvette Cooper to the Department of Health, where she will drive much-needed reforms to the broken social care system.

‌



The Cabinet continues to take shape but these appointments show us what the PM's key priorities are.

And while he has packed his Cabinet with experienced people, there is only one vision here - and it's his.

News.title: Andy Burnham's Cabinet - Who's in and who's out as Angela Rayner returns and Rachel Reeves loses job
News.content:
Andy Burnham's Cabinet - Who's in and who's out as Angela Rayner returns and Rachel Reeves loses job

Andy Burnham has unveiled his top team as Rachel Reeves and David Lammy departed the government, with the new PM pledging 'the moment when Britain starts to believe again'

'We will be better' says new PM Andy Burnham

Andy Burnham has announced a major change in personnel at the top of government hours after becoming Prime Minister.

‌



Chancellor Rachel Reeves was among the high-profile names axed as the new PM installed his top team - with John Healey named as her surprise replacement. Shabana Mahmood remains Home Secretary, while Ed Miliband was named as Foreign Secretary. And there was a return to government for Angela Rayner less than a year after she stepped down as Deputy PM.

‌



Wes Streeting became Defence Secretary, while Lucy Powell took over as Education Secretary from Bridget Phillipson. Ms Phillipson remains in Cabinet as Minister for Women and Equalities.

‌



Other high-profile departures include Keir Starmer's deputy PM, David Lammy., as well as Liz Kendall, Peter Kyle and Steve Reed. There was a return to the top table for Angela Rayner and Louise Haigh.

WASPI new hope as Andy Burnham set to meet campaign over redress options READ MORE :

View 10 Images Andy Burnham pledged an overhaul of British politics after becoming PM (Image: Ben Birchall/PA Wire)

Who's in:

John Healey - Chancellor of the Exchequer

‌



In one of his first surprise moves as PM, Andy Burnham announced John Healey as his new Chancellor, replacing Rachel Reeves.

It comes just weeks after his dramatic resignation as Defence Secretary - lashing out at the Treasury for not setting aside enough cash for defence.

One of the longest-serving MPs on the Labour benches, Mr Healey has been in Parliament since 1997 and held government roles under Tony Blair, Gordon Brown and Keir Starmer.

‌



Mr Healey last month threw Mr Starmer's government into turmoil, saying the PM's Defence Investment Plan failed to meet the challenges the country faces.

A respected figure on the international stage, Mr Healey has also been a housing minister and junior Treasury minister in the early 2000s - so he does have experience in his new field.

View 10 Images Former Defence Secretary John Healey succeeds Rachel Reeves as Chancellor (Image: TOLGA AKMEN/POOL/EPA/Shutterstock)

‌



Shabana Mahmood - Home Secretary

Some Whitehall mischief in recent days saw Shabana Mahmood linked with the Chancellor job. But Andy Burnham had other ideas and decided to keep her in post.

Ms Mahmood is a lightning rod figure for the Labour left - but has a record for delivery which few can match. It has been well known that she wants to remain in the Home Office.

‌



Just last week she set out a controversial Immigration and Asylum Bill, with measures including charging successful asylum seekers £10,000 to cover the cost of support they received.

A separate set of hardline immigration polices, which include doubling the standard time a person qualifies for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) sparked a backbench fury last year. Ms Mahmood, who as a youngster helped her dad run a corner shop, often observes that she is the most right-wing person in the room.

A lawyer who studied at Oxford, the Cabinet member also chairs Labour's National Executive Committee (NEC) and was initially Justice Secretary when Labour came to power. She held a junior shadow Treasury role under Ed Miliband, but refused to serve on the frontbench under Jeremy Corbyn.

‌



View 10 Images Shabana Mahmood is a key member of Mr Burnham's top team (Image: Getty Images)

Ed Miliband - Foreign Secretary

If some reports were to be believed a few weeks ago, Ed Miliband was in line to become Chancellor under Andy Burnham.

‌



But the former Labour Party leader has instead been appointed Foreign Secretary - the same post his former nemesis, David Cameron, took in the last months of the Tory government. An experienced operator, Mr Miliband has served as Energy Secretary since the general election, becoming the face of the government's Net Zero drive.

He has been an MP for over two decades, representing Doncaster North since 2005. Following Gordon Brown's resignation, he became leader of the Opposition. He beat rivals including his brother David and - awkwardly - Mr Burnham, who was eliminated in the first round.

A popular figure on the Labour left, he was thought to be on the cusp of becoming PM at the 2015 general election following positive polling - but a wipeout in Scotland proved costly and the Tories got a comfortable majority.

‌



Louise Haigh - First Secretary of State and Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster

View 10 Images Louise Haigh managed Mr Burnham's by-election campaign (Image: PA)

One of Andy Burnham's key allies in Parliament, Louise Haigh returns to the Cabinet after more than 18 months on the backbenches.

‌



She was Keir Starmer's pick as Transport Secretary when Labour returned to government. During her five months in office she pushed through groundbreaking legislation to bring railway companies into public ownership.

Ms Haigh also secured more than £1billion to improve bus services across the country. But she was forced to quit after it emerged she had pleaded guilty to fraud by false representation in 2014 by reporting a work mobile phone stolen - only to later find it in a drawer.

Earlier this month Ms Haigh, a key figure on the Labour 'soft left', revealed Mr Burnham had been planning what he would do in No10 for more than a year. She said: "He has spent that time thinking very deeply about how the country is run, what holds regions like Greater Manchester, and therefore most regions and the devolved nations of this country, back."

‌



Pat McFadden - Work and Pensions Secretary

One of Keir Starmer's closest allies, Pat McFadden has a reputation as a safe pair of hands across Westminster.

He was shifted to the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) last year in a reshuffle after welfare reforms championed by Liz Kendall had to be torn up. Mr McFadden was drawing up his own proposals under Mr Starmer, but Andy Burnham has already indicated he does not favour headline-grabbing cuts.

‌



The Wolverhampton South East MP was Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster from 2024, having previously held ministerial roles under both Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.

His calm demeanour is respected across government, and he is often dispatched to face the media on difficult days.

View 10 Images Yvette Cooper has been appointed Health Secretary

‌



Yvette Cooper - Health Secretary

Yvette Cooper is one of the most experienced figures in Andy Burnham's new team.

Since 2024 she has held two of the great offices of state - firstly as Home Secretary and then as Foreign Secretary. She was Work and Pensions Secretary and chief secretary to the Treasury under Gordon Brown, and held junior ministerial roles under both Gordon Brown and Tony Blair.

‌



Ms Cooper stood for party leader in 2015 after Ed Miliband stood down, losing out to Jeremy Corbyn. She is another name who has been linked with the Chancellor's job.

Angela Rayner, Housing and Local Government Secretary

The former Deputy PM is back in government following months of speculation about a leadership challenge.

‌



Angela Rayner was made Housing, Communities and Local Government Secretary following the general election and championed the landmark Employment Rights Act. A popular figure on the left of the party, she has spoken out against Shabana Mahmood's immigration reforms, branding them "un-British" - but will have to fall in line when she returns to government.

It also emerged she had warned Keir Starmer against appointing Peter Mandelson as ambassador to the US in 2024. She was forced to quit after it emerged she had underpaid stamp duty on a flat purchase in Hove by £40,000.

Ms Rayner admitted the error, stating it was not intentional, and was later cleared of wrongdoing by HMRC.

‌



View 10 Images There was a return to the Cabinet for Manchester MP Lucy Powell (Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire)

Lucy Powell, Education Secretary

There is a return to the Cabinet for Labour deputy leader Lucy Powell, who was sacked by Keir Starmer a year ago.

‌



Ms Powell, who served as Leader of the House of Commons from July 2024 to September 2025, is a popular figure on the Labour left. She was voted deputy party leader in a run-off following Angela Rayner's resignation - but not rewarded with a government role.

The Labour stalwart, an MP since 2012, has held shadow Cabinet posts under Keir Starmer and Jeremy Corbyn - including shadow Education Secretary and Housing Secretary.

The Manchester Central MP will know Andy Burnham well, having worked with him both in opposition and during the PM's tenure as Mayor of Greater Manchester.

‌



Jonathan Reynolds, Business and Science and Technology Secretary

Jonathan Reynolds made a return to Cabinet in what appears to be two roles combined.

Mr Reynolds had served as Business Secretary until September last year, before becoming chief whip.

‌



While popular among Labour MPs, there was frustration at his performance as chief whip, with many suggesting they were wasting one of their best communicators in the wrong role.

Mr Reynolds previously served in Ed Miliband's shadow Cabinet, as well as Jeremy Corbyn's.

Anneliese Midgley, Chief Whip

‌



A key strategist in the Makerfield by-election, the Knowsley MP became an MP in 2024.

She welcomed Andy Burnham on stage at his victory rally last month, and was one of the two MPs chosen to formally introduce him for his Commons serving in.

On the left of the party, Ms Midgley was previously Jeremy Corbyn's chief of staff, and is secretary of the Trade Union Group of Labour MPs.

‌



No10 announced she is the new Parliamentary Secretary to the Treasury (Chief Whip). She will be a member of the Cabinet.

View 10 Images Lisa Nandy, pictured last month, is retained as Culture, Media and Sport Secretary (Image: Getty Images)

Lisa Nandy, Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport

‌



Ms Nandy was the first cabinet member to join Mr Burnham on the campaign trail in Makerfield, and has been tipped for a job in his cabinet.

During her 16 years in Parliament, she has served as Culture Secretary, as well as Shadow Foreign Secretary and Shadow Housing Secretary under Keir Starmer.

She was also Shadow Energy Secretary under Jeremy Corbyn, but stepped down in 2016 in protest at his leadership. Ms Nandy stood for Labour leader after Mr Corbyn's resignation in 2019, ultimately losing out to Mr Starmer.

‌



A centre left politician, she worked in the charity sector and as an advisor to former Labour MP Neil Gerrard before getting into Parliament.

Bridget Phillipson, full member of Cabinet as Minister for Women and Equalities

In recent weeks Ms Phillipson, Keir Starmer's Education Secretary, has been locked in a spat with Tory leader Kemi Badenoch, who labeled her a "spiteful class warrior".

‌



Since Labour's general election victory she has been a central figure in government, overseeing the strategy to tackle child poverty and recruit thousands of teachers.

Her argument with Mrs Badenoch stems from the policy of closing a VAT loophole for private schools. Last month, Ms Phillipson said she would have a t-shirt printed with the Tory leader's words on it, saying she is proud of her record pulling children out of poverty.

View 10 Images Wes Streeting is the new Defence Secretary (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Wes Streeting, Defence Secretary

A few weeks ago we were talking about Mr Streeting as a possible Prime Minister.

He delivered a massive blow to Keir Starmer when he stepped down as Health Secretary the day after the King's Speech in May. The Londoner has been an MP since 2015, and was one of the first names in Mr Starmer's cabinet after the general election.

‌



In opposition he held junior roles in the Treasury, Department for Education and as Shadow Secretary of State for Child Poverty. Mr Streeting, who said he grew up furious at politicians "denigrating single-parent families like mine", went on to study at the University of Cambridge.

He briefly quit the Labour Party over the decision to enter the Iraq War.

Other appointments confirmed late on Monday night include;

‌



Alex Norris MP as Lord Chancellor and Secretary of State for Justice

Dame Angela Eagle DBE MP as Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs

Miatta Fahnbulleh MP as Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero

Stephen Kinnock MP as Secretary of State for Wales

Sir Chris Bryant MP as Secretary of State for Northern Ireland

Rt Hon Ellie Reeves KC MP as Attorney General. She will attend Cabinet

Rt Hon Emma Reynolds MP as Chief Secretary to the Treasury. She will attend Cabinet

Kanishka Narayan MP as Minister of State (Minister for Artificial Intelligence) jointly in the Cabinet Office and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. He will attend Cabinet

Hamish Falconer MP as Minister of State (Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations) jointly in the Cabinet Office and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office. He will attend Cabinet

Who is out

View 10 Images There are no roles for Rachel Reeves and David Lammy in the new government (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Rachel Reeves

The highest-profile departure is Keir Starmer's Chancellor Rachel Reeves, who announced this afternoon she is not taking another government role.

It had been widely expected that Ms Reeves would be offered a role at the top table, albeit less senior than the one she previously held. In a message confirming her departure, she said: "The economy today is stronger, fairer and more resilient because of the choices we have taken as a Labour Government over the past two years.

‌



"Stability restored, investment delivered and reform to our economy under way. I said when I was appointed Chancellor that I would judge my time in office if the lives ordinary working class people have been improved. I’m proud to say that they have."

David Lammy

The former Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy announced he is out this afternoon.

‌



In a post on X, he wrote: "I am immensely proud of what we achieved, in Opposition and in Government. As Foreign Secretary and Deputy Prime Minister, I helped rebuild Britain’s relationships with our European allies after the catastrophic Brexit years, stood steadfastly with Ukraine in its darkest hours, championed a new partnership of equals with the Global South and was proud to play a leading role in Britain’s recognition of the State of Palestine."

He continued: "I will continue to serve the great people of Tottenham, support this Labour government from the backbenches and do everything I can to help defeat Reform again at the next general election."

Darren Jones

‌



Keir Starmer loyalist Darren Jones was among the high-profile casualties.

Mr Jones, a regular in TV studios in recent months defending his old boss, posted on X: "Andy Burnham has called to tell me I won’t be a part of his new Cabinet. I wish him and his team every success."

He went on: "I wish the new government every success. With Reform on the verge of imploding, an irrelevant Conservative Party and a tired SNP, there are big opportunities for Labour to push on."

‌



Liz Kendall

View 10 Images Liz Kendall is out of the Cabinet (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

The Technology Secretary Liz Kendall is out.

‌



Ms Kendall, who was Work and Pensions Secretary during the welfare rebellion last year, said the new PM will take the country from "strength to strength".

In a statement published on social media, the former Labour leadership contender siad: "I wish whoever takes on the science and technology portfolio the very best for the future. She or he is fortunate to be overseeing, what is to my mind, the most exciting and transformative brief in government."

Steve Reed

‌



Keir Starmer loyalist and former Housing Secretary Steve Reed was one of the first to announce he was out.

In a letter shared on social media, Mr Reed wrote to the new Prime Minister: "Dear Andy, serving as the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government has been the honour of my life and although I am disappointed to be leaving Government now, I wish your new team every success.

"We won power the hard way. I was part of the campaign that fought to save our party and take it back to power against all the odds after our worst-ever election defeat. In 2017, I set up a group that played a significant role in exposing and driving out the anti-Jewish racists who'd occupied our party and led it to being found institutionally racist. I was proud to be part of the team that then turned the party around under Keir's leadership and took us forward to a landslide election victory."

‌



Peter Kyle

Another name departing is Peter Kyle, who was Business Secretary this morning.

Mr Kyle is an ever-present in Cabinet since Labour came back to power, having been Technology Secretary from July to September 2025 before being moved in a reshuffle.

‌



It had been expected that the MP for Hove and Portslade would make way.

Lord Richard Hermer

Keir Starmer's attorney general, Lord Richard Hermer, was also among those leaving government.

Article continues below

He said in a post on BlueSky that it has been "the privilege of my life" to serve in the post for the last two years, adding he was especially proud of the Hillsborough Law and rebuilding the UK's reputation abroad.

"I will continue to support this Labour government from the backbenches, as it delivers the change this country desperately needs. Andy and his team know they have my utmost support, and I wish them nothing but success."

News.title: Who's in the cabinet?
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has started building his new cabinet after taking office following the resignation of Sir Keir Starmer.

Tap or click on a cabinet member in our interactive guide below to learn more about them and their role in government. The guide will be updated as new appointments are made.

News.title: Watch: Starmer resigns, Burnham becomes PM... the day in 101 seconds
News.content:
Andy Burnham has become the UK's prime minister today, replacing Keir Starmer.

The day began outside a busy 10 Downing Street where Starmer made his final address as PM, before he and Burnham visited King Charles in Buckingham Palace.

The new prime minister then gave his own speech in Downing Street saying he wants a "circuit-breaker for Britain" and bring some of the biggest changes that country has seen in 40 years.

News.title: Burnham promises help with your money. How could it affect you?
News.content:
In his first speech as prime minister, Andy Burnham has promised to give people more "breathing space" to help with the cost of living.

Policies will be announced on Tuesday - his first full day in the job. Although a few hours after taking office, the new prime minister confirmed he will be "looking at" the tax-free personal allowance ahead of his first Budget in the autumn.

Cost of living is a key issue for Burnham. Many people, he has previously said, can't go out for a pint on a Friday, can't take the kids out and can't go on holiday owing to the pressure on their finances.

The cost of living has dominated people's lives in recent years, and - to some extent - our politics too. Easing that pressure hasn't been easy.

So, if Burnham chooses to support people on issues such as energy bills and the cost of transport, allows people to earn more before being taxed, and makes care and somewhere to live more affordable - he'll face tough choices on funding those moves and managing the trade-offs that come with them.

And his new chancellor, John Healey, will be the one who has to deliver any changes, and outline how to pay for them.

News.title: Faisal Islam: The new PM has big ideas - but what will they cost?
News.content:
Up until this point, the new Prime Minister Andy Burnham has described his policy changes with a broad brush. From today, he faces the constraints, trade offs, and realities of high national office.

For example, Burnham has said Tuesday's announcements on cost of living support would be paid for. In other words, it would mean a tax rise or spending cut, so we will see rather quickly what the new PM prioritises when push comes to shove.

Meanwhile, the markets seem to have already reacted to the suggestion he would be using some "flexibility" in his borrowing rules to help with new announcements.

The UK government's 10-year borrowing rose above 5% on Monday after falling in recent days. It has not gone up in this way in other European economies.

The move was not huge, but it shows the sensitivities at a moment when Burnham is overhauling his cabinet - including replacing Rachel Reeves as chancellor with former defence secretary John Healey.

The "flexibility" Burnham was talking about is, I understand, about the treatment of financial institutions. This has occurred in some green energy policies and essentially helps exempt certain types of borrowing from the measures of debt. There is scope for this model to extend to housing and other infrastructure.

It was not a general suggestion of, for example, using up the increased headroom against the government's borrowing rules.

All this shows how every tricky decision and trade off is being watched by the country and the markets at the same time.

News.title: Chancellor Healey will be under pressure to deliver for armed forces
News.content:
When Healey resigned last month, he had been offered only an extra Â£13.5bn - what amounted to a 0.08% increase in the defence budget.

At the time he made clear that was not enough to keep the country safe and to meet rising threats.

Those close to him said in reality the offer amounted only to an extra Â£10bn, with the rest what they called "Treasury Trickery".

Healey's resignation letter also expressed his frustration that the government had no clear timetable to meet its promise of increasing the UK's defence spending to 3% of GDP.

He wanted to reach that target by 2030, the year when many in Nato have said the alliance must be ready for conflict.

But under Sir Keir, the 3% pledge remained vague - some time in the next parliament. A further Nato pledge to increase defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 appeared to be even more remote.

Now as Andy Burnham's chancellor, Healey will be under pressure to put his money where his mouth is.

But as chancellor he can't just focus on defence. There will be many competing demands.

And the extra spending he argued for as defence secretary is significant. According to calculations by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), reaching this 3% threshold will demand an additional Â£17.3bn per year by 2029â30. The overall defence budget would have to rise from more than Â£63bn a year to closer to Â£90bn by 2030.

Any increase in defence spending will increase the pressure for tax rises, though Healey has argued in the past for "creative funding options". That might suggest he has thought of other ways to fund the Ministry of Defence.

The Liberal Democrats have argued for defence bonds - though Sir Keir argued that was just another way of borrowing money.

But without extra funding, Healey has been clear Britain's armed forces will not be ready to meet rising threats. A revised DIP published following his resignation still had a Â£5bn black hole.

Key plans to transform the military with drones, and uncrewed warships and aircraft are still not fully funded. Defence chiefs have been emphasising the importance of learning the lessons from the war in Ukraine. But plans for new air defence systems and long-range weapons remain underfunded.

Now he's the chancellor, Healey will have the opportunity to set out a plan to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP himself.

If he is true to his word, it can only mean positive news for his successor as defence secretary.

News.title: Man, 28, charged with murder of Ann Widdecombe
News.content:
A 28-year-old man has been charged with the murder of Ann Widdecombe, police and prosecutors have said.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, is set to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

Counter Terrorism Policing said "determining the motivation, including any possible political motivation" remains "an active avenue" of investigation.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe, 78, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead on Thursday 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.

In a statement read outside New Scotland Yard, Laurence Taylor, head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing said: "I want to make it very clear that our investigation into [Kerry], determining his motivations and any wider activity he may have been involved in is continuing."

"As with all murder investigations, understanding the 'why' is a key part of our enquiries," he said, adding that it was "a particularly intensive and complex investigation".

Taylor said it remained the case that investigators were not looking for anyone else in connection with the incident.

He added that counter terrorism teams have gathered "a huge amount of information" over the last week, leading to more than 800 lines of enquiry.

The investigation, which remains ongoing, has been led by Counter Terrorism Policing South East, supported by Devon and Cornwall Police.

Frank Ferguson, of the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS)'s special crime and counter terrorism division, said: "Our prosecutors have worked closely with the police to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court, and we will continue working with them as their investigation progresses."

"We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial," Ferguson said.

"It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings."

News.title: Kevin Keegan, Liverpool footballer who managed England and Newcastle United, dies aged 75
News.content:
Former England captain and manager Kevin Keegan has died at the age of 75, seven weeks after he revealed he had been diagnosed with stage four cancer, his family have confirmed.

One of English football's most decorated players, Keegan enjoyed spells at Scunthorpe United, Liverpool, Hamburg, Southampton and Newcastle during an illustrious playing career.

He later went on to manage Newcastle, Fulham, England and Manchester City.

Keegan revealed he had stage four cancer in June, which is the most advanced stage of cancer and means the disease has spread to other parts of the body.

His family initially disclosed he was battling the disease in January, after he had "further evaluation of ongoing abdominal symptoms" in hospital.

A statement on behalf of the Keegan family said he was "surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments".

"Kevin, a double Ballon d'Or winner, was a much loved husband, father and grandfather," it continued.

"The family would like to thank Kevin's incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy."

Newcastle United paid tribute, describing Keegan as "one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club's history".

The club statement added: "Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.

"Kevin's impact will not be measured by appearances or results. It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired wherever he went, and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him."

Liverpool, for whom Keegan played for between 1971 and 1977, said Keegan's "indomitable spirit and remarkable contribution will be forever etched in our history and his legacy will live on".

Hamburg said football had lost one of its "defining figures" and they would always "cherish" his memory, while Fulham said Keegan "forged a strong connection" with the fans, who would "forever hold wonderful memories" of his short time at the club.

Keegan's first club, Scunthorpe, described him as "one of the best players of his generation", with an "inspirational demeanour" and "brilliant personality".

England and Manchester City both offered their condolences to the Keegan family, with the latter describing him as "one of the most iconic and fondly remembered figures in English football".

The Three Lions will celebrate Keegan's life when they host Spain in a Uefa Nations League match at Wembley on 26 September.

News.title: Ofcom launches investigation into Married at First Sight UK
News.content:
Married at First Sight UK is facing renewed pressure after the broadcast regulator launched an official investigation into the hit Channel 4 reality TV show.

In a statement on Monday, Ofcom said it was investigating "a fairness and privacy complaint" about the prime-time show.

In May, a BBC Panorama investigation revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show - allegations the men involved deny.

An Ofcom fairness or privacy complaint can be lodged by individuals who participated in TV or radio programmes. Complaints like these usually relate to claims of being treated unfairly or having unwarranted infringements of privacy on programmes.

It is understood the watchdog is considering a complaint of unjust or unfair treatment from a cast member of Married at First Sight UK.

At least one other cast member previously complained to Ofcom about their treatment on the show, but the watchdog dismissed their complaint as it found the broadcaster had no case to answer.

An Ofcom spokesperson said such complaints are considered "on a case-by-case basis through a detailed and careful assessment process".

News.title: South East Water hosepipe ban to affect 2.4 million people
News.content:
A hosepipe ban has been expanded to cover 2.4 million people across the south of England after record-breaking temperatures.

South East Water's ban now includes parts of Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire - an extra 1.5m customers. A ban in parts of Kent has been in force since 3 July.

Douglas Whitfield, SEW's water supply director, said it was "deeply sorry" and "incredibly grateful to everyone helping us protect water supplies" after exceptionally hot and dry weather.

Eastbourne MP Josh Babarinde said he was "appalled", calling it "the direct result of years of underinvestment in upgrading infrastructure and building resilience".

Under the restrictions, households in the affected area will be banned from using a hosepipe in their homes for tasks including cleaning, filling ponds, or watering plants.

The ban will officially come in from 00:01 BST on Saturday, but SEW has asked its customers to abide by the restrictions immediately.

The UK record for the hottest day in June was broken for a third day in a row last month, with temperatures reaching 37.3C, the Met Office said.

News.title: Sara Sharif killer wants inquest with jury
News.content:
The woman who murdered her stepdaughter Sara Sharif has asked for the inquest into her death to be held in front of a jury.

Beinash Batool and Sara's father Urfan Sharif were jailed for life in 2024 after the 10-year-old was found dead at the family home in Woking.

She had been violently abused in a "campaign of torture" lasting two years.

Bite marks, an iron burn and scalding from hot water were among dozens of injuries found on her body in a post-mortem examination.

On Monday, Batool's lawyer Dr Anton van Dellen said jurors would help determine if Sara was failed by people who were scared of being accused of racism.

"This is just the type of judgement where a diverse local jury would provide a helpful perspective," he added.

A review into the 10-year-old's death found that services in Surrey failed to properly investigate why Sara started wearing a hijab - that covered her bruising - for "fear of causing offence".

Neighbours also said they were worried about "being branded as being racist" if they reported concerns.

News.title: Ryanair profits drop as Iran war puts off passengers and lifts fuel costs
News.content:
Ryanair's profits have fallen sharply as war in the Middle East sent jet fuel prices soaring and customers reluctant to book flights.

The Irish airline's pre-tax profits dropped 34% to â¬593m (Â£503m) between April and June while sales were flat as the company was forced to cut fares to stimulate demand.

Ryanair also said it expects summer fares to be slightly lower than last year due to "consumer hesitancy" around air travel.

The price of fuelling a plane has jumped since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February and while Ryanair said it had "hedged" or struck deals for the most future fuel costs, those not included in these arrangements had more than doubled.

Crude oil prices hit $90 (Â£67) a barrel for the first time in a month on Monday, before falling back slightly, after a weekend of intense exchanges of fire between the US and Iran.

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz â an essential route for global oil and gas supplies â has ground to a halt.

An interim peace deal last month brought some respite to oil and energy prices, but they spiked again as negotiations broke down and fighting resumed.

The airline warned that its results for the year will be "highly sensitive" to external factors such as conflict escalation in the Middle East and Ukraine as well as the price of unhedged jet fuel.

Fares for for the key summer period between July and September are on track to be "modestly" lower than last year, with many passengers booking closer to departure than normal.

The firm's finance chief, Neil Sorahan, said flights on its popular Mediterranean routes were still full. "People [are] as keen to get away as ever, albeit booking just a little bit later," he said.

Between April and June, Ryanair's revenue ticked up 1% to â¬4.4bn.

While passenger numbers rose 6% to 6.1 million- helped by the Easter holiday in April - fares fell by 6% as the airline reduced fares to entice flyers concerned about the Iran war.

Ryanair's share price fell 5% on Monday.

Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said Ryanair was in a better position than many of its rivals, but nonetheless "visibility is worse than San Francisco airport when the fog sets in".

"The renewed escalation in hostilities in the Middle East is unhelpful and without a lasting resolution, challenging times for the airline and travel space look set to continue."

News.title: Ofcom unable to take further legal action against suicide forum
News.content:
Ofcom said it is unable to take further legal action against a pro-suicide forum which campaigners say has been linked to over 130 UK deaths.

The regulator said, external the site had blocked access for the "vast majority" of UK users, and it had "no further legal routes available" under the Online Safety Act.

But it accepted people would still be able to access the forum by using a VPN, which hides your location online.

Andy Burrows, chief executive of the Molly Rose Foundation, said the decision to take no further legal action would "result in more lost lives" and that announcing it on the day a new prime minister was named showed "an utter lack of moral courage".

In response, an Ofcom spokesperson said it had made the decision a "matter of days ago" following "months of work to exhaust all possible legal routes".

They said bereaved families were informed of the decision this morning after being contacted last week.

"In that context, we do not consider it appropriate to delay the announcement further to accommodate today's political developments," they said.

Meanwhile, Ofcom enforcement director Suzanne Cater said the regulator had used its powers "to the fullest extent possible".

"We'll continue to monitor the forum closely to check the geoblock remains in place," she said.

The geoblock means people based in the UK are unable to access the site, unless they mask their location through a VPN or similar means.

Ofcom said it was working with the government to explore whether its enforcement powers should be strengthened.

In particular, this concerns its ability to get a website blocking order through the courts, which would legally mandate internet service providers in the UK to block the website.

The regulator says it has reached the limit of what it can legally do under the Online Safety Act because the forum has implemented the geoblock.

The BBC has approached the government for comment.

News.title: 'Scrutiny' needed over baby's death, court hears
News.content:
Preston had been taken to Blackpool Victoria Hospital three times before his death and seen by a "battery of professionals" including medical staff, social workers and welfare officers from various bodies.

Wilson told the hearing an inquest had initially been opened shortly after Preston's death but was then suspended while police investigated, culminating in the trial and conviction of his adoptive parents.

Wilson said he had to consider whether an inquest should continue, given "relevant issues" had already been heard during the eight-week criminal trial.

However, while he said he would not make a final decision on Monday, subject to submissions from lawyers for other public bodies, it was "highly likely" one would take place, probably in the autumn of next year.

He said: "I feel there's sufficient reason to resume. There are acts and omissions of public authorities that need to be scrutinised in a public hearing in which Preston's family can participate.

"It's clearly going to be a wide-ranging inquiry."

The coroner said he was aware there had been calls for a public inquiry, but his role meant that was not a matter for himself to consider, but to proceed on the basis of whether or not to hold an inquest.

The court heard Oldham Safeguarding Children's Partnership, had resumed a review into Preston's death, following its suspension for the criminal trial to take place.

This review was likely only to be completed by January 2027, and the inquest cannot be held before then, the court heard.

Much of the hearing dealt with which people or public bodies should be legally represented at any inquest.

They included Preston's biological mother and grandmother, Sara and Debbie Davey, neither of whom were present for the hearing but were represented by lawyers in court.

Preston was born while his mother was in custody and a place in a mother and baby unit in prison was refused, the court heard.

Instead, he was taken from her by a court order from Oldham Council and placed with temporary adoptive parents before being adopted by Varley and McGowan.

News.title: Fire crews to remain at Arthur's Seat for days after blaze
News.content:
Firefighters are expected to remain at Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh "for a couple of days" following a large blaze on Sunday evening.

Small plumes of smoke could still be seen on Monday morning along Salisbury Crags and large swathes of vegetation below the cliff face had been burned black.

Six fire engines were sent to tackle the the grassfire on the slope between the Scottish Parliament and St Leonard's, with crews working overnight to douse the flames and dampen hotspots.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) said there were "no reported casualties" but Police Scotland said Queen's Drive, the road that encircles the Holyrood Park hills, remained closed to all vehicles.

It is the second fire in the last three months at the landmark, an ancient extinct volcano that offers panoramic views of the Scottish capital.

A Very High risk of wildfire warning for the central Highlands, southern and eastern Scotland has been extended to Friday as warm weather is forecast to continue.

The warning was extended by the SFRS, in conjunction with the Scottish Wildfire Forum (SWF).

News.title: Prisons minister Lord Timpson quits government
News.content:
The prisons minister has resigned from the government, the BBC has been told.

Lord James Timpson was appointed to the role in July 2024 after leaving his job as CEO of the Timpson group, a business which provides key cutting and shoe repair services and employs hundreds of former prisoners.

His arrival in government was greeted with much fanfare by some in the Labour Party and described as "radical" and "innovative".

But in a departing statement on Monday, seen exclusively by the BBC, Lord Timpson said he was stepping down and it was an "honour" to serve in the post.

His statement did not give a specific reason for resigning, but it is understood he feels he has done as much as he can in the role.

Prisons in England and Wales were at crisis point, reaching almost full capacity, when he first entered Sir Keir Starmer's government.

He oversaw the controversial early release scheme which saw tens of thousands of inmates let out to create more space in jails.

His critics will argue prisons continue to be violent, drug infused and overcrowded, while probation officers still report being overworked and unable to cope.

But figures do show assaults against staff and self-harm in prisons are falling.

Lord Timpson said in his resignation statement that he had left "our prisons and probation service in a much healthier and happier state than two years ago".

He added: "I'm proud to have become the longest-serving minister in this role for 15 years. I'm also proud that 75% of prisons and 90% of probation teams are now performing better than when I started.

"Self-harm, violence and assaults on staff are all down, and fewer people are leaving prison without a home to go to, a measure of dignity I care about deeply."

He also pointed to the Women's Justice Board he established, saying he "believe[s] most women should not be in prison at all" and "diverting them away from custody, helping them with often chaotic, damaged, and addicted lives, is one of the changes I'm proud to have achieved".

His critics may question why he is leaving before the Sentencing Act 2026 is enacted in September, when more people are expected to be released early and further criminals will serve their sentences in the community.

A source in the Ministry of Justice told the BBC: "We're gutted he's going but the new person is going to have their work cut out to get their head round what's round the corner."

News.title: Pupil not guilty of trying to murder history teacher after stabbing her in the head
News.content:
A pupil has been found not guilty of attempted murder after stabbing his teacher in the head with a kitchen knife.

The boy, 16, followed Vicki Williams into her empty classroom at Milford Haven Comprehensive School in Pembrokeshire, after asking for help with his history work on 5 February.

He pulled a knife from his bag and lunged at her. Williams told a jury at Swansea Crown Court she feared she would die.

On Monday, he was found not guilty of attempted murder but guilty of wounding with intent, and unlawful wounding. He will be sentenced on 3 September.

The boy had previously pleaded guilty to possessing a kitchen knife on the school grounds.

Judge Paul Thomas KC accepted a majority verdict on the charge of wounding with intent, which meant at least 10 jurors agreed following four hours deliberation.

During the attack, Williams grabbed the knife, pushed the boy back with her legs, and screamed.

She received injuries to her head, back and hands after the attack.

She said the look on the teenager's face was one of "pure hatred".

During a police interview, Williams said how the boy, who was 15 at the time and who cannot be named due to his age, came to her classroom "cool and collected" at the end of the school day to ask if his "work was correct".

She said that "got [her] confused" because he had "never seemed bothered before".

It was when he shut the door to the classroom, saying it was cold, that "alarm bells" began to ring in her head.

Williams said he was trying to "keep her talking" while he was "trying to find something in his bag".

"I ask him again, 'are you sure you're alright?' And then he pulls [the knife] out of the bag and lunges at me," she said.

The boy told the court Williams had seen him with the knife and "tried to grab it" from him. He said he "accidentally assaulted her" during the struggle.

She told the court she believed she was about to die, thinking: "I'm fearful that I am dying, I've seen the knife, I know I've been stabbed, all I'm thinking at that point is, 'I need help'."

Williams said the attack "came out of nowhere".

A number of Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City office items are being auctioned off by the club.

Among the of items up for grabs are the very coffee cups Guardiola used, offering fans a direct connection to his time at the club.

The auction features a wide array of memorabilia from Guardiola’s office, including his chair, desk lamp, and whistle, alongside several framed pictures.

Some of his training tops are also available, as is his winter jacket and collection of incense sticks, complete with matches.

For those interested in the tactical mind behind City’s success, a set of two pitch pads with Guardiola’s handwritten strategies, accompanied by his pens, is also up for grabs.

The auction features a wide array of memorabilia from Guardiola’s office, including his chair, desk lamp, and whistle, alongside several framed pictures ( PA )

While these personal effects are drawing significant interest, early bidding indicates that the most coveted item is a rare commemorative ball marking Erling Haaland’s achievement of 100 Premier League goals.

Only three such balls were ever produced, and bidding has already soared into four figures for the item, which is presented in a display box.

The auction is set to conclude at the end of the week, with some of the proceeds understood to be benefiting the club’s charity, City in the Community.

Guardiola left City this summer after a decade in which he won six Premier League titles, the Champions League, three FA Cups, and five League Cups.

The 55-year-old has now been linked with the vacant position of Italy boss.

The Azzurri missed out on a third successive World Cup in March after play-off final heartbreak at the hands of Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading to the departure of Gennaro Gattuso.

Italy icon Paolo Maldini, who has been newly appointed the technical director of the FIGC, travelled to Barcelona alongside advisor Leonardo to speak with the Catalan, who left City after 10 glory-laden years at the end of last season.

A four-year plan was outlined to Guardiola who is prioritising project over salary when deciding his next step.

It remains to be seen whether Guardiola is keen to take the job but the FIGC is making serious efforts to convince him, with Maldini and Leonardo speaking to Guardiola over three days.

Andy Burnham has made the surprise appointment of John Healey as his chancellor, as he ruthlessly purged the cabinet after entering Downing Street, promising a “circuit-breaker” moment for Britain.

It follows weeks of speculation that Mr Burnham was planning to give the job to Ed Miliband or Shabana Mahmood, but there were fears either choice would be divisive within the Labour Party. Mr Miliband will instead be foreign secretary and Ms Mahmood will remain as home secretary.

In a post on X, Ms Mahmood said she would continue with immigration reform. “It is an honour to remain as home secretary in Andy Burnham’s cabinet. I may be biased, but it’s the best job in the business,” she said.

Louise Haigh, who managed Mr Burnham’s Makerfield campaign, will be first secretary of state, chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster and minister for the Cabinet Office.

Mr Healey, who resigned from Sir Keir Starmer's government in a row over defence spending, gained respect in the party after a strong run as defence secretary – and his appointment shows Mr Burnham's commitment to bolstering Britain's military capabilities.

Mr Burnham used his first speech as prime minister to vow to end decades of failure by eradicating rough sleeping and overhauling social care, promising his arrival in Downing Street will be a “circuit-breaker” moment for Britain.

After meeting King Charles at Buckingham Palace, the new PM admitted politicians “needed to raise their game” and be better, insisting he would “make Britain believe and hope again” by winning over fed-up voters.

open image in gallery John Healey has been appointed chancellor ( Getty )

He reiterated his promise to move power outside of Westminster and said he would set out a 10-year plan later this year, adding: “Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again.”

In a sign of change, he purged Starmer loyalists including former chancellor Rachel Reeves and deputy PM David Lammy.

In a short speech delivered without a lectern, Mr Burnham said: “I am acutely conscious that I am the sixth person in the last 10 years to walk up this street, the seventh prime minister since 2016, making this a moment for reflection and new resolution.

“It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game and rise to the new challenge.”

In his first promise as prime minister, he said he would “end rough sleeping in our country”, having visited the homelessness charity The Passage in London’s Victoria earlier on Monday.

He also declared he would reduce Britain’s welfare bill by helping more young people into work, building more council homes and creating what he described as a “preventative state”, investing in people’s success rather than paying for failure.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham enters Downing Street after becoming prime minister ( AFP/Getty )

This, he said, “is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down, to meet our fiscal rules, and to honour our commitments on defence to our international partners”.

He made it clear that his first priority would be to tackle the cost of living crisis, teasing an announcement in the next 24 hours to address issues such as bus fare or rent freezes, or a reduction in energy bills.

Earlier, Sir Keir gave his goodbye speech in Downing Street before visiting Buckingham Palace.

He said he had offered Mr Burnham his “full support” and he was leaving “with good grace and a smile”.

However, some of the other cabinet ministers to lose their jobs were less generous.

open image in gallery Deputy prime minister David Lammy and chancellor Rachel Reeves have lost their jobs ( PA )

In a barbed remark, Steve Reed, who was ousted as communities secretary, wrote: “Keir Starmer showed me loyalty by appointing me to his cabinet. I make no apology for returning that loyalty. It’s what is expected of functioning teams, and I hope those who did not show loyalty to Keir will now show it to you.

“I’m proud I acted with integrity at every step over the turbulent last few months.”

Mr Lammy noted: “I would have been proud to continue serving in cabinet. But a new prime minister is entitled to build his own team.”

Speaking to journalists in the Downing Street rose garden, Mr Burnham made it clear that as well as ending rough sleeping, he wanted to ensure that he dealt with the social care crisis before his time in Downing Street came to an end.

The issue is unfinished business for Mr Burnham, who failed to get cross-party consensus in 2009 when he was health secretary, when his proposal for a levy was attacked by the Tories as “a death tax”.

Mr Burnham has made it clear that it is more personal to him now, with his father suffering from Alzheimer’s, making him unaware that his son is now PM.

He said: “I think the country needs to step back here and say, 'How have we let a situation kind of just roll on, where we know it's a major issue, and yet no one's got the courage to fix it?'

“I just think that's quite damning, really, of my generation of politicians. Has no one got the ability anymore to say: 'Right, it is a difficult thing, but we're going to do it'?

“If I look at the National Health Service right now, what I hear from people is that corridor care is becoming the norm all year round, not just in winter time, and the standards in relation to A&E are just not achievable in terms of the 90-plus per cent of people coming through in four hours.”

open image in gallery Starmer says goodbye to Downing Street as he hugs his wife Victoria ( Getty )

He will also look at the way people are being made to pay more income tax through thresholds being frozen, an issue he said was the biggest complaint from voters in Makerfield during the recent by-election campaign which brought him back into parliament.

Mr Burnham however insisted that he is “prudent” and will stick to the former chancellor’s fiscal rules on borrowing, which she set as chancellor before being sacked.

After his speech, Mr Burnham received hugs, applause and a kiss from his wife Marie-France van Heel, before the pair entered the black door of No 10 to be greeted by cabinet secretary Dame Antonia Romeo and clapped in by staff.

A state appeals court on Monday set aside convictions for two men involved in a 2020 plot to kidnap Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.

Pete Musico and Paul Bellar were convicted of providing material support for an act of terrorism. They, along with co-defendant Joe Morrison, were accused of having secondary roles in the scheme.

Morrison's conviction was thrown out in June in a precedent-setting decision. A different panel at the Michigan Court of Appeals said it was obligated to apply that ruling to Musico and Bellar as well.

The convictions were overturned on technical grounds. The appeals court said kidnapping is not an underlying violent felony that can support a conviction under Michigan’s terrorism law.

Attorney General Dana Nessel called it “linguistic gymnastics” and said she would ask the Michigan Supreme Court to take up the cases.

Morrison, Musico and Bellar were not charged with having a direct role in the plot to kidnap Whitmer. Bellar had moved out of state weeks before the FBI made arrests in October 2020, and Morrison and Musico said they, too, were no longer in contact with key figures.

But they had been members of a paramilitary group that earlier trained with Adam Fox, who was prosecuted in federal court as a leader and is serving a 16-year prison sentence for conspiracy.

As part of the plot, Whitmer was supposed to be kidnapped her from her vacation home just before the 2020 presidential election. Prosecutors said the conspirators were furious over tough COVID-19 restrictions that Whitmer and officials in other states had put in place during the early months of the pandemic, as well as perceived threats to gun ownership.

Whitmer, a Democrat, was never physically harmed. Undercover FBI agents and informants were inside Fox’s group for months, and the scheme was broken up.

The overall investigation, however, produced mixed results for state and federal prosecutors. Five of the 14 men were acquitted at trials.

The bodies of five family members have been recovered from a southern Utah canyon after heavy rains triggered flash floods on Friday, according to local authorities.

The victims include a fire captain from Provo, Utah, his wife and their three sons, the Associated Press reported. A daughter, who did not join the family on the excursion, survived.

Emergency responders first arrived at the Sunglow Campground, located in a red rock canyon near Bicknell, Utah, late Friday night after the body of a young male was discovered in a flood wash. Search teams recovered the remaining four bodies later that night and into Saturday, as reported by the Wayne County Sheriff’s Office.

“It is believed the family fell victim to flooding caused by heavy rains,” the sheriff’s office stated in a news release.

Though local law enforcement did not publicly name the victims, the Provo Fire Department confirmed that one of its leaders, Captain Spencer Long, died in the incident.

open image in gallery The bodies of five family members were recovered from a canyon near Sunglow Campground in Bicknell, Utah, after heavy rains triggered flash flooding on Friday, according to police ( U.S. Department of Agriculture )

Officials with the fire department posted to social media: “We are absolutely heartbroken by the death of Captain Spencer Long and his family. Our thoughts are with his family, friends, and colleagues during this difficult time. Out of respect for the family and the ongoing official process, we will not be commenting further at this time.”

The family had arrived at the campground on Friday for a day of hiking before the weather turned severe. Tributes from colleagues and community members have since highlighted the scale of the tragedy.

A GoFundMe page organized by a family friend identified the other victims as Long’s wife, Katrina, and their sons, Reid, Thayne and Gage. The online fundraiser was created to support the surviving daughter, Lydia.

open image in gallery The victims include Provo Fire Captain Spencer Long, his wife and three sons, while a daughter who did not join the hiking excursion survived ( Provo Fire and Rescue )

“Spencer and Katrina were loving, devoted parents whose greatest joy was their family,” Bree Nielson wrote on the page. “They touched the lives of so many with their kindness, generosity, and unwavering love. As Lydia begins the long journey of grieving and rebuilding her life, she is also facing many unexpected financial burdens.

“No amount of money can take away Lydia’s pain or replace the family she has lost. But together, we can help ease some of the burdens she now carries and remind her that she is not alone. Every donation, no matter the amount, is a meaningful expression of love and support.”

So far, Nielson has raised roughly $218,000 of her $250,000 goal.

Katrina Long was the co-founder of Summit Medical Spa, which also publicly acknowledged the tragedy.

“Katrina was an exceptional leader, an inspiring businesswoman, and an extraordinary person whose generosity and love for others touched countless lives,” the company shared on Facebook. “Our hearts are with all of their loved ones as we grieve the unimaginable loss of Katrina, her husband, and their three beautiful boys.”

Barstool Sports founder Dave Portnoy has proposed a number of changes to the rules of football, or soccer, following the conclusion of the FIFA World Cup.

Spain defeated Argentina 1-0 after extra time in the final Sunday, bringing to an end a wildly popular tournament that was jointly hosted by Canada, the United States and Mexico.

There were several on-field controversies in the game, including a disallowed goal for Spain’s Nico Williams that was ruled out due to an earlier foul by Mikel Merino, who was judged to have stepped on the foot of Argentine defender Nicolás Otamendi.

Speaking on talk show Wake Up Barstool, Portnoy argued that the fact Spain did go on to win the game “avoided a near-international incident.”

He continued: “That goal that they called back against Spain was an awful call. That was a brutal call. That was a goal. I know that they’re going to show the super-replay of the guy stepping on the other guy’s foot, and there are a lot of things that we’ve talked about on this panel — I loved the tournament — that we have to fix.”

Dave Portnoy wants to ‘Americanize and fix soccer’ after World Cup controversies ( Getty )

Portnoy argued that after his proposed rule changes, the goal by Williams would have stood.

“If you let us get our hands on this game and really Americanize it... If you accidentally step on a guy’s foot, that’s not a flag,” said the 49-year-old. “It’s not a penalty. It’s not a flag in the NFL if you accidentally bump into each other. So you’ve got to pick that up. That should have been a goal. Thankfully we didn’t have to worry about it.”

Portnoy also said he would change the offside rule to make it more lenient.

“You’ve got to change this, clearly,” he argued. “It’s got to be that your entire body has to be ahead, not one tiny body part.”

This amended version of the offside rule is similar to a change proposed by former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger, which aims to encourage more attacking football by deeming an attacker onside if any part of their body capable of scoring is level with the second-last defender.

Known as the “daylight rule”, the new version is being trialled in Canada.

The 2026 World Cup already featured several changes that were described as “Americanization” by critics, including hydration breaks which effectively divided the game into four quarters and a 27-minute-long Super Bowl-style halftime show for the final that divided fans.
