Best known for his role in the “Jackass” movie franchise, Wee Man has made a name for himself by performing stunts on film that the average viewer should never try at home. In addition, he’s a pro skateboarder and was a host on the Fox Sports Net television show “54321.” Despite his impressive resume, his background is more diverse than most people would assume.

Wee Man’s legal name is Jason Shannon Acuña, and he is of Mexican and German descent. He’s spoken openly in the past about growing up eating tacos and menudo. The “Jackass” actor, idolized for getting into cages with bulls, bungee jumping and funny pranks, also has an entrepreneurial side, having been a long-time investor in the popular Mexican-American franchise Chronic Tacos.

Kat Von D

A well-known public figure in her niche, Kat Von D may look like the reincarnation of Amy Winehouse, yet is actually a Mexican-born tattoo artist from Nuevo León.

She’s most recognized for her work on the TLC reality show “LA Ink.” On the show, she set the record for the most tattoos done in 24 hours at 400 and was named to the Guinness Book of World Records for that milestone — a record that has since been surpassed.

In addition, Von D has also released a makeup collection with Sephora in 2008, released two studio albums and written two New York Times bestselling books.

Anthony Quinn

If you’re a fan of old movies and love trivia, Anthony Quinn could be defined as a legend of Hollywood. In the 1950s, he cleaned up at the Oscars — winning two Best Supporting Actor awards, one in 1952 for “Viva Zapata!” and another in 1956 for “Lust for Life.” What many U.S. audiences didn’t know at the time, however, was that he was also Mexican.

His legal name was Manuel Antonio Rodolfo Quinn Oaxaca. What’s also intriguing is the fact that he was born in Chihuahua at the midpoint of the Mexican Revolution in 1915. It’s said his father was Irish and his mother was from Mexico, yet in his biography, “The Original Sin: A Self-Portrait,” he claimed his Irish father was just a story made up by Hollywood publicists. In other words, he was as proud to be Mexican as they come. That alone deserves to be celebrated as much as his Oscars.

Hubertus von Hohenlohe-Langenburg

Most people know a famous Mexican soccer player or boxer, but what about one who’s a well-known skier? Hubertus Hohenlohe-Langenburg is a pioneer in niche sports in Mexico, having competed in six Winter Olympics as an alpine skier and founded the Mexican Ski Federation in 1981.

His family story is also one that could be turned into a scripted television series. Hohenlohe is a descendant of German royalty, being the son of Prince Alfonso of Hohenlohe-Langenburg and Princess Ira von Fürstenberg. He was born in Mexico City, moved to Spain and then eventually settled in Austria.

In addition, Hohenlohe is a photographer and businessman and was even a pop singer who went by the stage names Andy Himalaya and Royal Disaster.

Lupita Nyong’o

Having won an Oscar for Best Supporting Actress in the film “12 Years a Slave” in 2014, Lupita Nyong’o has gone on to be one of Hollywood’s brightest stars, appearing in “Black Panther” and “Star Wars: The Force Awakens.” But the most intriguing thing about her is her cultural background. Not only does she hold U.S. and Kenyan citizenship, but she also carries Mexican citizenship.

Her father is a Kenyan politician who was teaching in Mexico City when she was born. Although she grew up in Kenya and later came over to the United States to study at Yale University, she has always maintained that she is Kenyan-Mexican.

So who else should have been mentioned on our list? Let us know in the comments below.

Ian Ostroff is an indie author, journalist, and copywriter from Montreal, Canada. You can find his work in various outlets, including Map Happy and The Suburban. When he’s not writing, you can find Ian at the gym, a café, or anywhere within Mexico visiting family and friends.

World.title: Zacatecas AG: Multihomicide of 10, including officials, may be linked to extortion and collusion
World.content:
The murders of 10 men whose bodies were found in three different municipalities in the state of Zacatecas on Saturday could be linked to extortion and collusion between criminals and public officials, the Zacatecas attorney general said Sunday.

The bodies — including that of Ignacio Castrejón Valdez, a former mayor of Sombrerete, Zacatecas — were found in the municipalities of Morelos, Pánuco and Saín Alto, all located north of Zacatecas City. Five of the bodies were found hanging from a bridge in Pánuco.

Among the other victims were Fidel Alvarado de la Torre, an official with the Fresnillo municipal government, and Andrés Vázquez Gurrola, an ex-councilor in the municipality of Canatlán, Durango.

In a video message on Sunday, Zacatecas Attorney General Cristian Paul Camacho said that “various pieces of evidence have been collected, which indicate that the main lines of investigation involve possible acts of extortion and collusion by public officials.”

“This investigation must be carried out in a very exhaustive and very professional way,” he said, adding that a financial probe could be part of it.

Camacho said that authorities had obtained video footage that allowed them to establish the vehicles that were used in “the criminal events” — i.e., those used to dump the bodies in public places.

“It is necessary to inform that at this time a search warrant is being executed at a property in the municipality of Fresnillo, where it has been determined at least two of the victims were there before they were killed,” he said.

“… At a different place, a vehicle related to the events was seized.”

Camacho said that eight of the victims were from Zacatecas and two were from the neighboring state of Durango.

“Among the victims is the ex-mayor of Sombrerete, Ignacio Castrejón Valdez, and two officials from the municipality of Fresnillo. One of them worked as the director of social development and one was a Civil Protection member,” he said.

Referring to ex-municipal councilor Andrés Vázquez Gurrola, Camacho said that another victim was a lawyer and former police officer from Durango. Six others were businessmen in various fields including agriculture, entertainment and construction. One of the businessmen owned a bar.

Camacho said that eight of the victims were strangled to death, while two others, including Alvarado, the social development director in Fresnillo, were shot. He said that bullet casings recovered by authorities were being subjected to an “exhaustive analysis” in order to establish whether perpetrators of the murders had used the same weapons in other crimes.

According to the attorney general, four of the victims stopped communicating with their families last Thursday, while five ceased communication last Friday. The other victim ceased contact with his family on Saturday.

Camacho said that the Zacatecas Attorney General’s Office didn’t receive any reports that the victims had been abducted.

Citing the results of toxicology tests, Camacho said that five of the victims, including the two municipal officials from Fresnillo, had recently consumed drugs.

In the same video message, Rodrigo Reyes Mugüerza, general secretary of the Zacatecas government, said that it had been a “weekend of uncertainty … fear and concern” for residents of the northern state.

Homicides declined by more than 60% annually in Zacatecas in the first six months of 2026, according to government data, but Reyes said that “days like Saturday … remind us that the process of pacification is a complex and continuous process.”

He said that state authorities were carrying out an operation aimed at detaining those responsible for the murders and were committed to “minimizing the possibility of these events being repeated.”

“From the state government, we once again confirm our commitment to peace, to security and above all to solidarity with all the people of Zacatecas,” Reyes said.

At a press conference on Monday, Governor David Monreal Ávila conveyed his condolences to the victims’ families and declared that there will be no impunity for the murders.

“Far from intimidating us, expressions of barbarity like those of last Saturday force us to redouble efforts. They oblige us not to let our guard down, not to take a backward step or fear groups that violate peace,” he said.

The Morena party governor said that his government is supported by the federal government, and stressed that the state of Zacatecas has sufficient technology, equipment and trained security personnel.

“We’ll put all this capacity in play to shed light on the events of Saturday and, above all, to guarantee that they are not repeated and to ensure that whoever committed this atrocity receives the appropriate punishment,” Monreal said.

With reports from Aristegui Noticias, Reforma, El Financiero and El Sol de Zacatecas

World.title: Pre-Columbian skeletal remains discovered in Playa del Carmen cenote
World.content:
Deep in the underground waters of a cenote in Quintana Roo, divers have documented the skeletal remains of a young woman who may have lived in pre-Columbian times, Mexican authorities revealed last week.

Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) said custodians of the Yaakun cenote near Playa del Carmen reported the find after technical divers spotted submerged materials in late 2025.

Within months, underwater archaeologist Gustavo García García led a five-day survey, conducted at depths of 42 to 53 meters (138 to 174 feet), that confirmed a cluster of human bones and, about 30 meters away, ceramic vessels.

Preliminary analysis indicates the individual — who has been named Yatzil — was between 18 and 25 years old, based on skeletal features and limited dental wear.

Researchers have identified long bones, the pelvis, a cranium and part of a mandible with three molars.

Her remains, still submerged in a sloping chamber about 45 meters below the surface, are considered well preserved due to stable underwater conditions, including low light and temperature.

The ceramics — mostly globular pots likely used domestically in the eastern Maya region — may date to the Late Postclassic period (1200–1521 AD), according to INAH.

However, researchers are being cautious about assigning a precise date or cultural affiliation to Yatzil’s remains, noting that her chronology is still unknown despite the ceramics likely dating to the pre-Columbian period (before the Spanish conquest in the early 1500s).

INAH specialists say they will wait for DNA from a tooth scheduled to be removed in a second field session in 2027 before drawing firmer conclusions.

Authorities have launched the Cenote Yaakun Research Project to document and protect the site. A perimeter has been established, and divers are urged not to disturb the materials.

Culture Minister Claudia Curiel de Icaza emphasized the importance of working with the local communities on discoveries such as this one.

“Each archaeological find that we manage to protect,” she said in a press release, “strengthens our knowledge about the cultures that inhabited this territory and reaffirms that heritage is a shared responsibility.”

The Yaakun project is the latest underwater discovery on Mexico’s Caribbean coast, where at least 11 prehistoric skeletons were found in flooded caves and cenotes between Playa del Carmen and Tulum in recent decades. One of them, reported earlier this year, may be around 8,000 years old.

With reports from Infobae and Informador

World.title: MND Local: Two art exhibits, a global diving competition and a comedy show in Guadalajara
World.content:
This week, we take a look at two thought-provoking art exhibits now showing at the Museum of Art in Zapopan, an international diving competition and a comedian who brings joy and irreverence in wine drinking to the Guadalajara Metro Area (GMA).

Two exhibits at the Museum of Art Zapopan tackle timely themes

The current exhibition “Unlevel Playing Fields” (“Canchas Desiguales” in Spanish) by Costa Rican conceptual artist Priscilla Monge uses soccer to convey a deeper message about the human condition.

Monge’s transformation of a traditional soccer field into a sloped, irregular surface is meant to highlight that not everyone in Latin America and the world starts on a level playing field.

The exhibition arrives at a time when Mexico is beset by enormous economic inequality, something that’s readily apparent with the World Cup currently underway. While the matches are attracting the attention of millions, the live experience in Mexico was restricted to the wealthy, who could afford to pay prices that often exceeded the average monthly salary of ordinary Mexicans.

This interactive work will tour each of Mexico’s 2026 World Cup host cities: Guadalajara, Monterrey and Mexico City. Despite the differences among the venues, the exhibition poses the same questions to all: How do we play, participate and share a space when the conditions of the game are not the same for everyone?

Priscilla Monge is known for her thought-provoking, interactive art installations. Her work explores the power struggles and inequality embedded in modern societies with a mixture of humor and cynicism. Previously, her art has been exhibited at the Rufino Tamayo Museum in Mexico City, the Venice Biennale and the Tate Modern in London.

Yukinori Yanagi exhibit at Estación MAZ

Two blocks away in the brand-new Estación MAZ building across from the Line 3 light rail station, a new exhibit by Japanese artist Yukinori Yanagi, “The Pacific Ocean,” explores identity, nationalism and global conflict.

The Pacific Ocean’s name suggests peace and tranquility, but its history has been anything but. This vast sea has been the scene of some of the greatest violence of the twentieth century, from Japan’s imperial expansion across Asia to the Second World War, and the first use of atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

A core part of Yanagi’s work consists of revisiting these human tragedies that changed the course of history. Works like “Absolute Dud” (2007-2016) and “From the Sky” (2024) serve as symbolic recollections of the dire consequences of the Second World War. At the same time, he incorporates reflections on the limits of international boundaries and the dangers of excess nationalism.

Dates and locations: “Unlevel Playing Fields” runs through July 31 at the Museum of Art Zapopan (MAZ), Andador 20 de Noviembre, Zapopan Center.

“The Pacific Ocean” runs through Aug. 9 at Estación MAZ, Avenida de las Américas, Zapopan Center.

Cost: The MAZ in Zapopan is always free. Check the website to plan your visit.

Laugh about wine? Innovative stand-up comedy plus wine tasting in Zapopan

Who hasn’t had a good laugh about the pretentiousness of wine at some point in their life? Now, there’s a show where it’s safe to laugh and learn without fear of committing a social faux pas.

The brainchild of Australian comedian Merrick Watts, a certified wine taster, “An Idiot’s Guide to Wine: Comedy between Drinks” is a show that’s appeared at festivals, wineries and bars across Australia to sold-out crowds.

In Guadalajara, a new iteration of the show will feature a local comedian (and performed in Spanish), but the concept remains the same. During the set, the audience will enjoy wines from around the world, while learning about aromas, grape varieties and winemaking styles.

Your biggest challenge at this show won’t be trying to seem knowledgeable about wine but not spilling your glass while laughing. So don’t worry if you can distinguish between a Malbec and a Merlot. The point is no-pressure learning while having a good time.

For those who don’t wish to imbibe, non-alcoholic drinks will be available for an extra charge.

Date: Saturday, Oct. 10 and Saturday, Nov. 14 at 6 p.m. and 9 p.m.

Location: A 70-minute set at Escenik Teatro Bar in Zapopan.

Cost: Available now from Feverup, starting from 570 pesos.

World.title: Quintana Roo moves to guarantee pet spaces at hurricane shelters
World.content:
Nearly two months into the tropical storm season, the Yucatán Peninsula state of Quintana Roo is now encouraging public hurricane shelters to feature specific provisions for pets.

The new recommendation — established in the Operating Guide for Public Temporary Shelters in Case of Hurricane, as published in the state government’s Official Gazette — is meant to guarantee adequate conditions for families who come to these spaces during an emergency.

“The guide is intended for state and municipal authorities … and for pet owners,” said Javier Carballar Osorio, director of the state’s Institute of Biodiversity and Protected Natural Areas of the State (Ibanqroo).

The measure acknowledges that many people are unwilling to leave their pets behind in risky situations, prompting state authorities to mandate the well-being of such animals in civil protection protocols.

Although officially just a recommendation, its inclusion in the Official Gazette establishes a criterion that state and municipal authorities must consider when selecting and preparing buildings that will function as shelters during the current hurricane season.

The new guidelines recommend that spaces for pets must be integrated within the same shelters intended for people. The document specifies the minimum requirements that buildings operating as temporary shelters must meet with regard to safety, accessibility and hygiene.

Supporters of the new guidelines say it addresses a reality that has become evident in recent emergencies — that many families prefer not to go to a shelter if they cannot bring their pets with them, effectively jeopardizing their own safety.

By calling for spaces for pets within the shelters, the authorities seek to reduce that impediment and encourage greater participation of the population in evacuation protocols.

Before this, Quintana Roo had opted to enable separate shelters for companion animals, especially after the passage of Beryl, a Category 5 hurricane, in 2024.

In 2025, Ibanqroo teamed up with the International Fund for Animal Welfare to prepare and distribute information packets to the state’s 11 municipalities for the implementation of temporary shelters for dogs and cats during a disruptive event or threat.

With reports from El Economista and Quadratín

World.title: Farmacias Similares, Stori launch credit card featuring Dr. Simi
World.content:
The Mexican pharmacy chain Farmacias Similares and fintech firm Stori have launched a new co-branded credit card, which is expected to help millions of Mexicans who are not enrolled in the formal financial system access credit.

The card is adorned with the Farmacias Similares mascot, Dr. Simi, a mustachioed character wearing a white lab coat, who has become a Mexican cultural icon.

The Farmacias Similares x Stori card is the company’s latest effort to connect its credit products with a retailer following the 2024 launch of Stori SHEIN, expanding the ultra-fast-fashion brand’s reach in the Mexican market. It also aims to provide credit for people who cannot easily access traditional financial institutions.

Around 51% of Mexico’s population is unbanked, according to the 2023 World Bank Financial Inclusion National Survey. This is largely because Mexico continues to have a large informal workforce, at almost 55% of workers, who contribute around 25.4% of GDP, according to Mexico’s National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI).

“We want to tear down the barriers that separate Mexicans from credit and demonstrate that money can also be on the ‌side ⁠of the most important thing we have, which is health,” said Stori’s co-founder and chief governance officer, Marlene Garayzar.

The card offers users a 25% discount on their first purchase and a monthly discount of up to 10% on purchases at Farmacias Similares’s physical and online stores, so long as the card was used as payment elsewhere during the previous month.

Farmacias Similares is popular for offering a wide range of low-cost generic medicines and is now one of Mexico’s most well-known retail brands, operating over 11,000 stores across the country and launching in Texas in 2025.

Stori was founded in Mexico in 2018 and has expanded rapidly by offering credit products ⁠to people with limited or no formal credit history, with a customer base of around 5 million.

With reports from Reuters, El Economista and PCMI

World.title: Sheinbaum highlights opportunities for diplomacy at Sunday’s World Cup final: Monday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

⚽ World Cup final attendance takes center stage: Monday’s mañanera came a day after President Sheinbaum attended the FIFA World Cup final in New Jersey, seated with President Trump, First Lady Melania Trump and Prime Minister Carney — a trip with added weight given the tense state of the Mexico-U.S. relationship.

Monday’s mañanera came a day after President Sheinbaum attended the FIFA World Cup final in New Jersey, seated with President Trump, First Lady Melania Trump and Prime Minister Carney — a trip with added weight given the tense state of the Mexico-U.S. relationship. ✈️ A last-minute military flight to NYC: Sheinbaum said she’d planned to skip the final until Trump personally invited her by phone on Friday. A canceled commercial flight forced a military flight instead, landing the delegation in the northeastern U.S. at 2 a.m. Sunday.

Sheinbaum said she’d planned to skip the final until Trump personally invited her by phone on Friday. A canceled commercial flight forced a military flight instead, landing the delegation in the northeastern U.S. at 2 a.m. Sunday. 🤝 Brief chats with Trump’s cabinet: Sheinbaum said she spoke with Commerce Secretary Lutnick, U.S. Trade Representative Greer and Secretary of State Rubio at the match, describing the exchanges as short but cordial. Greer is expected in Mexico City Wednesday or Thursday.

Sheinbaum said she spoke with Commerce Secretary Lutnick, U.S. Trade Representative Greer and Secretary of State Rubio at the match, describing the exchanges as short but cordial. Greer is expected in Mexico City Wednesday or Thursday. 🇲🇽🇺🇸 USMCA talks resume: Sheinbaum confirmed a new round of Mexico-U.S. USMCA review talks begins Monday, saying she’d also briefly discussed trade with Trump and Carney at the stadium and hopes for agreements this week.

Sheinbaum confirmed a new round of Mexico-U.S. USMCA review talks begins Monday, saying she’d also briefly discussed trade with Trump and Carney at the stadium and hopes for agreements this week. 🏛🦅 Defending the relationship with Trump: Asked about her personal rapport with Trump, Sheinbaum said Mexico must always seek good relations with the U.S. president, citing shared geography, diplomacy and the 40 million Mexicans living in the U.S., while stressing disagreements needn’t become personal.

Asked about her personal rapport with Trump, Sheinbaum said Mexico must always seek good relations with the U.S. president, citing shared geography, diplomacy and the 40 million Mexicans living in the U.S., while stressing disagreements needn’t become personal. 🎤 Pushing back on critics: Sheinbaum argued she’d have been criticized either way — for skipping the final or for attending it — and noted neither Trump nor Carney attended their own countries’ World Cup openers. She framed the closing as a joint moment for the three co-hosts.

Why today’s mañanera matters

Today’s mañanera came a day after President Claudia Sheinbaum attended the FIFA men’s World Cup final between Spain and Argentina at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, just west of New York City.

Sheinbaum was seated with U.S. President Donald Trump, First Lady Melania Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, among other officials, and participated in the post-match trophy ceremony.

The Mexican president’s attendance at the match, which Spain won 1-0 in extra time, was significant as it came at a crucial time in the Mexico-U.S. relationship. Sheinbaum’s brief visit to the U.S. came ahead of the commencement on Monday of a new round of trade talks between Mexico and the United States, which announced at the start of July that it had declined to extend the USMCA for an additional 16 years.

Beyond trade, there are tensions in the Mexico-U.S. security relationship for a range of reasons, including the CIA’s alleged participation in a drug lab raid in Chihuahua in April without the knowledge or authorization of the Mexican government, and U.S. prosecutors’ drug trafficking accusations against Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya and nine other current and former Sinaloa-based officials.

In addition, the Mexican government recently filed criminal complaints in the United States as it seeks thorough investigations into the deaths of Mexicans in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention centers and in ICE operations.

Therefore, Sheinbaum’s remarks on Monday morning about her face-to-face interactions with U.S. officials, including Trump, took on added significance, even though she didn’t provide many details about them.

Sheinbaum explains why she decided to attend the World Cup final

Sheinbaum told reporters that before Friday, the only invitation she had received to attend the World Cup final was from FIFA.

“I was weighing up whether to go or not, but I had thought I wouldn’t attend,” she said.

Sheinbaum said she spoke by telephone to Trump on Friday and he personally invited her to attend the final.

“He said, ‘Claudia, are you going to come?’ And I said, ‘Well, if you invite me, President Trump.’ And he said, ‘Yes, you’re invited. Come. You’re going to be seated with us,’” she explained.

Sheinbaum said she consequently decided to go to the match. She noted that she and five aides got tickets to fly to New York from Cancún, but their flight was canceled due to stormy weather in New York.

Sheinbaum said she spoke to Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla Trejo and organized a military flight to the United States.

“We arrived at about 2 in the morning [on Sunday]. Thank you to all the compatriots who waited for us outside the hotel. And early [on Sunday] we went to the stadium,” she said.

Sheinbaum: ‘I had the opportunity to speak to some Trump administration secretaries’

Sheinbaum said she had the opportunity to speak to some Trump administration secretaries who attended the World Cup final on Sunday.

She said she spoke to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

🇲🇽⚽ La final del Mundial también sirvió para la diplomacia. @Claudiashein aseguró que conversó brevemente con Donald Trump y Mark Carney sobre las negociaciones del T-MEC. Además, sostuvo encuentros con Marco Rubio, Felipe VI y Pedro Sánchez durante su visita a Nueva York.… pic.twitter.com/qB3mIFq0qi — Alicia Salgado (@AliciaSalgadoMX) July 20, 2026

“In reality, they were little moments,” Sheinbaum said without providing details of the conversations.

She said that all the U.S. officials at the stadium were “very respectful” and “pleasant.”

“[There was] an atmosphere of a lot of cordiality, also with the King of Spain, … with the Prime Minister of Spain,” Sheinbaum said.

“It was a good environment,” she said.

Sheinbaum says she spoke about trade with Trump and Carney

Sheinbaum said that she, Trump and Carney had the opportunity to briefly discuss trade, but didn’t provide many details of the conversation.

“With Canada [the United States] has other issues, the issue of security, because Canada belongs to NATO,” she said.

“… Remember that today this second round of conversations about the review of the USMCA begins and we hope to be able to reach some agreements this week,” Sheinbaum added.

She said she would welcome Ambassador Greer to Mexico City on Wednesday or Thursday.

In remarks early in her press conference, Sheinbaum also highlighted her social media post on Sunday after the completion of the World Cup.

In that post, she congratulated Spain and said that the three World Cup host countries — Mexico, the United States and Canada — showed that “when we work together, we are capable of making great projects reality and leaving a legacy of cooperation, friendship and hope for the world.”

Later in the press conference, when asked about her personal relationship with the U.S. president, Sheinbaum said that she and Trump “have sought a good relationship.”

“I think that Mexico must always seek a good relationship with the president of the United States and his government,” she said.

“First of all because we’re neighbors. Secondly because we always have to prioritize diplomatic relationships and promote a good-neighbor policy. And thirdly because there are 40 million Mexicans who live in the United States,” Sheinbaum said.

“In addition, there has to be respect between people. We can disagree with President Trump on issues, but we have no reason to make this a personal matter,” she said.

Sheinbaum said she spoke to Trump on Sunday about the aim of “reaching an agreement” regarding USMCA at this week’s bilateral trade talks.

“We didn’t go much beyond that,” she said.

“… And I raised other issues we want to talk about. Obviously we referred to Mexicans in the United States and other issues,” Sheinbaum said.

Damned if you do and damned if you don’t

Sheinbaum said that whether she went to the World Cup final or not, she would have faced criticism.

🗳️⚽️ Claudia Sheinbaum entrega el Balón de Oro a Rodri La presidenta de México entregó el reconocimiento al mejor jugador del Mundial 2026 al capitán de España, tras la victoria 1-0 sobre Argentina en la final disputada en Nueva Jersey. 🇪🇸🏆 pic.twitter.com/Mev8cxW9Ka — LuisCardenasMX (@LuisCardenasMx) July 19, 2026

“If we hadn’t gone, what would they have said?” she asked, referring to government critics.

“How is it possible that they leave Mexico’s position in a World Cup empty? Sheinbaum said.

“… If we go, [they say] ‘Why is she going? How is it possible?’” she said.

“‘What lack of coherence! How is it possible that she smiles alongside President Trump? … Why did she go to the closing [of the World Cup], but not the opening?’” Sheinbaum said before noting that neither Trump nor Carney attended the opening matches of the tournament in their respective countries.

“The closing was a matter of the three of us being together because the three of us, North America, organized [the World Cup],” she said.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily. com)

World.title: Uber Pours $500M More Into Argentina, Totaling $1B Bet
World.content:
Argentina · Companies

Key Facts —New investment. Uber committed an additional US$500 million on July 17, 2026, bringing its total three-year pledge in Argentina to US$1 billion. —Uber Eats returns. The funds will officially relaunch Uber Eats in Argentina after the food delivery service ceased operations in the country in 2020. —Platform unification. Uber plans to integrate its ride-hailing and delivery services into a single app, likely leveraging its Uber One subscription program. —Market scale. Over 20 million people have used Uber in Argentina, and more than 1 million individuals have earned income through the platform as drivers or delivery partners. —Reform confidence. Uber executives directly linked the investment to confidence in the economic reforms under President Javier Milei, with Argentina ranking among Uber’s fastest-growing markets globally.

Uber is making its largest bet yet on Argentina’s economic recovery. The San Francisco-based ride-hailing and delivery giant confirmed on July 17, 2026, an Uber Argentina investment of an additional US$500 million, doubling its total three-year commitment to US$1 billion. The announcement, made after company executives met with Economy Minister Luis Caputo, signals strong foreign confidence in President Javier Milei’s reform agenda and sets the stage for the return of Uber Eats to the South American nation.

Where the Fresh Capital Is Headed

The new US$500 million package is earmarked for three specific areas over the next three years, running through 2029. First, Uber will broaden its core ride-hailing operations, which already span more than 50 cities across all Argentine provinces. The company entered the market in Buenos Aires in 2016 and has since grown into a nationwide network.

Second, and perhaps most notably for consumers, the funds will finance the official relaunch of Uber Eats. The food and supermarket delivery arm originally exited Argentina in 2020, but the company now sees a clear path back, focusing on “last-mile” logistics. The move follows Uber’s broader regional play, including the acquisition of Delivery Hero’s PedidosYa assets in Latin America, which strengthens its hand against local delivery competitors.

Finally, Uber intends to unify its mobility and delivery services so users can access both without switching between separate apps. The integration is expected to lean heavily on Uber One, the company’s subscription program that bundles ride discounts and free delivery perks into a single monthly fee.

A Vote of Confidence in Milei’s Argentina

The timing of the announcement is no accident. Uber executives explicitly tied the fresh capital to their confidence in the economic direction charted by President Javier Milei, a libertarian economist who took office promising aggressive deregulation and pro-market reforms. Economy Minister Luis Caputo described his meeting with Uber’s leadership as “excellent,” stating on social media that the investment arrives alongside “confidence in the economic course delineated by our president.”

For international investors watching Latin America, the move is a concrete signal. Classifying Argentina as one of its fastest-growing markets globally, Uber is putting capital to work at a scale that suggests it believes the country’s volatile economic history is taking a stabler turn. The first US$500 million tranche of this commitment was announced back on March 17, 2025, meaning the company has now locked in a US$1 billion spending plan in just over a year.

Scale, Jobs, and the Road Ahead

Uber’s existing footprint in Argentina is already substantial. The company reports that more than 20 million people have used its services in the country, and over 1 million individuals have generated income through the app as drivers or delivery partners. While the company did not specify an exact number of new jobs the US$500 million will create, it framed the investment as a commitment to local “talent” and “technological” growth, implying a significant scaling of operations and support staff.

The relaunch of Uber Eats will likely create a fresh wave of delivery-partner opportunities, adding to the platform’s role as a key income generator in a country where flexible work remains in high demand. The announcement also coincides with Uber’s 10th anniversary in Argentina, marking a decade since its contentious 2016 launch in Buenos Aires, where it initially faced fierce opposition from local taxi unions and regulators before gradually cementing its place in the transportation landscape.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is Uber investing in Argentina?

Uber announced an additional US$500 million on July 17, 2026. Combined with a previous US$500 million announced in March 2025, the company’s total three-year investment commitment in Argentina now stands at US$1 billion.

Is Uber Eats returning to Argentina?

Yes. The new investment includes funds to officially relaunch Uber Eats in Argentina, focusing on food and supermarket delivery with an emphasis on last-mile logistics. The service originally left the Argentine market in 2020.

Why is Uber investing so heavily in Argentina now?

Uber executives cited confidence in the economic reforms under President Javier Milei. The company views Argentina as one of its fastest-growing markets globally and believes the stabilizing economic direction warrants major long-term capital deployment.

World.title: Tren Maya’s Yucatán Food Trains Launch at US$304
World.content:
Mexico · Travel

Key Facts —Price for foreigners. The all-inclusive gastronomic tour package costs 1,550 Mexican pesos, approximately US$304 per person. —Route structure. Trips are same-day roundtrips departing from Cancún Airport or Mérida Teya station, featuring onboard brunch and a five-course dinner. —Featured stops. Destinations include the UNESCO-listed Chichén Itzá ruins, the yellow-painted town of Izamal, and the walled city of Campeche. —Culinary partners. The program is a collaboration between Tren Maya, Mexico’s national restaurant chamber CANIRAC, and regional hotel associations. —Booking method. Gastronomic packages are sold through Tours Experiencia Maya and partner operators, not on the standard Tren Maya ticket site.

Foreign travelers exploring Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula can now turn a train ride into a rolling feast. Tren Maya gastronomic routes are operating as all-inclusive day trips that combine high-speed rail, archaeological wonders, and multi-course regional dining, with foreigner packages priced at 1,550 Mexican pesos (about US$304).

How the Gastronomic Trains Work

Each gastronomic route is designed as a same-day roundtrip, eliminating the need for overnight lodging. Passengers board at either Cancún Airport or Mérida Teya station in the morning and are served brunch shortly after departure. The train then stops at a Pueblo Mágico – one of Mexico’s designated “magical towns” – or a major archaeological zone for exploration, before guests reboard for the return journey.

The culinary centerpiece is a five-course dinner prepared onboard by certified local chefs. Dishes are rooted in Yucatecan tradition and change depending on the destination. On the Cancún-Izamal-Cancún loop, travelers sample panuchos, salbutes, relleno negro, and turkey in escabeche. The Mérida-Valladolid-Mérida route highlights cochinita pibil, sopa de lima, and queso relleno. The Campeche-bound train leans into coastal flavors with seafood stews and fresh catches from the Gulf of Mexico.

Routes, Ruins, and Regional Flavors

Five confirmed gastronomic itineraries are running as of early 2026. The Cancún-Chichén Itzá-Cancún option is the most archaeology-focused, delivering travelers to the UNESCO World Heritage site for a guided visit before an evening of Mayan-inspired cuisine. Another route heads to Izamal, known as the “Yellow City” for its sun-colored colonial buildings, where the onboard menu spotlights escabeche turkey and relleno negro.

From Mérida, passengers can choose a Valladolid itinerary that pairs colonial architecture with poc chuc – traditional Yucatecan grilled pork – or a Campeche route that explores the fortified walls of San Francisco de Campeche, another UNESCO site, alongside Campechean stews. A fifth route, Ruta Edzná, focuses entirely on the lesser-visited Edzná ruins deep in Campeche state, offering a quieter archaeological experience.

Pricing and How to Book

The gastronomic tour package is priced at 1,550 Mexican pesos for foreigners, which converts to roughly US$304 at current exchange rates. Mexican nationals pay a slightly reduced rate of 1,400 pesos (about US$275). This all-inclusive fee covers the roundtrip train ticket, onboard brunch, the archaeological or town stop, and the five-course dinner.

These packages are not sold through the official Tren Maya website, where standard point-to-point tickets range from 431.50 to 1,862 pesos (US$85 to US$365) depending on distance and class. Instead, the gastronomic experiences are booked via Tours Experiencia Maya or affiliated tour operators. Regular Tren Maya tickets, for travelers who simply want to ride the railway, remain available on the official site with payment processed through BBVA Mexico.

The Bigger Tourism Picture

The gastronomic routes are part of a broader strategy by Tren Maya, the national restaurant chamber CANIRAC, and regional hotel associations to transform the railway into more than just transportation. By embedding local chefs and regional ingredients directly into the journey, officials aim to channel tourism spending into communities that have historically been overlooked by mass-market resort tourism.

The 100-mile-per-hour rail service itself was built to connect Cancún’s beach zone with inland colonial cities and Mayan archaeological sites, replacing long bus rides and shared taxis. Trains offer multiple classes, including economy, a dining car called Janal, and sleeper cabins branded P’tal. While a separate two-day food festival called “Sabores de la Ruta del Tren Maya” is scheduled for August 23-24, 2026 at Parque de las Palapas, that event is a stationary food fair and not a new train route launch.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does the Tren Maya gastronomic tour cost for foreigners?

The all-inclusive package costs 1,550 Mexican pesos, approximately US$304 at current exchange rates. This covers the roundtrip train journey, onboard brunch, a stop at an archaeological site or Pueblo Mágico, and a five-course dinner prepared by local chefs.

Can I book the gastronomic route on the official Tren Maya website?

No. The gastronomic packages are sold through Tours Experiencia Maya and partner tour operators. The official Tren Maya website only sells standard point-to-point tickets, which range from about US$85 to US$365 depending on distance and class.

Is the August 23, 2026 date a new route launch?

No. August 23-24, 2026 marks the “Sabores de la Ruta del Tren Maya” food festival at Parque de las Palapas, a stationary event showcasing regional cuisine. The gastronomic train routes described here are already operating as of early 2026 and are not tied to that festival date.

World.title: Steelmaker Ternium Slashes 2025 Dividend to US$2.20
World.content:
Latin America · Companies

Key Facts —Dividend revision. Ternium’s board cut the fiscal year 2025 dividend proposal from $2.70 to $2.20 per ADS in April 2026. —Final payment. The remaining net dividend of $1.30 per ADS was paid to shareholders on May 15, 2026. —2025 earnings. Full-year 2025 net income reached $303 million, weighed down by a $405 million deferred tax asset write-down at its Brazilian unit Usiminas. —Q4 performance. Fourth-quarter 2025 revenue slipped 2.6% year-over-year to $3.78 billion, with earnings per share of $0.62 missing analyst estimates. —2026 outlook. The company expects higher shipments and improved EBITDA margins in Mexico and Brazil during the first quarter of 2026.

Luxembourg-based Latin American steelmaker Ternium has completed its Ternium dividend 2025 payout cycle with a reduced figure, finalizing a $2.20 per American Depositary Share (ADS) distribution after a board-level revision in April 2026. For foreign investors tracking the New York Stock Exchange-listed company (NYSE: TX), the adjustment reflects a cautious approach following a fiscal year marked by a major deferred tax write-down, even as the company signals a brighter operational outlook for its core Mexican and Brazilian markets.

Dividend Breakdown: What Was Paid

Ternium’s board of directors initially proposed a fiscal year 2025 dividend of $2.70 per ADS. However, on April 15, 2026, the company revised that proposal downward to $2.20 per ADS, equivalent to $0.22 per share. The final net portion of this distribution, $1.30 per ADS ($0.13 per share), was paid out on May 15, 2026, effectively closing the book on the 2025 dividend cycle. No new dividend announcements for 2026 have been made as of mid-July.

At the time of the revision, Ternium‘s share price hovered around $43.27, giving the reduced $2.20 annual dividend a yield of approximately 5.1%. While earlier drafts based on the original $2.70 proposal had suggested a yield closer to 6%, the final figure remains notable for income-focused investors. The stock was trading near $43.57 during intraday activity on February 18, 2026, though updated share prices for July 2026 are not available in recent disclosures.

2025 Earnings: The Write-Down That Shaped the Payout

The dividend revision cannot be separated from Ternium’s full-year 2025 financial performance, reported on February 18, 2026. The company posted a net income of $303 million for the year, a figure deeply impacted by a $405 million write-down of deferred tax assets at Usiminas, its Brazilian steelmaking affiliate. This non-cash accounting charge significantly eroded bottom-line results, prompting a more conservative capital-return strategy.

In the fourth quarter alone, Ternium generated $171 million in net income, which included a $94 million gain from deferred taxes. Quarterly revenue reached $3.78 billion, representing a 2.6% decline compared to the same period in 2024. Earnings per ADS came in at $0.62, missing analyst consensus estimates by $0.15. The mixed results underscored the challenges in a global steel market still navigating uneven demand and pricing pressures.

2026 Outlook: Mexico and Brazil Drive Optimism

Despite the cautious dividend action, Ternium’s forward guidance strikes a more optimistic tone. The company expects Adjusted EBITDA to increase in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the fourth quarter of 2025. This anticipated improvement is pinned on higher shipment volumes, primarily in Mexico, and better Adjusted EBITDA margins in both Mexico and Brazil. Management attributes the margin recovery to rising revenue per ton, though it notes this will be partially offset by higher costs per ton.

For the full year 2026, analysts project earnings per ADS of $6.05. If Ternium maintains an expected annual dividend of $1.80 per ADS, the implied payout ratio would sit at a comfortable 29.8%, suggesting ample room for the company to fund its distribution from profits. The strategic focus on Mexico and Brazil as operational drivers is clear, though the company’s public disclosures do not provide detailed mid-2026 data on market conditions in Argentina or the specific impact of Chinese steel import pressure on the region.

What Foreign Investors Should Watch

For expats, tourists-turned-investors, and global market watchers following Latin America, Ternium offers a window into the region’s industrial health. The company’s ADR structure makes it easily accessible on the NYSE, but its fortunes are tied to construction, automotive, and infrastructure cycles in Mexico and Brazil – two of the area’s largest economies. The 5.1% dividend yield, based on the revised $2.20 payout, remains competitive in a global context, but it comes with the volatility typical of commodity-linked equities.

Key signposts for the months ahead include any updates on Usiminas’ tax-asset recovery, quarterly shipment data out of Mexico, and broader trade policy shifts that could affect steel flows into the Americas. While the 2025 dividend chapter is closed, the 2026 story will hinge on whether Ternium can convert its guided margin improvements into the earnings growth that analysts are penciling in.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Ternium’s final 2025 dividend per ADS?

Ternium’s board revised the 2025 dividend to $2.20 per ADS, down from an initial $2.70 proposal. The final net payment of $1.30 per ADS was distributed on May 15, 2026.

Why did Ternium cut its 2025 dividend?

The reduction followed full-year 2025 net income of $303 million, which was heavily impacted by a $405 million write-down of deferred tax assets at its Brazilian unit Usiminas, prompting a more conservative payout.

What is Ternium’s business outlook for 2026?

Ternium expects higher shipments and improved EBITDA margins in Mexico and Brazil during Q1 2026. Analysts forecast full-year 2026 earnings of $6.05 per ADS, which would comfortably cover an expected $1.80 annual dividend.

World.title: Peru Economy May 2026: Fishing Crash Hits Growth
World.content:
Peru · Economy

Key Facts —GDP growth. Peru’s economy grew 1.80% year-on-year in May 2026, down from 3.73% in April and the slowest expansion in 2026. —Fishing collapse. The fishing sector contracted 73.10%, driven by El Niño conditions that warmed Pacific waters and drove away anchovy stocks. —Manufacturing drag. Manufacturing fell 10.67%, weighed down by a 41.70% drop in fishmeal and oil processing and a weak textile production cycle. —Trade leads. The trade sector grew 6.91%, accounting alongside other services and mining for roughly 95% of the month’s overall expansion. —Year-to-date. Cumulative growth for January through May 2026 stood at 3.20%, with annualized growth reaching 3.54%.

Peru’s Peru economy May 2026 expanded just 1.80% compared to the same month a year earlier, decelerating sharply from April’s 3.73% pace and marking the weakest monthly performance of the year, the national statistics agency INEI reported on Wednesday.

For readers unfamiliar with the region, INEI is Peru’s official body responsible for collecting and publishing economic and demographic data. Its monthly GDP reports are the primary gauge of the country’s economic health, much like the Bureau of Economic Analysis releases in the United States.

El Niño slams fishing and manufacturing

The dramatic slowdown was driven overwhelmingly by climate. El Niño conditions warmed the Pacific Ocean off Peru’s coast, drastically reducing the availability of anchovy and other hydrobiological resources.

As a result, the fishing sector collapsed by 73.10% year-on-year, the single worst-performing segment of the economy in May.

That collapse spilled directly into primary manufacturing, where fishmeal and fish-oil processing plummeted 41.70%. Combined with a downswing in the textile industry’s production cycle, overall manufacturing contracted 10.67% compared to May 2025, acting as the heaviest drag on the headline GDP figure.

To understand why this matters so much, it helps to know that Peru is the world’s leading producer of fishmeal, a high-protein feed ingredient used in aquaculture and livestock farming globally. The anchovy fishery off its coast is among the richest on the planet, but it is also among the most sensitive to ocean temperature shifts.

When El Niño arrives, warmer waters push the nutrient-rich cold currents deeper or farther offshore, scattering the anchovy schools and making them far harder to catch.

Trade, mining, and construction provide support

While fishing and manufacturing cratered, several large sectors kept the economy in positive territory. The trade sector – which spans wholesale, retail, and automotive sales – surged 6.91% year-on-year.

Alongside other services and mining, it accounted for roughly 95% of the month’s total growth.

Mining and hydrocarbons returned to expansion after three consecutive months of decline, growing 2.60%. Construction also posted a solid 4.66% increase, while electricity, gas, and water output rose 5.21%.

Accommodation and restaurants grew 5.05%, and government services added 3.69%, rounding out a picture of an economy where domestic demand and services largely offset the climate-driven supply shock in primary industries.

On a month-on-month basis, however, economic activity fell 1.11% from April, underscoring the abruptness of the May deceleration.

The resilience in trade and services tells an important story about Peru’s economic structure. While the country is famous for its commodity exports, a large and growing portion of its workforce earns a living in commerce, tourism, and public services.

When these sectors hold up, they act as a shock absorber, preventing a climate-driven downturn in one industry from turning into a broad recession.

Broader trends and the 2026 outlook

Despite the weak May print, Peru’s cumulative growth for the first five months of 2026 stands at 3.20%. The annualized rate – measured from June 2025 through May 2026 – reached 3.54%, indicating that the economy entered this soft patch from a position of relative strength.

The agriculture and livestock sector barely moved the needle, growing just 0.10%, as a 1.99% increase in livestock output was largely canceled out by weakness elsewhere. Telecommunications expanded a modest 0.65%, while finance and insurance rose 1.79% and transport, storage, and courier services grew 2.42%.

Analysts caution that El Niño‘s intensity in the coming months will be critical for the fishing sector’s recovery and, by extension, for manufacturing. A prolonged warm-water event could continue to weigh on primary industries, though robust trade and services activity may keep overall growth in positive territory.

What to watch next is whether the central bank adjusts its monetary policy stance in response to this slowdown. A single weak month does not usually trigger a rate change, but if the fishing and manufacturing weakness persists into the third quarter, policymakers may face pressure to support domestic demand.

Another open question is how global fishmeal prices will react to the supply disruption from Peru, and whether competing producers in other parts of the world can fill the gap without pushing up costs for the aquaculture industry.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Peru’s economy slow so sharply in May 2026?

The slowdown was primarily caused by El Niño, which warmed Pacific waters and devastated the fishing sector. Fishing output fell 73.10%, and the shock spilled into manufacturing – especially fishmeal processing – which contracted 10.67% overall.

Which sectors performed well in Peru in May 2026?

Trade grew 6.91%, construction rose 4.66%, and electricity, gas, and water expanded 5.21%. Mining and hydrocarbons returned to growth at 2.60%, and accommodation and restaurants increased 5.05%.

What is Peru’s cumulative growth so far in 2026?

For January through May 2026, Peru‘s economy has grown a cumulative 3.20%. The annualized rate from June 2025 to May 2026 is 3.54%, reflecting solid momentum before the May slowdown.

World.title: EU Charges Mexican Giant Cemex with Price-Fixing Cartel
World.content:
Latin America · Companies

Key Facts —Charges filed. The European Commission issued formal cartel charges against Cemex on July 20, 2026, for alleged price-fixing of construction chemicals. —Product in focus. The investigation targets additives for cement, concrete, and mortar, not cement itself. —Markets affected. The alleged collusion took place in France, Germany, and Spain between 2021 and 2022. —Potential penalty. If found guilty, Cemex could face fines of up to 10% of its global annual revenue. —Prior probe closed. A separate seven-year EU investigation into the cement sector involving Cemex was dropped in July 2019 due to insufficient evidence.

The European Commission has formally charged Mexican cement giant Cemex in a Cemex EU cartel charges case, alleging the company conspired with rivals to fix prices of construction chemicals across three major European economies. The charges, announced July 20, 2026, follow dawn raids conducted in October 2023 and mark a significant escalation in Brussels’ scrutiny of the building-materials supply chain.

What the EU is Alleging

The European Commission’s statement of objections accuses Cemex and several other companies of colluding between 2021 and 2022 to artificially raise prices of chemical additives used in cement, concrete, and mortar. The alleged coordination took place in France, Germany, and Spain, three of the European Union’s largest construction markets.

According to the Commission, the firms exploited cost spikes triggered by the Covid-19 pandemic and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Investigators claim the companies used press releases distributed through trade associations to signal and coordinate price increases, rather than competing fairly during a period of genuine supply-chain disruption.

The charges target construction chemicals specifically, not cement. This is an important distinction: Cemex, the world’s third-largest cement producer, is not accused of fixing cement prices in this case.

Other companies charged include Swiss specialty-chemicals group Sika, Germany’s MC Bauchemie, Italy’s Mapei, France’s Chryso, and Master Builders Solutions, along with several trade bodies.

Potential Fines and Next Steps

If the Commission ultimately finds Cemex and its co-accused guilty of breaching EU antitrust rules, each company could be fined up to 10% of its global annual turnover. For Cemex, a multinational with operations spanning the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia, that represents a potentially substantial financial hit.

Cemex has confirmed it is cooperating with authorities and providing requested information and testimonies. The company now has the right to examine the Commission’s evidence and submit a formal reply to the statement of objections.

There is no fixed deadline for the EU to conclude its investigation, and companies can challenge any final decision before European courts.

The charges stem from dawn raids – surprise inspections – conducted by Commission officials in October 2023. Such raids are a common preliminary step in EU cartel probes, allowing investigators to gather documents and digital evidence before companies have time to alter or destroy them.

A Look Back: The Closed Cement Probe

For international readers following Cemex‘s regulatory history in Europe, the new charges may sound familiar. The company was previously caught up in a much broader EU investigation into alleged price-fixing and import-export restrictions in the cement sector itself. That probe, which also involved France’s Lafarge, Germany’s HeidelbergCement, and Switzerland’s Holcim, lasted seven years.

In July 2019, the Commission scrapped the entire cement-sector case, concluding there was insufficient evidence to substantiate the claims. The investigation had begun with dawn raids back in November 2007, underscoring how long such antitrust inquiries can drag on without yielding penalties.

The contrast between the two cases highlights the EU’s shifting focus. While cement-price collusion proved difficult to prove, regulators are now targeting adjacent markets like construction chemicals, particularly where they suspect companies exploited pandemic and war-related cost volatility to coordinate price hikes.

Why This Matters for Latin America’s Multinationals

Cemex is one of Latin America’s most internationally exposed industrial companies, with a deep footprint across Europe. The case serves as a reminder that Brussels remains one of the world’s most aggressive antitrust enforcers, willing to pursue complex, cross-border cartel investigations that can take years to resolve.

The EU has a long track record of scrutinizing the cement and construction-materials sector. Previous merger reviews include the 2014 approval of Cemex’s acquisition of Holcim’s Spanish operations and the 2015 decision to block HeidelbergCement and Schwenk’s attempt to buy Cemex’s Croatian assets, citing concerns the deal would control 45% to 50% of the market and push prices higher.

For investors and expats watching Latin American companies navigate European regulations, the July 2026 charges signal that even when one probe closes – as the cement case did in 2019 – regulatory risk can resurface in related markets. The construction-chemicals case is now one of the most significant antitrust actions facing a major Latin American multinational in Europe.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Cemex being charged for fixing cement prices?

No. The July 2026 charges relate to construction chemicals – additives for cement, concrete, and mortar – not cement itself. A previous EU cement-sector probe involving Cemex was closed in 2019 without charges.

What is the maximum fine Cemex could face?

Under EU cartel rules, the Commission can impose fines of up to 10% of a company’s global annual turnover if it finds a breach. The final amount depends on the gravity and duration of the infringement.

Which countries are involved in the alleged cartel?

The European Commission says the alleged price-fixing took place in France, Germany, and Spain between 2021 and 2022.

World.title: Brazil’s Pix Payment System Eyes Global Expansion at $660B
World.content:
Brazil · Markets

Key Facts —Massive user base. Pix has 200 million monthly active users, including 25 million businesses, as of early 2026. —Staggering volume. The system processes roughly 8.6 billion transactions per month, totaling R$3.4 trillion (approximately US$660 billion). —Financial inclusion engine. Over 70 million Brazilians entered the formal financial system for the first time thanks to Pix since its 2020 launch. —Global ambitions. Brazil’s central bank has explicit plans to take Pix cross-border, with fintechs already enabling its use for international payments. —US trade scrutiny. In July 2025, the US Trade Representative opened an investigation into Pix, labeling it a potential discriminatory ‘national payment standard’.

Brazil’s ubiquitous instant payment system, Pix, is no longer just a domestic powerhouse processing a staggering US$660 billion each month. With its Pix global expansion plans now firmly underway, the central bank-backed network is stepping onto the international stage, challenging traditional card networks and drawing a mix of admiration and trade friction from abroad, including a formal investigation by the United States.

A Domestic Giant with Global Dreams

To understand why Pix’s international move matters, you first have to grasp its jaw-dropping scale at home. Launched by Brazil’s central bank in late 2020, the system has achieved near-total saturation in record time.

By the first quarter of 2026, Pix counted 200 million monthly active users – a figure that includes 175 million individuals and 25 million businesses. That represents well over 80% of the country’s entire population, with 93% of Brazilian adults actively using the platform.

The transaction volumes are equally staggering. Brazilians make about 8.6 billion Pix transfers every month, moving R$3.4 trillion (roughly US$660 billion). To put that in context, Pix now moves 8.6 times more value than all credit and debit card transactions in Brazil combined. In 2024 alone, the system processed 68.7 billion transactions worth around US$5 trillion, accounting for a full 14% of all instant payments made globally that year.

How Pix is Going Cross-Border

Brazil’s central bank has not hidden its ambition to take this homegrown success story global. As early as late 2024, officials outlined a concrete strategy to enable cross-border payments via Pix, allowing the system to be used for international transfers, travel spending, and e-commerce with foreign merchants.

Fintech companies like PagBrasil have already begun rolling out Pix-based solutions for international travelers and cross-border shoppers.

The appeal for foreigners is straightforward: Pix transactions clear instantly, 24/7, often at zero cost for individuals. For a tourist visiting Rio de Janeiro, paying a street vendor by scanning a QR code with a Pix-enabled app is faster and cheaper than using a credit card. For an expat sending money home, Pix promises to slash the high fees and multi-day waits typical of traditional international wire transfers. The system’s domestic dominance also suggests a ready-made user base of millions who would eagerly use Pix abroad if given the chance.

Financial Inclusion and E-Commerce Dominance

Pix’s global push is built on a foundation of radical financial inclusion. Since its debut, the system has brought more than 70 million Brazilians into the formal financial system – people who had never before made an electronic transfer.

By eliminating fees for individuals and requiring only a smartphone, Pix turned bank accounts from a luxury into a utility.

This inclusion engine is now reshaping commerce. Analysts project that Pix will capture 50% of Brazil’s entire e-commerce market by 2028, surpassing credit cards as the preferred online payment method.

For foreign investors and companies looking at Latin America’s largest economy, ignoring Pix is no longer an option. Any business selling to Brazilian consumers – whether a global e-commerce platform or a local restaurant – must integrate Pix or risk losing access to the vast majority of the country’s purchasing power.

US Scrutiny and Trade Tensions

Pix’s rise has not gone unnoticed in Washington. In July 2025, the Office of the United States Trade Representative opened a formal investigation into Brazil’s digital trade and electronic payment services.

The probe specifically flagged Pix as a potential ‘national payment standard’ that could discriminate against US-based payment companies like Visa and Mastercard.

The investigation highlights a growing tension: Pix’s state-backed, fee-free model is difficult for private-sector competitors to match. While the US has not yet imposed any measures, the probe signals that Pix’s global expansion could face regulatory headwinds.

For now, Brazil’s central bank continues to promote Pix as an open, inclusive system that benefits consumers and merchants alike. For international readers, the key takeaway is that Pix is a financial force that is here to stay – and it is increasingly a factor in trade relations between the Americas.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly is Pix?

Pix is an instant payment system created by Brazil’s central bank. It allows individuals and businesses to send and receive money in seconds, 24/7, using just a phone number, QR code, or key.

For individuals, transactions are typically free.

Can foreigners use Pix?

Yes, but currently you generally need a Brazilian bank account or a digital account with a participating fintech. As Pix expands globally, cross-border options for tourists and international transfers are being developed by companies like PagBrasil.

Why is the US investigating Pix?

The US Trade Representative opened an investigation in July 2025 to determine whether Pix acts as a discriminatory ‘national payment standard’ that unfairly disadvantages US-based payment companies operating in Brazil.

World.title: Brazilian Author Felipe Cattapan Brings Apocalyptic Love Story to London
World.content:
Brazil · Culture

Key Facts —Author. Felipe Cattapan is a Brazilian writer, conductor, and lecturer at the University of the Arts Bern in Switzerland. —Book. ‘Um Espaço além do Tempo, um Tempo além do Espaço’ combines a theater play and a novella centered on unconditional love during an apocalypse. —Venue. The presentation takes place at the Biblioteca Brasileira Casa do Livro, a Brazilian cultural library in London. —Date. The event is scheduled for July 26, 2024, from 2 PM to 4 PM local time. —Publisher. The book is published by Kotter Editorial, which operates in both Brazil and Portugal.

Brazilian author and conductor Felipe Cattapan London readers will get a rare chance to meet the Rio de Janeiro-born writer this July, as he presents his latest book, a genre-blending work that fuses a theater play with a novella, at a Brazilian cultural hub in the UK capital.

A Book That Defies Genres

The work, titled “Um Espaço além do Tempo, um Tempo além do Espaço” (which translates to “A Space Beyond Time, A Time Beyond Space”), is not a straightforward novel. Published by Kotter Editorial, a house with a presence in both Brazil and Portugal, the book contains two distinct yet thematically linked unpublished pieces: the theater play “X Minutos” (X Minutes) and the novella “Emulação” (Emulation).

The central thread is unconditional love set against an apocalyptic backdrop. Cattapan uses this extreme setting to explore human relationships across time and space, creating what his announcement describes as a guide to a “different level of consciousness.” His writing style uniquely blends prose and poetry, a technique heavily inspired by his parallel career in classical music.

For a foreign audience, this hybrid format is worth understanding. In Brazilian literary culture, it is not unusual for authors to move fluidly between forms—poetry, theater, and prose—often within a single volume.

Cattapan’s decision to pair a play with a novella reflects a broader Lusophone tradition where the boundaries between literary genres are treated as porous, inviting the reader to experience the same emotional core from different structural angles.

From Piano in Rio to Podium in Europe

For international readers unfamiliar with his work, Felipe Cattapan’s path is deeply interdisciplinary. Born in Rio de Janeiro, he first studied piano in his home city before moving to Europe to pursue orchestral and choir conducting. His credentials include studies at the prestigious Conservatoire National Supérieur de Musique in Paris and the École Normale de Paris, followed by a contemporary music conducting degree in Lugano, Switzerland.

Since 2010, he has worked professionally with literature, writing poems, short stories, and theater plays in his native Brazilian Portuguese. His first edition was published in 2018.

Today, he balances his writing with a role as a lecturer at the University of the Arts Bern in Switzerland, where he also directs interdisciplinary projects that sit at the interface of literature and music.

This dual life as a conductor and writer is central to understanding his literary voice. Musicians who turn to literature often bring a distinct sensitivity to rhythm, silence, and structure.

In Cattapan’s case, the prose-poetry blend he employs is not merely decorative; it mirrors the way a musical score alternates between tension and release, a quality that likely shapes how the apocalyptic love story unfolds on the page.

Event Details for London Attendees

The London presentation is scheduled for July 26, 2024, running from 2 PM to 4 PM local time. The venue is the Biblioteca Brasileira Casa do Livro, a Brazilian library in London that serves as a cultural bridge, often hosting Lusophone authors and artists.

The event follows what was described as a successful launch in Zurich, Switzerland, on May 27, 2024.

The book is written entirely in Portuguese, so the event will be most accessible to Portuguese speakers or those with a deep interest in Brazilian literature in its original language. No entry fee or ticket price was specified in the author’s announcement, suggesting a free, open-door cultural event typical of such library-hosted literary afternoons.

For anyone planning to attend, it helps to know that the Biblioteca Brasileira Casa do Livro occupies a special niche in London’s multicultural landscape. Such libraries function as more than book repositories; they are community living rooms where the Brazilian diaspora and UK-based Lusophiles gather for readings, workshops, and conversations that rarely make it into mainstream British arts listings.

An afternoon event of this kind typically includes a reading by the author, a moderated conversation, and an open question session, all conducted in Portuguese.

The broader significance of this London date lies in what it says about the circulation of contemporary Brazilian literature. While translated Brazilian classics occasionally surface in English-language bookshops, living authors writing in Portuguese often reach international audiences through exactly this kind of grassroots, community-anchored event.

It is a reminder that a book’s journey beyond its home market frequently depends on cultural institutions that operate below the radar of large publishing fairs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Felipe Cattapan presenting a book in London in 2026?

No. According to the author’s own announcement and available sources, the confirmed London event at the Biblioteca Brasileira Casa do Livro took place on July 26, 2024. There is no evidence of a 2026 London presentation.

What is Felipe Cattapan’s book about?

The book “Um Espaço além do Tempo, um Tempo além do Espaço” combines a theater play and a novella. It explores unconditional love in an apocalyptic setting, crossing themes of time, space, and human relationships in contexts of existential tension.

In what language is the book written?

The book is written in Brazilian Portuguese. The London event was hosted at a Brazilian cultural library, and the presentation was conducted in that linguistic context.

World.title: Zema Privatization Plan Targets Petrobras, Banco do Brasil
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts —The proposal. Romeu Zema pledges to sell Petrobras and Banco do Brasil if elected president in October 2026. —The revenue goal. Sale proceeds would fund roads, railways, waterways, and ports, not pay existing federal debt. —The economic team. The plan is coordinated by Carlos Da Costa, a former secretary in the Bolsonaro administration. —The inspiration. The platform is structurally modeled on Javier Milei's free-market reforms in Argentina. —The legal hurdle. Privatizing Petrobras requires a constitutional amendment passed by Brazil's Congress.

Zema privatization of Brazil’s two largest state-owned enterprises took center stage this month as presidential pre-candidate Romeu Zema formally launched his 2026 economic platform in São Paulo.

Romeu Zema is a Brazilian politician and businessman serving as governor of Minas Gerais.

The Zema Privatization Blueprint

Romeu Zema, the former governor of Minas Gerais state and a member of the Novo party, first floated the idea in an April 26 Instagram video. He formally presented the plan on July 18 at the 10th National Meeting of the Novo party.

The proposal calls for selling Brazilian oil giant Petrobras and lender Banco do Brasil as a starting point. Zema then aims to privatize every federal state-owned enterprise without exception.

Petrobras is the world’s largest oil producer by output and a symbol of Brazilian industrial might. Banco do Brasil, one of the country’s oldest financial institutions, holds a vast network of accounts and credit operations touching millions of citizens and businesses.

For foreign investors, these two firms are pillars of the state’s direct involvement in strategic sectors. Selling them would mark the most radical redefinition of Brazil’s economic model in decades.

Funding Infrastructure, Not Paying Bills

Zema argues that revenue from the sales must build roads, railways, waterways, and ports. He explicitly ruled out using the money to pay Brasília’s bills.

He claims the federal government spends more than it collects, creating a debt near R$9 trillion (US$1.77 trillion). Privatization, he says, would cut corruption and lower interest rates.

The distinction is crucial for his campaign narrative: he wants voters to see the sell-off as a long-term investment in the country’s notoriously bottlenecked logistics network. Brazil’s infrastructure gap has long been cited by exporters and agribusiness as a primary brake on competitiveness.

By ring-fencing the proceeds for ports and highways, Zema hopes to appeal to the powerful farm caucus and industrial sectors that lose billions annually to clogged transport routes. For expats and foreign traders, smoother logistics would directly lower the cost of moving goods from the interior to global markets.

The Exploration and Production segment explores, develops, and produces…

Milei-Style Shock Therapy for Brazil

The economic plan is coordinated by Carlos Da Costa, a former secretary to Paulo Guedes under ex-President Jair Bolsonaro. It is structurally modeled on Argentine President Javier Milei’s aggressive free-market reforms.

Zema wants to eliminate the so-called ‘Custo Brasil,’ an estimated R$1.7 trillion (US$335 billion) annual drag on production. He blames tax complexity and high capital costs for the inefficiency.

The ‘Custo Brasil’ encapsulates the extra expenses businesses face in Brazil that they would not encounter in more efficient economies. For international companies weighing a Brazilian expansion, this cost is often the invisible wall that makes the market uncompetitive.

By invoking Milei’s name, Zema signals to investors that he would pursue a no-compromise deregulation agenda. However, Brazil’s fragmented political system requires constant negotiation with a sprawling Congress, making a pure shock-therapy approach harder to execute.

Steep Political and Legal Hurdles

The proposal has drawn sharp criticism from the left-wing Workers’ Party (PT) and other groups. They view Petrobras and Banco do Brasil as strategic national assets.

Privatizing Petrobras requires a constitutional amendment, a heavy lift without a broad coalition in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies and Senate. The sheer size of the entities would also make any sale a complex multi-year process.

Brazil’s 1988 Constitution grants the state a monopoly over oil exploration and production, a legal shield that cannot be removed by a simple presidential decree. Amending the constitution demands a three-fifths majority in two rounds of voting in both legislative houses.

Beyond the legal text, nationalist sentiment around Petrobras runs deep across the political spectrum. The company was born from a ‘O Petróleo é Nosso’ (The Oil is Ours) campaign in the 1950s, and any attempt to sell it touches a raw cultural nerve.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For the foreign community eyeing Brazil, a successful Zema privatization push would reshape the investment landscape overnight. A privately run Petrobras could prioritize profitability over political pricing, potentially unlocking higher dividends and attracting fresh foreign capital into the pre-salt oil fields.

A privatized Banco do Brasil might streamline lending and reduce the state’s habit of using the bank for subsidized credit programs that distort markets. For expats managing cross-border finances, a more market-oriented banking sector could simplify access to credit and investment products.

However, the transition period would likely bring volatility. The Brazilian real could swing sharply on election polls, and the timeline from a potential October 2026 victory to an actual asset sale would stretch years, filled with legal challenges and public hearings.

For tourists and short-term visitors, the immediate impact is minimal. A successful infrastructure push funded by privatization could eventually improve the airports, highways, and port terminals that make traveling and doing business in Brazil a famously endurance-testing experience.

What Happens Next

The campaign is still in its early stages, with the first round of the presidential election scheduled for October 4, 2026. Zema must first secure the Novo party’s formal nomination and then build enough national name recognition to challenge better-known figures in a crowded field.

Even if he wins, the privatization timeline would begin only after the January 2027 inauguration. The constitutional amendment process alone could consume the first year of a new government, followed by the technical work of valuing two of Latin America’s largest companies and structuring an international tender.

For now, the Zema privatization plan serves as both a campaign differentiator and a litmus test for how much appetite Brazilian voters have for radical economic change. Foreign capitals and multinational boards will be watching closely to see whether this bold promise gains traction or fades under the weight of political reality.
