World.title: People’s photos are helping scientists record marine life in real-time in the Canary Islands
World.content:
With more than 85,000 recorded and validated sightings in the waters of the so-called ‘Lucky Islands’ or Macaronesia, scientists from the RedPROMAR project have recorded more than 5,000 species of living organisms in this part of the North Atlantic.

 

Dennis Rabeling, a diving instructor at Euro-Divers Lanzarote, is one of its main contributors. He dives every day and uploads thousands of photos of marine flora and fauna to the website of this European project, which is co-funded by the Government of the Canary Islands. He has contributed to the discovery of three species previously unknown in the Canary Islands, one of which is named after him: Gibberula Dennisi. “With RedPROMAR, if you upload your photos, you become another pair of eyes on the water. In this way, scientists can identify new species that we did not previously know lived here. Today, during a thirty-minute dive, we saw around twenty or thirty species, perhaps even more," he explains.

Through this project, ocean culture is brought into the classroom, and the classroom is brought closer to the sea. This year, secondary school pupils from Juan Francisco Rodríguez García’s class at IES Yaiza have studied how human activities affect the marine environment, recorded a podcast on tropicalisation and its consequences, and undertaken a field trip to Órzola, in the north of Lanzarote, to learn ‘in situ’ which species live in the sea and how RedPROMAR works.

“We’ve taught them about a tool which allows any member of the public, including them, to take a photo of a particular species and geotag it using the same app, in order to provide better scientific data and contribute to scientific research” Juan Francisco Rodríguez García Environmental educator and teacher, IES Yaiza

An experience their pupils will never forget. Aroa says, “I didn’t even know most of the species. I hadn’t heard those names before at all. Take the manatee, for example. When an animal tries to bother it, it releases a kind of purple ink to scare it away. It’s really amazing."

The total budget for the project is just under two million euros, of which 85% has been funded by the European Cohesion Policy and the remaining 15% by the Canary Islands Government.

The pieces of the photo jigsaw speak

This project began in the Canary Islands and has since expanded its scope to Cape Verde, Madeira and the Azores. Each geotagged photo is checked by a team of experts. Marc Martín Sola, a marine biologist at Gesplan and a technician with RedPROMAR, says that “citizen science data is like a jigsaw puzzle, in which observers provide us with small pieces that, taken individually, may not make sense”, but when put together, they are valuable to the scientific community and to the authorities.

“By putting all these pieces together, we can see things that we wouldn’t be able to see individually; for example, introduced species or protected species, and we can better assess a species’ distribution or breeding season” Marc Martín Sola Marine biologist at Gesplan and technician with RedPROMAR

The platform also serves as an early-warning system for the arrival of alien species and the proliferation of species linked to human activity or climate change. “There are specific times when we receive a lot of reports, a lot of sightings of a particular species, and this usually coincides with ‘arribazones’ (washed ashore) – the mass arrival of organisms, whether alive or dead, on the coast,” explains Marc. “In 2024, we had more than a hundred sightings in just a few months. "Citizen science enables us to detect and record these sudden surges that might otherwise go unnoticed by the scientific community and thus keep a record of when and where they have occurred," he concludes.

World.title: From 'Following' to 'The Odyssey': All Christopher Nolan movies ranked from weakest to strongest
World.content:
From sci-fi thrillers to historical dramas via layered mysteries and three hugely successful Batman films, few directors inspire as much devotion as Christopher Nolan.

 

You know the fans we're talking about. The Nolanites who gush about every film and batter away recurring criticism of style-over-substance, emotional coldness, or the fact that he'd do well to forgo non-chronological narrative tampering in order to prioritise three-dimensional female characters that aren't just there to be dead wives.

Then there are those who recognise these pitfalls but can't deny that the Oscar winner continues to wow with an eclectic filmography featuring reoccurring motifs, arresting visual flourishes, and an ability to command top-notch talent both in front and behind the camera.

Whichever camp you're in, and whatever you may think of his box-office dominating latest, The Odyssey, Euronews Culture looks back and re-assesses all of the director's movies from weakest to strongest.

13) Following (1998)

Following Momentum Pictures

Every director has to start somewhere, and for then-28-year-old Christopher Nolan it was a 70-minute black-and-white drama about an obsessive writer. The 'Young Man' (Jeremy Theobald) follows strangers around London for inspiration and gets in over his head when he breaks his one rule: never follow the same person twice. This cerebral neo-noir is striking due to its Hitchcockian effectiveness, and features some of Nolan's treasured themes - principally topics of obsession and identity. Following is a decent entry point into Nolan's world and it's impressive to watch it with his second film (Memento) in mind to appreciate quite how the director evolved in leaps and bounds. Beyond that perspective and his debut being a micro-budget curio in his filmography (it was reportedly made for $6000), Following does remain a promising, if sluggish, character study.

12) Tenet (2020)

Tenet Warner Bros. Pictures

You can't accuse Tenet of not being ambitious. It's a high-concept and technically impressive espionage story which trusts the audience to keep up with time inversion and palindromic shenanigans. But it's the movie which showed that Nolan's reach exceeded his grasp. John David Washington plays a secret agent (eyerollingly dubbed “The Protagonist”) trying to prevent a war between the present and the future. It's thrilling in theory but baffling in execution. Tenet gets increasingly frustrating when it becomes a checklist of Nolan's most irritating foibles: pseudo-profundity lost in clumsy dialogue, underwritten female characters, oppressive sound mixing, and stunning style over pretentious substance. Even if you do embrace the advice given by a Tenet scientist ("Don't try to understand it, feel it"), you'll still be confronted with an emotionally cold effort which is convinced it's a lot cleverer than it actually is.

11) Insomnia (2002)

Insomnia Warner Bros. Pictures

Nolan's third film may not one of his most memorable, but it's certainly underappreciated. Insomnia is a remake of Erik Skjoldbjærg’s 1997 thriller starring Stellan Skarsgård, and follows a veteran detective (Al Pacino) who teams up with a small-town investigator (Hilary Swank) to solve a Laura Palmer-reminiscent murder in a remote part of Alaska. Remote and bathed in perpetual sunlight. It’s a captivating detective drama, and what it lacks in ambitious scope it makes up for in upended tropes, an audaciously bleak ending, as well as a stellar performance from Robin Williams playing against type. Granted, Insomnia feels like it was a studio-mandated assignment for Nolan (who delivered his first film for Warner Bros.), but as far as psychological thrillers go, it deserves your time of day.

10) The Dark Knight Rises (2012)

The Dark Knight Rises Warner Bros. Pictures

It's a shame that Christopher Nolan's Dark Knight Trilogy ended with a bit of a whimper with The Dark Knight Rises. Sure, Tom Hardy was great as Bane and Anne Hathaway impressed as Catwoman, but in making the story's scope wider (Charles Dickens' "A Tale of Two Cities" was a reference point for Nolan), something got lost along the way. The script isn't as tight, the plot holes are glaring, and some of the acting is questionable... Quite how that was the take chosen for Miranda Tate (Marion Cotillard)'s death, we'll never know... Nothing here reaches the same heights as Batman Begins or The Dark Knight. Granted, the latter was a tricky act to follow (more on that later), but it's undeniable that this closing chapter settles for satisfactory.

9) Dunkirk (2017)

Dunkirk Warner Bros. Pictures

From the very first shot, Dunkirk announces itself as something special. And it is: an astonishingly well-made World War II film that is split between land, sea and air. All three parts are intercut together while maintaining their individual pace. A week for land; a day for sea; an hour for air. By segmenting his depiction of the Dunkirk evacuation into these timelines and making them share a common theme (survival), Nolan delivers a technically accomplished experience whose visuals take precedent over traditional narrative storytelling. While it's a technical marvel which throws you into the action, Dunkirk does suffer from keeping the audience at an emotional distance when it comes to the many protagonists. As for the ending, some shots are jaw-dropping but their impact is dented by a clichéd ending featuring Commander Bolton (Kenneth Branagh) saying he's stayng "for the French." Groan.

8) Interstellar (2014)

Interstellar Warner Bros. Pictures

Interstellar is Christopher Nolan aiming to make this generation's 2001: A Space Odyssey, only with a more emotional core. By charting how an astronaut (Matthew McConaughey) leaves behind his children (not that you'd know, as most of the focus is on his daughter Murph) in a quest to save humanity by finding a new world to replace a dying Earth, Nolan attempts to prove some of his detractors wrong. He can put aside the coldly clinical and is capable of embracing feelings. For much of the runtime, the self-serious theoretical astrophysics blend well with the human drama, and some sequences are jaw-dislocatingly good. The "wave planet" and its time distortion is a particular highlight. The snag is that while Interstellar is never not awe-inspiring, thanks in large part to Hoyte van Hoytema's cinematography, the dialogue is distractingly on-the-nose and the final act fumbles the father-daughter story when it all goes M. Night Shyamalan in a five-dimensional space bookshelf. It's an imperfect film - made worse by countless film bros insisting that you the reason you don't love it more is because you don't understand it. But there's no denying that ambitious sci-fi never looked this spectacular.

7) The Odyssey (2026)

The Odyssey Universal Pictures

You've resurrected Batman, performed a dream heist (Inception), gone into outer-space and finally won several Oscars for your three-hour biopic about the birth of the atomic bomb... What do you do next? Embrace your inner Kubrick by fearing no scale nor scope and adapt the borderline unadaptable oldest known work of literature. As if that wasn't enough, you shoot it all in IMAX for a world first. Nolan’s take on Homer's epic is without a doubt his most ambitious undertaking, and there's so much to admire about this monumental technical achievement. Also worth singling out is his departure from the traditional Homeric world, preferring a tale in which the supernatural elements are dialled back to make way for a modernist reading of Odysseus' psyche. However, the filmmaker's proclivity for non-linear plot structures proves to be a thorn in his side. The Odyssey is often crippled by clumsy editing choices and pacing issues in its first half, and he never spends enough time on the dangerous adventures to make thrills truly register. Once it does coalesce into something more focused in the final act, you'll have felt awe but not much in the way of character-driven emotion. Even if it isn't the flat-out masterpiece many are hailing, there's no denying that no one could have accomplished something so bold.

6) Oppenheimer (2023)

Oppenheimer Universal Pictures

You’ve got to hand it to Oppenheimer - a three-hour biopic about a bunch of scientists, generals and lawmen talking to each other became 2023’s most unlikely blockbuster pairing with Barbie. It had no right being as gripping as it was. Based on Kai Bird and Martin J Sherwin’s non-fiction book "American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer", Nolan’s chronologically skewed epic gives spectators an exhaustive look at the rise and fall of the theoretical physicist who oversaw the Manhattan Project and introduced nuclear weapons to humanity. It's an American tragedy which benefits from the talents of an all-star cast led by Cillian Murphy and his note-perfect performance. Themes of guilt hit hard; the pace feels more deliberate compared to The Odyssey; and Ludwig Göransson's score is still his crowning achievement. One sizeable issue remains: Nolan still can’t write female roles – which is glaring here considering Oppenheimer features two complex women played by the immensely talented Emily Blunt and Florence Pugh.

5) Batman Begins (2005)

Batman Begins Warner Bros. Pictures

The Batman franchise was dead and buried after 1997’s Batman & Robin, and it took Christopher Nolan to revive the Caped Crusader for a new generation of cinemagoers. Starting with the very origins of Bruce Wayne before he donned the cowl, Nolan approached this superhero story much like he did The Odyssey: out with the myth and in with the character-driven story of a traumatised man. His hyper-realistic take on the Bat dispelled memories of Burton’s gothic treatment and Schumacher’s campy kitsch, and reinvented the franchise by showing that a grown-up Dark Knight was possible. Kudos to Christian Bale for understanding the assignment and making the parallels and conflicts between Bruce Wayne and Bats so engaging. It was the thrilling start of something special – but we’ll get to that in a bit.

4) Inception (2010)

Inception Warner Bros. Pictures

From this point in the ranking, there are nothing but triumphs. But because decisions have to be made, it's 2010's Inception which narrowly misses the podium. Following Leonardo DiCaprio as a grief-stricken widower who specializes in a form of corporate espionage involving the theft of information from a mark’s subconscious, Inception is one of the most original blockbusters of the 21st century. Getting the balance just right between cerebral and thrilling, Nolan proved that an A-list populated Hollywood action caper could be Bond-indebted and audaciously mind-melting. Moreover, the director gave the audience credit by trusting them to keep up during the matryoshkadream ride. Beyond the now parodied Hans Zimmer score and its blaring horns, Inception remains the bar to clear when it comes to films that both dazzle and challenge.

3) Memento (2000)

Memento Newmarket

Nolan's second film is the one that put him on the map as a singular talent to watch. His sophomore effort is an engrossing and twisty noir about a man (Guy Pierce) unable to create short-term memories. As if that wasn't tough enough to deal with, our hero is trying to solve his wife's murder. Before Inception upped the stakes in terms of scope, Memento showed that Nolan was capable of making thrilling and challenging films which didn't talk down to audiences. Since its release, there have been misguided corners of the internet keen to dismiss Memento as "gimmicky". It's anything but. Beyond the chronological momentum of the monochrome scenes and the backward trajectory of the colour frames, Nolan takes the time to explore themes of grief, guilt and self-deception within a fractured mind. His film still stands as a groundbreaking mystery thriller that proves the director is at his nonlinear best when he keeps a tight grip on the narrative and never forgoes psychological depth for structural flourishes.

2) The Dark Knight (2008)

The Dark Knight Warner Bros. Pictures

After Batman Begins, Nolan originally had no plans to return to Gotham. Everyone was glad he did, as The Dark Knight still stands to this day as one of the – if not the – greatest comic book / superhero movie ever made. Continuing his deconstruction the Batman myth, Nolan saw fit to shake things up and introduce the franchise's most beloved antagonist: The Joker. Despite initial bellyaching from fans that Heath Ledger was miscast as the Clown Prince of Crime, the latter delivered an Oscar-winning performance that was elevated to iconic following the actor's untimely death. Beyond the performances and thrills, The Dark Knight is an expansive and thematically rich blockbuster which continues to divide cinemalovers. Which is the superior middle instalment: The Empire Strikes Back or The Dark Knight ?

1) The Prestige (2006)

The Prestige Warner Bros. Pictures

Based on Christopher Priest’s novel about dueling turn-of-the-century magicians - the charismatic Robert Angier (Hugh Jackman) and the technically skilled Alfred Borden (Christian Bale) - The Prestige didn't make much of a splash when it came out. Turning 20 this year, it takes the top spot. Structured in three fiendishly orchestrated parts mirroring (and adopting) the stages of a magic trick (The Pledge / The Turn / The Prestige), this is Nolan at his most disciplined when it comes to his time-based perspective shifts. The structure directly complements the narrative, making it a necessary formal trick. The Prestige is also Nolan at his most diligent when it comes to character development, and the way he explores themes of obsession and sacrifice hit home. Moreover, Nolan makes his film enticingly metatextual, a layered slight of hand that becomes not only about two ego-driven characters chasing the perfect illusion but about the medium of cinema itself. Fans may argue that The Odyssey is Nolan's most awe-inspiring feat, but this may just be about the scale and... whisper it... recency bias. They should consider The Prestige as the film which continues to leave spectactors open-mouthed. The twists stun upon first viewing; its layers deepen with repeated watches; and it continues to impress 20 years later. “You don’t really want to know the secret; you want to be fooled.” Too true. The Prestige is not only the greatest film ever made about magic, but Nolan's finest achievement to date.

The Odyssey is out in cinemas now.

World.title: IRGC pledges 'unforgettable lesson' for US as Iran signals return to talks
World.content:
Iran's IRGC vowed on Monday to deliver an "unforgettable lesson" to the US, telling Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei in a formal statement that it regarded his message as "a binding command, a divine covenant and a clear roadmap," as Tehran simultaneously signalled that a return to talks remained possible if its national interests were respected.

 

"Now, as criminal America has once again chosen the path of error, aggression, and adventurism, we remain committed to this pledge: we will deliver, with power, determination, wisdom, and authority, the 'unforgettable lesson' that you promised," the IRGC said.

"A lesson that will prevent any aggressor from repeating its mistakes, break the ambitions of any aggressor, and record in history the truth of the Iranian nation's unwavering will."

The IRGC pledged it would "never tie the destiny of this land to the promises of an enemy whose record is filled with broken commitments, deception, and hostility toward the Iranian people."

The declaration came as Iranian and US forces exchanged strikes for the ninth consecutive day, as the US confirmed the deaths of at least three of its personnel.

Iran's Health Ministry said at least 50 people had been killed and more than 500 injured in US strikes on southern Iranian provinces since the start of July.

Cities in northwestern Iran, Tabriz and Urmia, were targeted for the first time in the latest wave of attacks, killing at least one person and injuring several others, according to Iranian state sources.

Two men wade in the waters of the Strait of Hormuz with vessels anchored in the background, off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Sunday, July 12, 2026. (Razieh Poudat/ISNA via AP) AP Photo

A Malta-flagged vessel also caught fire in Omani waters, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported, around 15 kilometres northwest of Kumzar.

IRGC-affiliated media said the ship was carrying Saudi oil bound for the United States and was using the southern approaches of the Strait of Hormuz. The fire had not been extinguished, and the vessel was drifting without power at the time of publication.

Diplomatic signals emerge amid continued strikes

Despite the military exchanges, Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said diplomacy remained open.

He described intermediaries as having exchanged messages with Iran in recent days and said Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni's visit to Islamabad was part of Tehran's response to those communications.

Momeni, who has a background in the IRGC, may be carrying a message from President Masoud Pezeshkian on possible negotiations, Iranian media reported.

Mediators have reportedly sought a 10-day ceasefire to revive the framework deal, which was put on ice last week after an apparent resumption of all-out hostilities.

Baghaei said diplomacy and military defence were "two powerful pillars" for protecting Iran's national interests. He said Article 5 of the interim deal gave Tehran a future role in discussions over Strait of Hormuz management with Oman and other regional countries, and contained no provision allowing the US to launch military action based on its own interpretation.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran, "or at least some people inside Iran," wanted to control the strait and use it as leverage.

"We're always open to diplomacy. It has to be real. It has to be a deal that they're willing to live by," he said before departing for the Philippines.

Iranian military officials have argued that fighting must continue until a new deterrence balance is established.

"Rationality dictates that the war should continue until it reaches a point where it creates complete deterrence for the Iranian nation," Brigadier General Akrami-Nia said.

Parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf accused Washington of bad faith.

"The Americans keep bringing new military equipment into the region while claiming they are seeking to end the war," he said.

Pezeshkian said Iran had not withdrawn from any provisions of the framework deal and would stand "until the last breath" in defending the country.

Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not appeared publicly since the start of the war, described Trump's signature on the interim ceasefire agreement as "worthless and invalid" in a message read out on state-run television.

The prolonged absence of the ayatollah has added uncertainty to an already opaque chain of command, with the IRGC increasingly visible as the key decision-making body in the ongoing war.

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.

World.title: US imposes new 50% tariff on many Canadian goods
World.content:
The tariffs will cover products including wine and hockey sticks, but not energy or fish. The move is the latest trade escalation between the US and its northern neighbor under the Trump administration.

US President Donald Trump's administration on Monday announced it was imposing 50% tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods.

The White House said the tariffs would take effect in 30 days and cover "products ranging from wine to hockey sticks to cement."

Trump signed the three proclamationsunder Section 338 of the Tariff Act ​of 1930 — a nearly century-old trade law that allows for tariffs of up to 50% on imports from ​specific countries.

However, the new tariffs will not apply to energy, potash (used in agricultural fertilizer), fish, critical minerals and goods already covered by existing tariffs under Section 232 of the law which relates to national security.

Trump threatens new Canada tariffs as wildfire smoke spreads To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

White House accuses Canada of 'discriminatory treatment'

The White House said the move was a response to Canada's "discriminatory treatment" of American goods.

Specifically, it said Canada imposed tariffs and quotas on US-manufactured cars that it did not apply to cars from other countries, and it said all but two Canadian states and territories have restricted the distribution of American alcohol.

"Over the past year and a half, only two countries have chosen to retaliate against President Trump’s tariffs rather than negotiate a deal with the United States: the People’s Republic of China and Canada," the White House said.

World.title: Iran war: US launches fresh strikes as Trump vows revenge
World.content:
07/20/2026 July 20, 2026 US launches fresh strikes on Iran

The US has launched strikes on Iran for the 10th night in a row.

"The strikes are designed to further degrade Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz," the US military's Central Command said on social media.

Iran's semi-official Mehr News Agency reported that air defenses were activated near the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant on the southern coast. The complex has been hit by previous waves of US strikes.

Strikes between the US and Iran have escalated in an attempt to control the Strait of Hormuz.

On Friday, Iranian strike on an air base in Jordan killed two US service members and left a third unaccounted for. Another US soldier was reported dead in Iraq on Saturday due to a "controlled detonation" of a downed Iranian drone.

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that whenever Iran killed an American soldier, they would "pay for that killing many times over."

World.title: Mexican drug lord ‘El Mayo’ sentenced to life without parole in US prison
World.content:
Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada, a co-founder of the Sinaloa cartel and one of the world's most notorious drug traffickers, was sentenced to life in a US prison.

Mexican drug trafficker Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole on Tuesday for co-founding and leading the notorious Sinaloa cartel.

Zambada was one of the most prominent Mexican drug traffickers to face sentencing in a United States court since Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman was sentenced to life in prison in 2019.

"The almost unimaginable amount of drugs attributable to him and the number of murders that we can document is enough to justify Congress's decision to make this a mandatory life sentence," US District Judge Brian Cogan said.

The 76-year-old Zambada apologized "for the harm I caused and for the example I set," urging future generations to "choose a different path."

Zambada apologizes before sentencing

He was arrested in July 2024 after he said he was kidnapped in Mexico and flown to Texas.

Zambada helped found and lead the Sinaloa cartel, becoming one of the most wanted figures for US intelligence and law enforcement agencies for decades.

According to prosecutors, he ordered torture and plotted murders, including the killing of his own nephew, as the cartel flooded the US with tons of cocaine, fentanyl, methamphetamine and other drugs.

U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said Zambada had spent nearly four decades 'poisoning American communities' for profit and ordering the murders of anyone who stood in his way, and that all ended with his sentencing Image: Leonardo Munoz/AFP

He pleaded guilty to charges that included engaging in a continuing criminal enterprise and racketeering conspiracy, acknowledging culpability for 85 underlying crimes. In exchange, prosecutors did not seek the death penalty.

"I grew up in an environment where violence and crime seemed normal, but now I know that's no excuse," Zambada said in court on Monday. "There comes a time when every person must take responsibility for their decisions. I didn't, and many people paid the price."

"El Chapo" partner joins cartel leaders serving life terms

Zambada's former partner "El Chapo" is already serving a life sentence in the United States.

He was convicted in 2019 and is serving a life sentence at the federal Supermax prison in Florence, Colorado.

Together they built the Sinaloa cartel into one of the world's most powerful drug trafficking organizations.

Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman was sentenced to ​life in prisonin 2019 Image: Paul Ratje/REUTERS

The Sinaloa cartel is one of six Mexican drug gangs that US President Donald Trump has designated as Foreign Terrorist Organizations.

Zambada was arrested with El Chapo's son, Joaquin Guzman Lopez, one of El Chapo's sons, who has pleaded guilty to federal drug charges. He has yet to be sentenced.

Zambada's arrest led to a splintering of the Sinaloa cartel, pitting his loyalists against backers of Guzman's sons, dubbed the Chapitos, or "little Chapos."

World.title: AliExpress hit with record EU fine
World.content:
The Chinese retailer has become the latest major online marketplace to face penalties under the EU’s Digital Services Act.

AliExpress said it plans to appeal a penalty imposed by European Union (EU) regulators, who found shortcomings in the firm's efforts to curb illegal, unsafe and counterfeit goods.

The largest Chinese e-commerce platform in the EU, AliExpress, has been fined €550 million ($629 million) for failing to tackle sales of illegal, unsafe and counterfeit products.

"The spread of counterfeit clothing, unsafe toys, dangerous cosmetics and other illegal and harmful products is not an unavoidable cost of shopping online - it is a failure by AliExpress to comply with its obligations under the Digital Services Act," European Commission Vice President Henna Virkkunen said on Monday.

It is the largest fine ever imposed under the Digital Services Act (DSA), which sets out clear rules for online services in the EU, targeting especially very large online platforms.

AliExpress said it will appeal the "disproportionate" fine, saying it considers the penalty excessive.

AliExpress faces October 20 deadline

The online retail giant, which belongs to the Alibaba Group, must pay the fine and has until October 20, to submit a plan to address the breaches. EU regulators will then review the plan, after which the company could face further penalties.

A year ago, AliExpress agreed to tighten controls on illegal and potentially dangerous goods, such as medicines and supplements. But the European Commission said the measures did not fully resolve its broader concerns.

The commission said AliExpress:

Failed in some cases to penalize traders selling illegal products, allowing them to continue operating on the platform.

Lacked sufficient staff to effectively review potentially illegal listings.

Inspectors faced excessive workloads, hampering oversight efforts.

Some illegal products were recommended or promoted before being removed from the platform.

But AliExpress said the EU's decision "ignores our sound risk management framework and the significant, proactive enhancements we have made."

The company also said it has worked with the Commission to meet its "evolving expectations."

DSA used to rein in Big Tech

According to the EU, AliExpress has 193 million users in the bloc, ahead of online fashion giant Shein and retailer Temu, which have 156 million and 130 million users, respectively.

"One in five Europeans say they shop once a month from Shein, Temu and AliExpress," Virkkunen said.

Temu was fined €200 million in May, while Elon Musk's social media platform X was fined in December last year, both for DSA violations.

World.title: England and Liverpool foortball legend Kevin Keegan dies aged 75
World.content:
English former striker and manager Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75 after a battle with cancer. He was a two-time European footballer of the year with Hamburg.

The death of Kevin Keegan, regarded as one of the greatest football players of his generation, was announced in a statement released by his family on Monday.

"It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75," the statement read.

"Kevin had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments. A double Ballon d'Or winner, Kevin was a much-loved husband, father and grandfather."

Born in Doncaster, South Yorkshire on February 14, 1951, Keegan got his big break when he was signed by Liverpool's legendary manager Bill Shankly in 1971.

At Anfield, Keegan struck up a striking partnership with Welshman John Toshack, going on to win the First Division title three times as well as the FA Cup, the UEFA Cup twice and the 1977 European Cup. He made 323 appearances, scoring 100 goals for Liverpool.

Success in the Bundesliga

From Merseyside, Keegan moved on to the Bundesliga's Hamburg, where he was twice named European Footballer of the Year, which is now called the Ballon d'Or, in 1978 and 1979. With Hamburg, he won the Bundesliga in 1978-79 and played in another European Cup final, a 1980 loss to Nottingham Forest. He left the club having scored 32 goals in 90 appearances.

Hamburg were among the former teams to pay tribute to Keegan in a statement on their website on Monday.

"In Kevin Keegan, world football loses one of its most defining figures. Hamburger SV will always cherish the memory of its former title-winning player and two-time Ballon d'Or winner," the statement said.

Our thoughts are with his family, his friends, and all those who shared his journey. Rest in peace, "Mighty Mouse."

Return to England

Following his stint in West Germany, Keegan returned to England with Southampton in the summer of 1980 before moving to Second Division Newcastle, helping the club win promotion back to the top flight – before retiring as a player.

He won 63 England caps, scoring 21 goals, playing at the 1982 World Cup and was also later captain of the national team.

Stepping into management

In 1992, Keegan moved into management at Newcastle, leading them into the Premier League and to within touching distance of the 1995-96 title, but they missed out to Manchester United.

The club also paid tribute to Keegan in a statement issued on Monday afternoon, describing him as "the beating heart of Newcastle for generations of supporters."

After leaving St James' Park in January 1997, a brief stint at Fulham followed before he became England manager in 1999. After overseeing a disappointing Euro 2000 campaign, Keegan resigned minutes after a 1-0 defeat by Germany in World Cup qualifying, the last match played at the original Wembley Stadium.

He later managed Manchester City, before returning to Newcastle.

Keegan's family had revealed in January that he had been diagnosed with cancer, which later spread to stage four.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

World.title: Russia says bus strike kills 5 in border region with Ukraine
World.content:
The strike comes as Ukraine launched more than hundreds of drones at Moscow after a Russian missile barrage on Kyiv, as President Zelenskyy sought to calm growing tensions over Ukraine’s military leadership.

Russia said Monday that a Ukrainian strike on a bus in the border region of Belgorod killed five civilians, including a minor, and left three others critically injured.

The attack came after a Ukrainian retaliatory strike on Moscow, with city officials reporting that more than 400 drones targeted the Russian capital.

The latest escalation followed Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities over the weekend.

Russian strikes targeted the eastern cities of Pavlograd and Kramatorsk in Ukraine Image: REUTERS

In eastern Ukraine, Russian attacks on Pavlograd and Kramatorsk killed two people in each city, according to local authorities.

Officials also reported one person killed in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia during Russian bombardment.

Both sides have previously denied targeting civilians.

Ukraine launches large-scale drone attack on Moscow

Ukraine targeted the Russian capital with more than 400 drones from Sunday into Monday, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.

He added that most of the drones were intercepted, but Moscow region Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said at least 10 people were wounded by Ukrainian drones.

Several residential buildings and civilian infrastructure facilities were also damaged.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces were targeting Russian logistics facilities and an oil depot in the region.

"We are responding, justly, to every Russian strike against our cities and communities," Zelenskyy said in a post on X.

Ukraine rejects rumors of military leadership shake-up

Meanwhile, Ukraine's military publicly denied rumors that Zelenskyy was firing the chief of Ukraine's armed forces, Oleksandr Syrskyi.

Zelenskyy has faced criticism over the dismissal of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov last week.

There have been days of protests in Ukraine following Fedorov's removal, as a long-running dispute between the reform-minded minister and Syrskyi spilled into the open.

Zelenskyy appointed Yevhenii Khmara, the acting head of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU), as acting defense minister and asked parliament to approve him for the position.

On Monday, he posted several messages on social media showing him meeting with Ukraine's top military commanders to discuss the latest developments in the war, which has dragged on for more than four years.
