World.title: Whistleblower's fight to unmask one of WA's worst child abusers
World.content:
As one of Western Australia's most monstrous serial paedophiles approaches the end of his prison term, the whistleblower who helped bring his crimes to light is publishing her account of the story.

WARNING - This story contains descriptions of sexual abuse and self-harm that some readers may find distressing.

Dennis John McKenna abused 28 boys over the course of two decades while serving as warden of the St Andrew's Hostel in Katanning, 287 kilometres south-east of Perth in WA's Great Southern.

Made aware of the abuse shortly after arriving in town in 1985, Maggie Dawkins reported McKenna's horrific crimes to local police, a local councillor and state government authorities.

No-one listened, and she was run out of town.

The abuse continued for years as a result.

While the demolition of the site in 2024 wiped the location of McKenna's crimes from the map, Mrs Dawkins's account, entitled To Be Believed — A West Australian Scandal, captures the harrowing story of those who survived his abuses, and the serious failings of WA authorities to stop him.

The Katanning Residential College was bulldozed in 2025. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

Trusted with harrowing story

Mrs Dawkins became aware of the first of many of those stories shortly after arriving in Katanning in 1985, working for a government-backed youth employment and support program.

She said one boy approached her, trusting her with his and his friends' stories in the hope of halting the abuse.

"I'd never heard the word rapist. I didn't know what it was," she said.

Maggie Dawkins played a vital role in exposing Dennis McKenna. (ABC News: Shannon Pearce)

"This young man, who was clearly distressed and embarrassed and all those dreadful feelings of shame, was trying to explain to me that this was going on at the hostel on a regular basis.

"I didn't know how to cope with this."

But reports to her line manager, local police and a local councillor fell on deaf ears.

Local figures berated her for "besmirching" McKenna, who had recently been named Katanning's Citizen of the Year.

Confronting the abuser

Mrs Dawkins took matters into her own hands and confronted McKenna herself.

She said she approached him and he told her he had "friends in high places".

" As he was throwing me out of town, he told me he had friends in high places. He held all the cards. "

It was not until years later, when the Blaxell inquiry investigated abuse at the hostel, that Mrs Dawkins realised just how many people knew of the abuse and did nothing.

"It just made me sick. It was incredibly soul-destroying," she said.

"The kids and parents of the kids who attended the hostel never had a chance."

Years waiting for justice

Mrs Dawkins then spent the next five years trying to unmask the ongoing abuse inside the walls of St Andrew's, which was later rebadged as the Katanning Residential College.

McKenna used the hostel as a base to sexually abuse school-aged boys. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

In 1990, five years after she raised the alarm, Operation Paradox, a national police effort to raise awareness of child sex abuse and encourage victim survivors to come forward, resulted in multiple complaints against McKenna.

He was arrested soon after, and eventually found guilty of 19 offences.

Since then, McKenna has been charged with a further 44 offences for the abuse of 28 boys, and remains locked up at Acacia Prison in Wooroloo east of Perth.

McKenna is due to complete his prison sentence later this year. (ABC News)

Why come forward

Both Mrs Dawkins's brave fight and her account have been lauded by those who survived McKenna's abuse.

After a football game in August 1990, McKenna sexually abused Todd Jefferis.

The unvarnished story of the abuse and grooming he suffered features throughout the book.

St Andrew's Hostel survivor Todd Jefferis spearheaded the campaign to demolish the building. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Mr Jefferis said Mrs Dawkins's work provides a platform for other whistleblowers to speak out about abuse.

"It certainly tells the truth about what really went on and how far-reaching it was," he said.

" If you've been abused or are being abused, the ability to go and speak out and have someone believe you is incredibly important. "

McKenna's evil left a deep scar on Kaye Anderson's family.

Her eldest sons, Ray and Quenton, were targeted and sexually abused by McKenna in 1985.

Ray, Quenton, Bevan, Nathan and Damian Anderson. (Supplied: Kaye Anderson)

Mrs Anderson also lost sons Nathan and Damien, in what she believes to be a direct result of their older brothers' deaths.

She said Mrs Dawkins revealed more of the story than she ever understood.

"I absolutely applaud her for standing up to an absolute mongrel bastard," she said.

"I just pray to God that it will [encourage more people to come forward]."

Listen to Maggie Dawkins's interview with Nadia Mitsopoulos on 102.5 ABC Perth and on local radio across WA from 9am today.

World.title: Football world 'devastated' by death of English icon Keegan
World.content:
Former England captain and manager Kevin Keegan has died aged 75.

Keegan's family and Newcastle United revealed in January that the two-time European Footballer of the Year was undergoing cancer treatment, without disclosing details of his illness. His death was confirmed by Newcastle overnight.

Last month, Keegan, who was nicknamed "King Kev" and "Mighty Mouse" and was one of the most influential figures of his generation in English football, revealed he had stage four cancer.

Fans lay flowers at St James' Park, Newcastle United's home ground, in memory of Keegan after his death. (Getty Images: Owen Humphreys)

"We are devastated to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan, one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club's history," Newcastle said in a statement.

"As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James' Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be.

"As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an entertainer."

Glittering career as player and manager

Keegan became one of English football's biggest superstars in his time with Liverpool from 1971-77. (Getty Images: Harry Ormesher)

Keegan began his career at Scunthorpe United before joining Liverpool in 1971.

He made 323 appearances for Liverpool in all competitions, scoring 100 goals over six seasons. He won three First Division titles, the FA Cup, two UEFA Cups and the 1977 European Cup during a glittering spell at Anfield.

After moving to Hamburg, Keegan was named European Footballer of the Year in 1978 and 1979, becoming the only British player to win the Ballon d'Or twice. He later returned to England to play for Southampton and Newcastle before retiring in 1984 at the age of 33.

Keegan scored 21 goals in 63 appearances for England between 1972 and 1982, captaining the side 31 times.

He moved into management at Newcastle in 1992, guiding the club into the Premier League and transforming it into one of England's most entertaining sides.

Keegan's team came agonisingly close to winning the 1995-96 Premier League title before they were overtaken by Manchester United.

Although the title race did not go Keegan's way, his rant aimed at United manager Sir Alex Ferguson in the heat of the race went down in football folklore.

After leaving St James' Park in January 1997, he had a brief spell at Fulham before taking charge of England in 1999 following Glenn Hoddle's departure.

He resigned after Euro 2000 and a defeat by Germany at Wembley Stadium, famously saying he was "not good enough" to do the job, at a media conference. He won seven of his 18 matches in charge.

Keegan later managed Manchester City before leaving the club in March 2005 and initially announcing his retirement from football. He made an emotional return to Newcastle in 2008, though his second spell at the club lasted only eight months.

A lasting legacy

A statement from Keegan's family, quoted by British media, said on Monday: "It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75.

"The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments."

Tributes poured in for Keegan, with Liverpool saying in a statement: "Our 'Mighty Mouse', his legacy at Liverpool will be forever etched in history."

England Football wrote on X: "We are incredibly saddened by the news that Kevin Keegan OBE has passed away," while former Newcastle striker Alan Shearer wrote: "My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss".

Reuters

World.title: Council's beach access changes spark accessibility concerns
World.content:
Elisa Wood says her 12-year-old daughter, Sophie, loves sitting on the beach watching the family's border collie while her brother and father surf.

But that is no longer possible after the Sunshine Coast Council changed its dog policy across the region, leaving the family's local off-leash beach at Point Cartwright only accessible via stairs.

"Getting down the steps or walking across an extended soft sand is just not physically manageable for her or us," Ms Wood said.

Her daughter was born with polymicrogyria, a congenital brain condition which means she is non-verbal and frequently requires a wheelchair.

Elisa Wood says family time has become "disjointed". (ABC News: Nykayla Dux)

"It was a space where we could be in a beautiful environment with our puppy dog and Soph, and that's not really achievable now," Ms Wood said.

"It is really disappointing."

Environmental concerns drive changes

Council's new laws, which changed where dogs can go across the Sunshine Coast and reduced the size and number of dog beaches, came into effect on July 3.

There are no wheelchair-friendly off-leash dog beaches across the nearly 50 kilometres of coastline between Peregian Beach and Golden Beach.

Four beaches, Mooloolaba, Alexandra Headland, Caloundra and Dicky Beach, do have capacity to support accessible access, but equipment, including wheelchair matting, must be pre-arranged with the local surf lifesaving club.

None of these beaches permit dogs.

In a statement to the ABC, a council representative said the changes were to balance dog exercise opportunities with community safety, shared use of public spaces and environmental protection.

The council representative said the process involved a Human Rights Assessment and "extensive community consultation" including with representatives from disability organisations.

Elisa Wood (centre) says the council changes are "really disappointing". (ABC News: Nykayla Dux)

"Council recognise that beaches and parks play an important role in recreation, connection and wellbeing for our community, and acknowledges that changes to familiar places can be difficult."

The council did not respond to the ABC's questions about providing access to a dog beach for people with disabilities but referred to its 2024-2028 All Abilities Action Plan online.

The five-year plan currently does not specify plans for an accessible dog beach.

Richard Fuller from the University of Queensland's School of the Environment said dogs in South-East Queensland were a "major source of disturbance" for migratory shorebirds that travelled thousands of kilometres from Siberia and Alaska.

"It's already illegal to significantly disturb migratory birds, so council does have an obligation to act in this space," Professor Fuller said.

"Importantly, a controlled dog has a much smaller impact than one running loose."

Disability groups call for compromise

Queenslanders with Disability Network said an accessible off-leash beach was one of very few, genuinely inclusive recreation spaces for people with disability.

"Losing that tends to bring isolation, with real flow-on effects for mental health and community belonging," deputy chief executive officer Paige Armstrong said.

Ms Armstrong said addressing environmental concerns could be managed while ensuring accessibility.

"Environmental protection and accessibility don't have to be a trade-off," she said.

"That means retaining or creating a genuinely accessible pathway to at least one off-leash area and co-designing any changes with the people who actually use the space."

Paige Armstrong says beach accessibility is important. (Supplied: Queenslanders with Disability Network)

Less than 2 per cent of beaches across Australia are accessible

Accessible Beaches Australia works toward creating more equitable beach access nationally.

Project officer Bern Walker said the council's change was "extremely disappointing".

"Out of the 12,000 beaches in Australia, less than 2 per cent are actually accessible to people with disabilities and mobility limitations, and very few of those are accessible all the time," she said.

"By not including access for [people with disability], the message that you're saying is you are not welcome and you are less valued than other people in society."

Bern Walker (right) from Accessible Beaches Australia with founder Shane Hryhorec. (Supplied: Accessible Beaches Australia)

Ms Walker said community and stakeholder engagement was crucial.

Ms Wood said she was involved in the council's community consultation phase, including submitting feedback advocating for accessibility, however felt "overwhelmingly ignored".

"It's really disheartening when that process just seems to have very little impact on the decision-making.

"I would love them to reconsider and create more balance to allow even just limited access for people like Sophie and our family with their dogs so that we can share the area like everyone else."

In a statement, council said there was no intention to review the policy and a formal review would only commence in 2030.

World.title: PM backs bid for future NT AFL team, no promises on funding
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has backed the prospect of an AFL team in the Northern Territory, but has stayed tight-lipped on whether his government would help fund it to get off the ground.

With a 20th AFL licence up for grabs, the NT has been touted as one of the top options to take it home, with Western Australia and the ACT also billed as possible contenders.

It comes as Tasmania prepares to enter the AFL with the Devils in 2028, bringing the competition a step closer to becoming truly representative of each state and territory.

This year's Tiwi Islands grand final marks the first time a sitting PM has ever attended the iconic match. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Despite being known as a breeding ground for some of the competition's most exciting talent, from regions like Gove and the Tiwi Islands, the NT has never had a top-tier team.

Mr Albanese visited the Tiwi Islands on Sunday, the first time a prime minister has travelled to the islands north of Darwin in more than 25 years, where he voiced his support for an NT team.

"I'd love to see a team here in the territory, as I'm sure all Territorians would," he said.

"It's a while off, [but] we'll continue to talk and engage with the AFL as well."

Anthony Albanese met with local players at the Tiwi Islands grand final on the weekend. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Mr Albanese was asked whether the Commonwealth would help finance an AFL team in the NT as it has done to help create an NRL team in Papua New Guinea.

"I don't run the AFL, so I'll wait, and certainly any submissions from the AFL [for funding] would be welcome," he said.

"We'll engage constructively with the AFL as well.

" The Northern Territory has a great history of producing great footballers. "

'We have the raw talent'

Reacting to the prime minister's comments, Northern Land Council (NLC) chair Matt Ryan said an AFL team would bring huge social benefits to the jurisdiction.

'Work to do': AFL targets Indigenous player boost The AFL is considering a range of measures to boost the number of Indigenous players in the league following a significant decline in recent seasons.

"We have the raw talent, and I think we can do it," he said.

"I would push that 100 per cent."

When asked if the NLC would be prepared to consider helping with funding the establishment of a team, alongside possible federal financial support, Mr Ryan said, "I think we should all chip in".

"It's our team and I think we should sponsor or support them," he said.

Mr Ryan said he believed the establishment of an NT team would help offset the falling number of Indigenous players in the league.

Tiwi Islands women's footy player Mara Munkara, who played in the weekend's grand final, said an NT team would "mean a lot to the Tiwi people".

"It could bring excitement, everyone happy, everyone around Northern Territory," she said.

Mara Munkara says an NT AFL team would bring a lot of excitement to the Territory. (ABC News Pete Garnish)

A task force has been formed in the NT to try to build the case a local team to be created.

A business case published in 2024 included the recommendation for the federal government to fund construction of a new stadium in Darwin's CBD, to help bolster the jurisdiction's chances for a team.

The AFL has been contacted for comment.

World.title: 'Surreal' sense of grief at packed town meeting after alleged Layla Jeffery murder
World.content:
More than 300 people filled the Donald Memorial Hall in western Victoria last night for an emotional public meeting about the alleged murder of 13-year-old Layla Jeffery.

Remains believed to be Layla's were found in bushland near the Richardson River close to the Donald Police Station on July 9, and a 16-year-old boy has since been charged with murder.

Residents submitted dozens of questions to police and council before the meeting, hoping for an update on the investigation.

Senior Detective Inspector Dave Dunstan addresses the Donald community at a meeting on Monday night. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

Authorities were able to answer some questions. But they repeatedly told the crowd there were others they simply could not.

Mental health support agencies also addressed the crowd. They acknowledged there was a lot of "anger" in the community.

They described that emotion as a normal stage of grief.

Layla Jeffery, 13, was last seen in Donald on July 4. (Suppied: Victoria Police)

'This will take time'

Victoria Police Senior Detective Inspector Dave Dunstan said police would continue visiting Donald for at least another two months as they follow up leads, review evidence and revisit key locations.

They warned court proceedings could take years to finalise and told the community not to expect a quick resolution.

"This will take time," Senior Detective Inspector Dunstan said.

"We don't want to give anyone false hope that this will be resolved quickly."

Police said they could not give specific answers about the case because doing so could risk the integrity of the court proceedings and coroner's inquiry.

Police search for evidence in the Richardson River in the days after Layla Jeffrey’s body was found. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

"If we start discussing evidence here, we risk jeopardising the case," senior Detective Inspector Dunstan said.

He said authorities were being particularly cautious because the alleged murderer was a child in custody who is set to face the Children's Court.

A line search being conducted in Donald. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

Mayor's warning

Buloke Mayor Cr Graeme Milne delivered a blunt warning to the community about what he described as "very insensitive" rumours and speculation circling on social media.

"There's been a number of text messages and emails, and other social media stuff where people are building a platform for themselves," Cr Milne said.

Buloke mayor Graeme Milne addressed 300 community members at the Donald Memorial Hall. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

"We've seen suspicion and innuendo that probably has no basis. It doesn't help the inquiry, and it doesn't help Layla's family."

He said unsubstantiated claims were fuelling anger in the town that was already reeling.

"A lot of this finds its way back to family and friends," Cr Milne said.

"They don't need that sort of stuff circulating around. Neither do councillors or support agencies."

The mayor told the crowd to "pull up" anyone spreading misinformation or disinformation.

"We're not going to put up with it," Cr Milne said.

" If we have to, police will call on people making untruths, and I will not defend them. "

Thanks for 'thorough investigation'

Cr Milne said many community members wanted to know more about the alleged murderer.

He told the ABC, authorities were "extremely limited" in what they could say about the teenage boy's background and history.

"They are genuine questions, but they don't all need to be answered yet," Cr Milne said.

"We are not going to do anything that jeopardises this case."

He said he understood if community members found that frustrating.

Mayor Graeme Milne laying flowers at Layla's memorial in Donald. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

"But if we have to put up with this for another couple of years to get the right outcome, then that's what we'll do," Cr Milne said.

" The community doesn't want anything less than a thorough investigation. "

Jodie Hollis, administrator at community progress group Donald2000, said the town was grappling with a "surreal" sense of grief.

"I can understand how everyone's so inquisitive, but it will all come out in time," Ms Hollis said.

Jodie Hollis speaks with the mayor at the community event in Donald. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

Ms Hollis said the community was grateful for the ongoing police presence in town and said most community members were feeling safe at home.

She said the size of the meeting showed how strongly the town had pulled together in response to the tragedy.

Community support

Lifeline, Headspace and other support agencies were in attendance.

They described the alleged murder as a community-wide trauma that would take years to work through.

Red Cross was among the support services at the meeting in Donald. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

They urged people to seek help early and encouraged people to use crisis support lines if needed.

Cr Milne said council would, in time, analyse what had happened and what the community had learned to inform an improved "health and wellbeing plan" for the shire.

"There will be learnings from this that we put into our next plan," Cr Milne said.

"But it's too early now to start rejigging things while the whole saga is still unfolding."

World.title: ‘Baked bean cans’: Emirates boss to reject Boeing planes
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation ‘Baked bean cans’: Emirates boss to reject Boeing planes Christopher Jasper July 21, 2026 — 8:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Boeing has been dealt a fresh blow after Emirates said it would refuse to take delivery of 10 aircraft, claiming that the much-delayed jets would be better off being turned into baked bean tins. The Dubai airline has ordered a total of 270 new 777X planes from Boeing at $US440 million ($629 million) apiece, with the first jet built in 2019. But repeated delays stemming from design modifications has meant Emirates is still waiting for the planes seven years later. Emirates president Sir Tim Clark said the company was unwilling to take the 10 aircraft because the design of the 777X had undergone so many significant changes that bringing them up to the latest standard would not be feasible. Bloomberg Sir Tim Clark, the president of Emirates, said the initial batch of 10 of the jets required such a patchwork of changes to update them that they were not fit for purpose. “We’re not taking that batch and that’s it,” he told The Telegraph at the Farnborough International Airshow. “As far as we’re concerned, what they do with them is up to them.”



Clark said he understood that Boeing had been trying to find a home for the aircraft, before adding: “Heinz would be interested – baked bean cans.” Related Article Exclusive

Aviation Some A380s grounded amid emergency inspections for wing spar cracks His refusal to take the planes will serve as a new setback to Boeing, which has been rocked by a string of safety crises in recent years. Clark said Emirates was unwilling to take the 10 aircraft because the design of the 777X had undergone so many significant changes that bringing them up to the latest standard would not be feasible. The 777X has suffered numerous problems that have pushed back entry into service from 2020 to next year at the earliest.



Those issues have included a thrust control issue that halted test flights in 2024 and an incident in 2020 that saw an aircraft’s nose pitch up without pilot input, delaying the programme by years. Clark said the airline was also concerned by the earlier-than-expected structural failure of a 777X during a ground-based stress test of the airframe. Emirates’ refusal to take the planes will serve as a new setback to Boeing, which has been rocked by a string of safety crises in recent years. AP He added: “The modifications for the airframe have been so significant since the early flights. And don’t forget we had a static-test failure as well.” He added: “I went on the first one in 2019, which was fully configured except for our first-class cabins, and here we are in 2026. It’s now seven years on. We’re not taking them.”



His comments came after it emerged one of the planes earmarked for Emirates had already been scrapped. The 400-seat plane was quietly “disassembled” in 2025 after sitting dormant for six years on an airfield close to Boeing’s Seattle manufacturing centre, The Air Current reported. Stephanie Pope, the head of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, said changes were made to the aircraft “as the maturity of the design progresses”. She said: “If you look at those early airplanes, you’ve then got to weigh how much change it’s going to take and the benefit from that. “We are always looking at how much that change is going to cost and what will be the capability of the airplane, and making sure we’re getting the right solution not only for Boeing, but for our customer.”



Related Article Billionaires Bezos’ whirlwind visit: How do the rich and famous get to the beach so fast? Flight tests on the 777-9, the first version of the new 777X plane, should be completed by the end of this year, after which the model will need to show it is capable of flying for long distances over water on a single engine, according to analysts at Jefferies. That should pave the way for the first aircraft to be delivered to Lufthansa before the end of 2027. Asked when British Airways expected to receive the first of 24 planes it has on order, Sean Doyle, its chief executive, said simply: “Good question.” Telegraph, London The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Officials got three of seven calls wrong at the weekend. Apart from that, the NRL was happy Christian Nicolussi Updated July 21, 2026 — 7:54am ,first published 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney Roosters forward Nat Butcher should not have been penalised for a high tackle, Melbourne were denied a legitimate try, and Manly’s Reuben Garrick was offside when he scored against the Titans. Aside from those three clangers, the NRL was more than satisfied with a string of other controversial calls made by referees and the bunker over the weekend. Loading This masthead pinpointed at least seven contentious calls in five games that were heavily criticised by coaches, players and commentators. They did not include queries St George Illawarra had with Valentine Holmes being penalised for an obstruction and Setu Tu being denied a try by a bunker ruling.



We revealed the bunker’s decision-making efficiency rate sat at an impressive 98 per cent just a month ago. But fans have been in the dark about the reasoning behind refereeing calls since the NRL scrapped head of football Graham Annesley’s weekly press conference a couple of years ago. In the hope of achieving some clarity, we asked the NRL for its thoughts about the weekend calls. Were Penrith robbed? The Panthers thought they had won a repeat set – and a chance to win the game – with two minutes of Thursday night’s match left after Brisbane’s Josiah Karapani was dragged into touch. Referee Todd Smith ruled a knock-on, which Penrith successfully challenged – but the bunker ruled Smith had blown the whistle before Karapani was taken into touch. Because it was a “mutual infringement”, Karapani was instructed to play the ball, rather than Penrith receive the ball back.



Penrith coach Ivan Cleary said after the game: “If we get the ball there, and we should have got it ... it’s just one of those nights”. The NRL, however, formed the view the decision was technically correct because the whistle was blown simultaneously as Karapani was being pushed into touch. If anything, Penrith could have been penalised for the second effort. Roosters Butchered Coaches Trent Robinson and Craig Bellamy both took issue with a few calls during Friday night’s Storm-Roosters clash.



Robinson was stunned Butcher was penalised for a high tackle on Alec MacDonald, which allowed Melbourne to march downfield and score two minutes later. Nat Butcher’s ‘hit’ on Alec Macdonald. Nine “It was completely laughable,” Robinson said of the penalty. The NRL agreed it should not have been given. Did Warbrick knock on? Bellamy could not understand why the Storm were denied a try in the first half, when Will Warbrick appeared to knock a ball back from a kick, only for Gerard Sutton to rule it a knock-on.



Bellamy broke into one of his famous colourful rants in the coach’s box. After several slow-motion reviews, the NRL were satisfied Warbrick got his hand in front of the ball and knocked it back. Walker shot clock Roosters halfback Sam Walker appeared to have taken a dropout after the shot-clock buzzer sounded in the 67th minute, which would have given Melbourne a penalty kick from in front to level the scores.



Loading “Six to eight weeks ago, we got done for taking too long with a line drop-out,” Bellamy said. But the NRL was satisfied the Walker kick and shot-clock buzzer were simultaneous, so Sutton was entitled to wave play-on. Similar situations occur on occasions with scrum-clocks. Was Dom Young taken out? Cronulla opened their account against the Knights with a try to Will Kennedy on Friday evening, but Ronnie Mulitalo appeared to deny Newcastle winger Dominic Young a fair chance at leaping for the ball.



Braydon Trindall sent the ball up, Mulitalo chased, but barely got off the ground – yet still did enough to impede Young. The NRL was comfortable Mulitalo had not taken his eyes off the ball, never looked at Young and had both arms extended in a catching position before he jumped, which meant there was a genuine contest, and no need to rule a “disruptor” penalty. Red V see red The Dragons have worked hard to address their sluggish second-half starts, so you could forgive them for being cranky when the Warriors went ahead in the 44th minute via Dallin Watene-Zelezniak from what they felt was a forward pass.



“It’s just not right,” co-captain Damien Cook said. “I feel sorry for the fans that have to watch that. But it’s happened too many times to us.” The NRL was comfortable it was not a forward pass, and other camera angles not shown on the live broadcast supported this view. Did Garrick jump the gun? Titans skipper Tino Fa’asuamaleaui made a beeline for referee Adam Gee after Reuben Garrick scored for Manly in the second half, wanting to know if the Manly centre was offside.



“It happened to Max Plath in Origin, that was the call; are you serious?” Fa’asuamaleaui asked Gee, referring to the Maroons being denied a try in similar circumstances in Origin III only a few weeks earlier. The decision did not cost the Gold Coast the win – and just as well, because the NRL, based on the available footage, believed Garrick was “marginally offside”. World.title: Joey Manu’s $1.6m contract call signals latest shift in cross-code talent stoush
World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 Joey Manu’s $1.6m contract call signals latest shift in cross-code talent stoush Dan Walsh Updated July 21, 2026 — 7:29am ,first published 11:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The PNG Chiefs are emerging as the NRL’s trump card in the cross-code battle for elite athletes as Joey Manu considers a multimillion dollar return to rugby league with the incoming franchise. Manu and his family toured the Chiefs’ Port Moresby facilities on Monday and the ex-Roosters star has been in talks with PNG officials for several weeks over a marquee deal to join Willie Peters’ inaugural 2028 roster. Loading Fellow code-hopper Zac Lomax is expected to make the same trip to PNG in the next week as he weighs up his own multi-year offer to make an NRL comeback with the Chiefs. Manu has been holidaying in New Zealand since the end of the French Rugby Top 14 season, where he has another year remaining on his contract with Racing 92.



The 29-year-old will return to France in September, where his deal is estimated to be worth as much as €1 million ($1.6 million) a season. French rugby’s four-month off-season had prompted the Warriors to enquire about Manu taking up a short-term NRL return this season, though that was ultimately knocked back by the Kiwi star. Former Rooster Joey Manu and his family at Port Moresby airport on Monday. A similar move from late May next year could yet make Manu an elite mid-2027 signing for NRL clubs. Sources speaking on the condition of anonymity due to ongoing negotiations have told this masthead that 2027 will be Manu’s last campaign in European rugby as he looks to move back closer to family in New Zealand.



A return to Japanese rugby, where Manu first landed in 2024 after wrapping up a 181-game Roosters career, is still a possibility. However, Manu is genuinely considering the PNG move given it offers a return to rugby league and the Chiefs are the only NRL outfit that can truly compete with the spending power of overseas rugby clubs. Joey Manu left the NRL as one of the best players in the game. NRL Imagery Manu’s current wage in France is roughly double the $800,000 the Roosters could offer him during his final year at the club, when he was widely regarded as the best centre in the game. The NRL’s salary cap is predicted to rise to at least $15 million in 2028, thanks to the record $5.3 billion broadcast deal.



But even with that potential 24 per cent increase, PNG would be the only NRL side able to match Manu’s potential earnings in overseas rugby without destabilising their salary cap due to their ability to offer players tax-free wages. The Roosters have repeatedly been mentioned in terms of bringing Manu back to the NRL, but this masthead reported in April that the club privately gave up that hope given his earning power in the rival code. Zac Lomax’s potential return to rugby league is gaining momentum. Getty Images Mark Nawaqanitawase has set the NRL alight in his two years of playing rugby league, but he will earn more than double his Tricolours wage when he links with Japan’s Saitama Wild Knights at the end of the year. Lomax, meanwhile, took a significant pay cut to join the Western Force after going all in on the aborted R360 project. He knocked back an approach to join the Storm next year and is chasing a Wallabies debut with an eye to playing in the 2027 World Cup.



Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Dean Young lands Dragons coaching job after challenge from old teammate Beyond that, either overseas rugby or linking with the Chiefs in 2028 present as the former NSW Origin star’s best chance to cash in given the estimated $350,000-a-year shortfall between his current earnings and his previous Parramatta deal. PNG have also made an offer to highly-rated 19-year-old Queensland Reds tyro Treyvon Pritchard, though as revealed by this masthead, the Roosters have also weighed in with a lucrative bid to lure him to the NRL. As for Manu and PNG, his existing Australian resident status also ensures any Chiefs contract would be tax-exempt. The club’s tax exemption deal is only in place between only the Australian and PNG governments, which reduces the financial lure for Kiwi and English players – including St Helens prop Matty Lees, who signed with the Chiefs last month.



Manu is also considered especially marketable in rugby league circles given his clean-cut looks, on-field prowess and cleanskin status, making him a natural fit for PNG’s lucrative third-party agreements. Earnings from those arrangements are also tax-exempt and star signing Jarome Luai is already tipped to earn more than double his $1.2 million Chiefs salary through endorsements in rugby league mad PNG. Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth says debates over Labor’s policies on the Middle East are a matter for the party, amid criticism from Israel over a to-be-debated draft.

The platform is set to call out settler violence in the West Bank, condemn a controversial new death penalty law and back two international courts considering genocide and war crimes charges against Israel.

Minister for Employment and Workplace Relations Amanda Rishworth says debates over Labor’s policies on the Middle East are a matter for the party, amid criticism from Israel over a to-be-debated draft. Alex Ellinghausen

Rishworth told ABC Radio National the debate is a matter for Labor’s upcoming national conference, but the government has been consistent in its desire for a two-state solution.

“We have unequivocally condemned Hamas, including for the atrocities of the seventh of October and its ongoing acts of terror ... we’ve also very clearly said that both Israelis and Palestinians deserve to live their lives free from terror and violence,” Rishworth said.

“We want to see a two-state solution in which Israelis and Palestinians can live in secure borders, and I think our Prime Minister and our government’s been pretty clear about that,” Rishworth said.

World.title: ‘We need to be better’: Arise, Andy Burnham, Britain’s seventh PM in a decade
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeUK politics ‘We need to be better’: Arise, Andy Burnham, Britain’s seventh PM in a decade David Crowe Updated July 21, 2026 — 7:02am ,first published 7:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has vowed to “bring back hope” to the country after being elevated to the leadership in a meeting with King Charles, declaring that the public deserves better from a new generation of politicians. Burnham promised to deliver help with the cost of living within his first 24 hours in the job, as he arrived at his official residence at 10 Downing Street to deliver his first remarks as prime minister in front of hundreds of reporters. Andy Burnham gives his first speech as prime minister outside 10 Downing Street. Getty Images “We have not been good enough, and we need to be better,” he said. “We will be.” The formal transfer of power concluded after the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer, visited King Charles at Buckingham Palace for a private meeting in which he officially resigned.



That meeting cleared the way for Burnham to visit the King soon afterwards and be invited to form government, elevating him to the top post. In a brief statement, the King confirmed that Burnham accepted the invitation and “kissed hands upon his appointment” – the traditional language used to describe a prime minister accepting the monarch’s invitation to lead government. King Charles welcomes Burnham to Buckingham Palace, where he was invited to form government. Getty Images Charles and Burnham. Getty Images The formal events were broadcast live on multiple television networks and online, while a helicopter flew overhead to capture the moments on a warm summer day in London.



Speaking outside Downing Street after the palace meeting, without notes or a lectern, Burnham said he was “acutely” conscious he was the seventh prime minister since 2016. “It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game and rise to the new challenge,” he said. Burnham and his wife, Marie-France van Heel, wave as they enter 10 Downing Street. AP Photo/Thomas Krych The couple is greeted inside the official residence by top political staff and other advisers. Getty Images “Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again, and that is our challenge: to make politics work, to make it work better.”



Burnham spoke directly to the main television camera to give a personal assurance to the British people that he would do better than previous prime ministers. “I know people at home are fed up with politics. I hear you,” he said, promising to deliver a “circuit breaker” for a system he said had taken wrong turns since the 1980s. Loading Burnham vowed to decentralise power from London, reindustrialise the economy, end rough sleeping, ensure stronger public control of key industries, build more homes and improve mental health support. He said he would outline help with the cost of living, in a funded government policy, within his first 24 hours.



“It’s about putting the right values and the right standards at the heart of government,” he said. “I will put the care of people at the heart of everything I do. I will give this my all, and I ask you all to pull with me. Burnham said his generation of politicians needed to “raise our game”. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth “Let’s build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose, and positivity. Let us make this the moment when Britain starts to believe again – the moment we bring back hope.” Upon those words, he entered 10 Downing Street with his wife, Marie-France van Heel, to be greeted by top political staff and other advisers.



Earlier, Starmer had left the official residence to give his final address as prime minister in front of dozens of ministerial colleagues, staff and family members including his wife, Victoria. “My work is done. In 6½ years, I took our party from a historic defeat in 2019, changed it so it was fit to face the country, and won a landslide general election victory in 2024,” he said. Keir Starmer receives applause as he leaves No. 10 Downing Street. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth Starmer and his wife, Victoria, depart Downing Street. Getty Images “Since then, it has been the privilege of my life to serve you and this great country as prime minister, and I am confident that Britain is now stronger and fairer than it was two years ago.”



Starmer said Burnham had his “full support”. “As I now pass the baton to Andy Burnham, I wish him every success,” he said. “I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything that we have achieved.” King Charles welcomes Starmer to Buckingham Palace, where he officially resigned as PM. Getty Images After being hugged by his wife and embracing some of his supporters, Starmer walked to a waiting car with Victoria and drove to the palace to see the King.



Buckingham Palace confirmed soon afterwards that Charles was “graciously pleased to accept” Starmer’s resignation – the same wording used for the statements about the departures of previous prime ministers. The meetings at Buckingham Palace formally concluded a long fight within the Labour Party to replace Starmer after growing discontent over his leadership, and a year of planning by Burnham and his allies to take power within the party. Sir Clive Alderton, left, principal private secretary to the King and Queen, and King Charles III’s Equerry, Major Ben Rigby, right, greet Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel at Buckingham Palace. Aaron Chown/Pool PA via AP In being named to the top post on Monday, Burnham became the nation’s seventh prime minister since 2016. One of Burnham’s biggest tasks on his first day was to appoint a Cabinet.



The key post of chancellor of the exchequer went to John Healey, the former defence secretary who quit the previous government a few weeks ago over funding plans for his department. His appointment as Treasury chief was a surprise. Related Article Updated

UK politics ‘Number 10 North’: PM-in-waiting vows major power shift out of London Healey replaces Rachel Reeves, the architect of much of Starmer’s economic agenda and some of the missteps that ate away at his support. Others leaving the Cabinet included David Lammy, who was deputy prime minister. Energy Secretary Ed Miliband was given the role of foreign secretary. He replaces Yvette Cooper, who was appointed health secretary, a demotion but a hugely important post for the Labour Party’s re-election prospects. Shabana Mahmood remains as home secretary. Burnham also brought back Jonathan Reynolds as business minister and Angela Rayner as housing minister. The full Cabinet will meets on Tuesday.



Bond market investors were watching the cabinet decision closely, given the country’s net public debt is £2.9 trillion ($5.6 trillion) – equivalent to 95 per cent of annual economic output – and rising. Related Article UK politics Four things to know about Andy Burnham, the man likely to be the UK’s next PM Burnham, who has spent the past nine years as mayor of Greater Manchester, set out broad themes about his plans in a speech three weeks ago, knowing he had the numbers within the Labour Party to lead the government. “We will create a more streamlined state with a clearer purpose to power up all parts of the country and put a laser-like focus on growth and regeneration – good growth,” he said. Burnham, however, captured attention with a related pledge to shift some of the powers of 10 Downing Street in London – near the major public service departments around Whitehall – so that a new unit of government would be responsible for northern England and other areas outside the capital.



Burnham called his proposed new office “Number 10 North”, and the phrase dominated media coverage of his speech, although he did not outline any details on how it would work. Labour has 403 seats in the House of Commons, giving it a comfortable majority. The Conservative Party has 117 seats, the Liberal Democrats have 71, Reform UK has seven and the Greens have five. Small parties and independents make up the rest. But the divisions within the Labour parliamentary party have weakened the government, while Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has made big gains in local government elections and has soared in the public opinion polls as a potential prime minister. Burnham’s rise began in earnest on May 19 when he overcame resistance from Starmer’s allies and gained party approval to run as the Labour candidate at a byelection for the seat of Makerfield, which he won on June 19. Starmer announced on June 22 that he would resign. With Labour MPs making it clear they wanted a new leader, Starmer set up an internal party timeline to decide his replacement. When party officials called for nominations, Burnham was the sole candidate – an extraordinary development given he had become a member of the House of Commons only days earlier.



While Burnham is the seventh prime minister in roughly a decade, he is also being described as the sixth prime minister in 10 years. Former Conservative prime minister David Cameron stepped down on July 13, 2016 – 10 years and one week ago. He was followed by Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak from the Conservative Party. They were followed by Starmer and Burnham. With wires. World.title: US launches new strikes after Iran-backed Houthis declare blockade of another key oil route
World.content:
Updated WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war US launches new strikes after Iran-backed Houthis declare blockade of another key oil route Nayera Abdallah , Eman Abouhassira and Timour Azhari Updated July 21, 2026 — 6:40am ,first published 5:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dubai/Riyadh: Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said they would impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, opening a potential new front against the US in its war with Iran and raising the threat to global energy supplies and trade beyond the Gulf. The Houthis made their announcement despite signs that Tehran and Washington want to resume diplomacy to halt a worsening cycle of attacks that has all but wrecked a fragile interim agreement signed last month. An image released by US Central Command shows service members aboard the amphibious assault ship USS Boxer supporting flight operations from the Arabian Sea. CENTCOM Iran’s Foreign Ministry said mediators had presented “proposals” to Tehran, signalling that diplomatic contacts remain active, but gave no details. Oil prices rose briefly after the Houthi statement, but later fell back as traders held out hope of a diplomatic breakthrough. The insurance cost of shipping goods through the Red Sea rose on the increased risks for merchant shipping.



Even so, the US President Donald Trump ordered a new round of strikes against Iran – the 10th consecutive night of attacks – that started about 6am on Tuesday (AEST). “The strikes are designed to further degrade Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz,” US Central Command said in a statement. Shortly after, Iranian state television said an explosion had been heard in the coastal cities of Bandar Abbas, Chabahar and Konarak. Air defence systems were also activated near Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant, Mehr reported. Iran had been pressing the Houthis to close the Bab el-Mandeb gateway to the Red Sea if the US continued to attack Iranian power infrastructure.



The full closure of the Bab el-Mandeb strait would reduce global oil supply by 7 per cent as it would leave most of Saudi oil exports unable to leave the region. The disruption would add to the huge cut to oil flows from the war in the Gulf, which has already reduced shipments by 10 per cent of global supply. In their statement, the Houthis’ armed forces said they were declaring “a maritime embargo against the criminal Saudi enemy, based on the equation of ‘an eye for an eye’, effective immediately” in response to what they called “an unjust and oppressive siege” imposed on Yemen by the Saudis. View post on X Saudi Arabia on Tuesday (AEST) condemned the Houthi naval blockade announcement and their statements accusing Riyadh of “besieging” the Yemeni people. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said it would respond to Houthis threats to ships with “force” and began to implement safety measures for its ships passing through Bab el-Mandeb Strait. “Such threats are a blatant violation of international law and falls under acts of maritime piracy,” the coalition said



“The question now is whether [the Houthis] will begin targeting vessels heading to Saudi ports. At this stage, there’s no clear answer,” said Mohammed Albasha, a Yemeni analyst and founder of Basha Report, a Washington-based risk advisory firm. “Even if no ships are attacked, the announcement alone is likely to disrupt shipping and create uncertainty for Saudi ports. Whether the Houthis move from threats to direct action remains the critical issue.” The group fired missiles at Saudi ​Arabia last week after accusing the kingdom of bombing an airport under their control, piercing a four-year truce in the conflict between ‌the kingdom and the Iran-aligned group In this photo released by the Pakistan’s Interior Ministry, Iran’s Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni, left, meets with his Pakistani counterpart Mohsin Naqvi, right, in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, on Monday. Pakistan’s Interior Ministry via AP Meanwhile, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Monday (Iran time) that Tehran had received a proposal from mediators for a 10-day ceasefire in efforts to salvage the interim deal, intended to pave the way to a lasting agreement to end the war that began on February 28 with US-Israeli attacks on Iran. Neither the ministry nor the official who spoke to Reuters gave any details on the putative ceasefire discussions. Two Pakistani government sources said separately that Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni had asked Pakistan to resume its mediation role in the conflict. He later arrived in Islamabad for further talks.



The diplomatic push followed another night of US strikes on Iranian cities and attacks by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards on US military assets across the region. Trump, under mounting political pressure at home over rising petrol prices since the war began and Iran effectively closed the vital Strait of Hormuz, defended the recent strikes on Iran as honouring the deaths of up to three American service members in recent Iranian attacks. First Lieutenant Tyler James Feehan and Private Isabella Gonzales were killed by an Iranian attack in Jordan. US Army Space and Missile Defence Command via AP Loading Two US Army soldiers killed in Iranian attacks on Jordan were identified on Monday as First Lieutenant James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii, and Private Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Carrollton, Texas, were killed in Jordan in Friday’s attacks.



An American service member was also killed in northern Iraq on Saturday during a “controlled detonation” of unexploded ordnance from a downed Iranian drone. “Every time Iran kills an American Soldier they will pay for that killing many times over! This directive has been passed on to Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Daniel Caine, and every Leader in the Military,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday. US President Donald Trump exits Air Force One on Sunday. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin The war has killed thousands of people, mostly in Iran and Lebanon, part of which has been occupied by Israeli forces following attacks on Israel by Hezbollah fighters who said they were acting in solidarity with Tehran. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun is due to meet Trump at the White House on Tuesday to present a plan on how to disarm Iran-aligned Hezbollah and secure an Israeli withdrawal.



Israel also still has forces in Gaza following two years of war ignited by the Palestinian militant group Hamas’ attack on southern Israeli communities on October 7, 2023. Hamas said on Monday it had named top negotiator Khalil Al-Hayya as its overall leader, a move that an analyst said could signal a tougher stance by the group towards calls for it to disarm. Related Article Middle East at war US launches new strikes as Iran continues to target oil tankers on the Strait of Hormuz US Central Command said its ninth consecutive night of strikes against Iran aimed at weakening its ability to attack commercial vessels in the strait. The US military also said it redirected seven commercial vessels and disabled one as part of a US naval blockade of Iranian ports. In Iran, explosions were reported in Tabriz, Chabahar, Konarak, Bandar Mahshahr and Bandar Imam Khomeini. One person was killed and several wounded southwest of Tabriz, according to state news agency IRNA. The IRGC said it targeted US aircraft at Jordan’s Aqaba airport with ballistic missiles, as well as military assets at Kuwait’s Al-Adiri camp and Ali Al Salem Air Base, and positions in Syria. Sirens sounded in Bahrain throughout Monday. Kuwait’s army said it again intercepted Iranian drones.

World.title: ‘This feels political’: Tate brothers to fight extradition to UK on rape, sex trafficking charges
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCrime ‘This feels political’: Tate brothers to fight extradition to UK on rape, sex trafficking charges David Fischer Updated July 21, 2026 — 6:32am ,first published 4:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Miami: Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate will fight extradition to the United Kingdom where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking, their lawyer said, suggesting their arrest in Miami was politically motivated without explaining why. The Tates appeared in federal court Monday (US time) for the first time since their arrest on Saturday (Sunday AEST) and are being held in federal detention. In the coming weeks, a US district judge will consider whether they meet the conditions for extradition. US Magistrate Lauren Louis set another hearing for Monday, July 27. Andrew Tate (left) and his brother Tristan, in Romania in January 2024. AP The brothers, normally photographed in tailored suits and stylish fitted shirts, wore tan jail uniforms and handcuffs during the brief hearing. Neither brother said a word during the hearing. Their attorney, Joseph McBride, insisted they should remain in the US.



“We are, of course, objecting to extradition because Andrew and Tristan are innocent,” McBride said after the hearing. “They’ve never done nothing wrong. They shouldn’t be extradited for crimes they did not commit.” The brothers were surprised when they were arrested, McBride said, adding that the attempt to have them extradited was politically motivated. “There’s no question about it,” he told reporters. Joseph McBride, lawyer for Andrew and Tristan Tate, arrives at court in Miami. AP Photo/Marta Lavandier He suggested the Tates’ case “had a lot to do with” former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s decision to step down, without providing any details, and said it was no coincidence that the brothers were arrested after meeting “friends in Washington, DC”. “We went to see our Congress people in DC and now we’re getting arrested. This feels political,” McBride said. He didn’t specify who the pair met with or what was discussed.



On Sunday, McBride said he was confident the extradition request would be denied. Prosecutors in Britain said the new charges relate to four new alleged victims and were brought after authorities received evidence from Bedfordshire Police in southeastern England. The allegations, spanning 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offences relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography”. A courtroom sketch shows Andrew and Tristan Tate appearing with their attorneys before judge Lauren Louis in a Miami court on Monday. AP McBride said none of the latest accusers have been identified, adding “we’d like to know who’s accused Andrew and Tristan of what.” The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other alleged victims in the UK between 2012 and 2015.



Their lawyer said in a statement on Saturday that he believed the arrests were “greenlighted by a low-level functionary” at the Justice Department without input from leadership. The Justice Department told The Associated Press that the arrests were approved by leadership of its Criminal Division. Loading The new allegations are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the Tates that has spanned the US, Britain and Romania. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing. Their social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny has made them among the world’s most polarising internet personalities.



The dual US and British citizens moved to Romania in 2016. They were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. Related Article Crime What to know about the Tates, the misogynist influencers facing rape, sex trafficking and child porn charges Last year, they were allowed to leave Romania and flew to Florida. The former professional kickboxers have millions of followers on social media and are vocal supporters of President Donald Trump. Andrew Tate, 39, first became known a decade ago when he was a contestant on the UK reality television show Big Brother. The self-described misogynist was booted from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman.



He has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms for violating hate speech guidelines, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram. Related Article Updated

Crime Manosphere influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate arrested in Miami He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women. The Tate brothers have consistently denied allegations of abuse and human trafficking, claiming their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes. World.title: ‘Baked bean cans’: Emirates boss to reject Boeing planes
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation ‘Baked bean cans’: Emirates boss to reject Boeing planes Christopher Jasper July 21, 2026 — 8:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Boeing has been dealt a fresh blow after Emirates said it would refuse to take delivery of 10 aircraft, claiming that the much-delayed jets would be better off being turned into baked bean tins. The Dubai airline has ordered a total of 270 new 777X planes from Boeing at $US440 million ($629 million) apiece, with the first jet built in 2019. But repeated delays stemming from design modifications has meant Emirates is still waiting for the planes seven years later. Emirates president Sir Tim Clark said the company was unwilling to take the 10 aircraft because the design of the 777X had undergone so many significant changes that bringing them up to the latest standard would not be feasible. Bloomberg Sir Tim Clark, the president of Emirates, said the initial batch of 10 of the jets required such a patchwork of changes to update them that they were not fit for purpose. “We’re not taking that batch and that’s it,” he told The Telegraph at the Farnborough International Airshow. “As far as we’re concerned, what they do with them is up to them.”



Clark said he understood that Boeing had been trying to find a home for the aircraft, before adding: “Heinz would be interested – baked bean cans.” Related Article Exclusive

Aviation Some A380s grounded amid emergency inspections for wing spar cracks His refusal to take the planes will serve as a new setback to Boeing, which has been rocked by a string of safety crises in recent years. Clark said Emirates was unwilling to take the 10 aircraft because the design of the 777X had undergone so many significant changes that bringing them up to the latest standard would not be feasible. The 777X has suffered numerous problems that have pushed back entry into service from 2020 to next year at the earliest.



Those issues have included a thrust control issue that halted test flights in 2024 and an incident in 2020 that saw an aircraft’s nose pitch up without pilot input, delaying the programme by years. Clark said the airline was also concerned by the earlier-than-expected structural failure of a 777X during a ground-based stress test of the airframe. Emirates’ refusal to take the planes will serve as a new setback to Boeing, which has been rocked by a string of safety crises in recent years. AP He added: “The modifications for the airframe have been so significant since the early flights. And don’t forget we had a static-test failure as well.” He added: “I went on the first one in 2019, which was fully configured except for our first-class cabins, and here we are in 2026. It’s now seven years on. We’re not taking them.”



His comments came after it emerged one of the planes earmarked for Emirates had already been scrapped. The 400-seat plane was quietly “disassembled” in 2025 after sitting dormant for six years on an airfield close to Boeing’s Seattle manufacturing centre, The Air Current reported. Stephanie Pope, the head of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, said changes were made to the aircraft “as the maturity of the design progresses”. She said: “If you look at those early airplanes, you’ve then got to weigh how much change it’s going to take and the benefit from that. “We are always looking at how much that change is going to cost and what will be the capability of the airplane, and making sure we’re getting the right solution not only for Boeing, but for our customer.”



Related Article Billionaires Bezos’ whirlwind visit: How do the rich and famous get to the beach so fast? Flight tests on the 777-9, the first version of the new 777X plane, should be completed by the end of this year, after which the model will need to show it is capable of flying for long distances over water on a single engine, according to analysts at Jefferies. That should pave the way for the first aircraft to be delivered to Lufthansa before the end of 2027. Asked when British Airways expected to receive the first of 24 planes it has on order, Sean Doyle, its chief executive, said simply: “Good question.” Telegraph, London The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Officials got three of seven calls wrong at the weekend. Apart from that, the NRL was happy
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Officials got three of seven calls wrong at the weekend. Apart from that, the NRL was happy Christian Nicolussi Updated July 21, 2026 — 7:54am ,first published 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney Roosters forward Nat Butcher should not have been penalised for a high tackle, Melbourne were denied a legitimate try, and Manly’s Reuben Garrick was offside when he scored against the Titans. Aside from those three clangers, the NRL was more than satisfied with a string of other controversial calls made by referees and the bunker over the weekend. Loading This masthead pinpointed at least seven contentious calls in five games that were heavily criticised by coaches, players and commentators. They did not include queries St George Illawarra had with Valentine Holmes being penalised for an obstruction and Setu Tu being denied a try by a bunker ruling.



We revealed the bunker’s decision-making efficiency rate sat at an impressive 98 per cent just a month ago. But fans have been in the dark about the reasoning behind refereeing calls since the NRL scrapped head of football Graham Annesley’s weekly press conference a couple of years ago. In the hope of achieving some clarity, we asked the NRL for its thoughts about the weekend calls. Were Penrith robbed? The Panthers thought they had won a repeat set – and a chance to win the game – with two minutes of Thursday night’s match left after Brisbane’s Josiah Karapani was dragged into touch. Referee Todd Smith ruled a knock-on, which Penrith successfully challenged – but the bunker ruled Smith had blown the whistle before Karapani was taken into touch. Because it was a “mutual infringement”, Karapani was instructed to play the ball, rather than Penrith receive the ball back.



Penrith coach Ivan Cleary said after the game: “If we get the ball there, and we should have got it ... it’s just one of those nights”. The NRL, however, formed the view the decision was technically correct because the whistle was blown simultaneously as Karapani was being pushed into touch. If anything, Penrith could have been penalised for the second effort. Roosters Butchered Coaches Trent Robinson and Craig Bellamy both took issue with a few calls during Friday night’s Storm-Roosters clash.



Robinson was stunned Butcher was penalised for a high tackle on Alec MacDonald, which allowed Melbourne to march downfield and score two minutes later. Nat Butcher’s ‘hit’ on Alec Macdonald. Nine “It was completely laughable,” Robinson said of the penalty. The NRL agreed it should not have been given. Did Warbrick knock on? Bellamy could not understand why the Storm were denied a try in the first half, when Will Warbrick appeared to knock a ball back from a kick, only for Gerard Sutton to rule it a knock-on.



Bellamy broke into one of his famous colourful rants in the coach’s box. After several slow-motion reviews, the NRL were satisfied Warbrick got his hand in front of the ball and knocked it back. Walker shot clock Roosters halfback Sam Walker appeared to have taken a dropout after the shot-clock buzzer sounded in the 67th minute, which would have given Melbourne a penalty kick from in front to level the scores.



Loading “Six to eight weeks ago, we got done for taking too long with a line drop-out,” Bellamy said. But the NRL was satisfied the Walker kick and shot-clock buzzer were simultaneous, so Sutton was entitled to wave play-on. Similar situations occur on occasions with scrum-clocks. Was Dom Young taken out? Cronulla opened their account against the Knights with a try to Will Kennedy on Friday evening, but Ronnie Mulitalo appeared to deny Newcastle winger Dominic Young a fair chance at leaping for the ball.



Braydon Trindall sent the ball up, Mulitalo chased, but barely got off the ground – yet still did enough to impede Young. The NRL was comfortable Mulitalo had not taken his eyes off the ball, never looked at Young and had both arms extended in a catching position before he jumped, which meant there was a genuine contest, and no need to rule a “disruptor” penalty. Red V see red The Dragons have worked hard to address their sluggish second-half starts, so you could forgive them for being cranky when the Warriors went ahead in the 44th minute via Dallin Watene-Zelezniak from what they felt was a forward pass.



“It’s just not right,” co-captain Damien Cook said. “I feel sorry for the fans that have to watch that. But it’s happened too many times to us.” The NRL was comfortable it was not a forward pass, and other camera angles not shown on the live broadcast supported this view. Did Garrick jump the gun? Titans skipper Tino Fa’asuamaleaui made a beeline for referee Adam Gee after Reuben Garrick scored for Manly in the second half, wanting to know if the Manly centre was offside.



“It happened to Max Plath in Origin, that was the call; are you serious?” Fa’asuamaleaui asked Gee, referring to the Maroons being denied a try in similar circumstances in Origin III only a few weeks earlier. The decision did not cost the Gold Coast the win – and just as well, because the NRL, based on the available footage, believed Garrick was “marginally offside”. World.title: Joey Manu’s $1.6m contract call signals latest shift in cross-code talent stoush
World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 Joey Manu’s $1.6m contract call signals latest shift in cross-code talent stoush Dan Walsh Updated July 21, 2026 — 7:29am ,first published 11:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The PNG Chiefs are emerging as the NRL’s trump card in the cross-code battle for elite athletes as Joey Manu considers a multimillion dollar return to rugby league with the incoming franchise. Manu and his family toured the Chiefs’ Port Moresby facilities on Monday and the ex-Roosters star has been in talks with PNG officials for several weeks over a marquee deal to join Willie Peters’ inaugural 2028 roster. Loading Fellow code-hopper Zac Lomax is expected to make the same trip to PNG in the next week as he weighs up his own multi-year offer to make an NRL comeback with the Chiefs. Manu has been holidaying in New Zealand since the end of the French Rugby Top 14 season, where he has another year remaining on his contract with Racing 92.



The 29-year-old will return to France in September, where his deal is estimated to be worth as much as €1 million ($1.6 million) a season. French rugby’s four-month off-season had prompted the Warriors to enquire about Manu taking up a short-term NRL return this season, though that was ultimately knocked back by the Kiwi star. Former Rooster Joey Manu and his family at Port Moresby airport on Monday. A similar move from late May next year could yet make Manu an elite mid-2027 signing for NRL clubs. Sources speaking on the condition of anonymity due to ongoing negotiations have told this masthead that 2027 will be Manu’s last campaign in European rugby as he looks to move back closer to family in New Zealand.



A return to Japanese rugby, where Manu first landed in 2024 after wrapping up a 181-game Roosters career, is still a possibility. However, Manu is genuinely considering the PNG move given it offers a return to rugby league and the Chiefs are the only NRL outfit that can truly compete with the spending power of overseas rugby clubs. Joey Manu left the NRL as one of the best players in the game. NRL Imagery Manu’s current wage in France is roughly double the $800,000 the Roosters could offer him during his final year at the club, when he was widely regarded as the best centre in the game. The NRL’s salary cap is predicted to rise to at least $15 million in 2028, thanks to the record $5.3 billion broadcast deal.



But even with that potential 24 per cent increase, PNG would be the only NRL side able to match Manu’s potential earnings in overseas rugby without destabilising their salary cap due to their ability to offer players tax-free wages. The Roosters have repeatedly been mentioned in terms of bringing Manu back to the NRL, but this masthead reported in April that the club privately gave up that hope given his earning power in the rival code. Zac Lomax’s potential return to rugby league is gaining momentum. Getty Images Mark Nawaqanitawase has set the NRL alight in his two years of playing rugby league, but he will earn more than double his Tricolours wage when he links with Japan’s Saitama Wild Knights at the end of the year. Lomax, meanwhile, took a significant pay cut to join the Western Force after going all in on the aborted R360 project. He knocked back an approach to join the Storm next year and is chasing a Wallabies debut with an eye to playing in the 2027 World Cup.



Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Dean Young lands Dragons coaching job after challenge from old teammate Beyond that, either overseas rugby or linking with the Chiefs in 2028 present as the former NSW Origin star’s best chance to cash in given the estimated $350,000-a-year shortfall between his current earnings and his previous Parramatta deal. PNG have also made an offer to highly-rated 19-year-old Queensland Reds tyro Treyvon Pritchard, though as revealed by this masthead, the Roosters have also weighed in with a lucrative bid to lure him to the NRL. As for Manu and PNG, his existing Australian resident status also ensures any Chiefs contract would be tax-exempt. The club’s tax exemption deal is only in place between only the Australian and PNG governments, which reduces the financial lure for Kiwi and English players – including St Helens prop Matty Lees, who signed with the Chiefs last month.



Manu is also considered especially marketable in rugby league circles given his clean-cut looks, on-field prowess and cleanskin status, making him a natural fit for PNG’s lucrative third-party agreements. Earnings from those arrangements are also tax-exempt and star signing Jarome Luai is already tipped to earn more than double his $1.2 million Chiefs salary through endorsements in rugby league mad PNG.
