World.title: ‘This feels political’: Tate brothers to fight extradition to UK on rape, sex trafficking charges
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCrime ‘This feels political’: Tate brothers to fight extradition to UK on rape, sex trafficking charges David Fischer Updated July 21, 2026 — 6:32am ,first published 4:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Miami: Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate will fight extradition to the United Kingdom where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking, their lawyer said, suggesting their arrest in Miami was politically motivated without explaining why. The Tates appeared in federal court Monday (US time) for the first time since their arrest on Saturday (Sunday AEST) and are being held in federal detention. In the coming weeks, a US district judge will consider whether they meet the conditions for extradition. US Magistrate Lauren Louis set another hearing for Monday, July 27. Andrew Tate (left) and his brother Tristan, in Romania in January 2024. AP The brothers, normally photographed in tailored suits and stylish fitted shirts, wore tan jail uniforms and handcuffs during the brief hearing. Neither brother said a word during the hearing. Their attorney, Joseph McBride, insisted they should remain in the US.



“We are, of course, objecting to extradition because Andrew and Tristan are innocent,” McBride said after the hearing. “They’ve never done nothing wrong. They shouldn’t be extradited for crimes they did not commit.” The brothers were surprised when they were arrested, McBride said, adding that the attempt to have them extradited was politically motivated. “There’s no question about it,” he told reporters. Joseph McBride, lawyer for Andrew and Tristan Tate, arrives at court in Miami. AP Photo/Marta Lavandier He suggested the Tates’ case “had a lot to do with” former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s decision to step down, without providing any details, and said it was no coincidence that the brothers were arrested after meeting “friends in Washington, DC”. “We went to see our Congress people in DC and now we’re getting arrested. This feels political,” McBride said. He didn’t specify who the pair met with or what was discussed.



On Sunday, McBride said he was confident the extradition request would be denied. Prosecutors in Britain said the new charges relate to four new alleged victims and were brought after authorities received evidence from Bedfordshire Police in southeastern England. The allegations, spanning 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offences relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography”. A courtroom sketch shows Andrew and Tristan Tate appearing with their attorneys before judge Lauren Louis in a Miami court on Monday. AP McBride said none of the latest accusers have been identified, adding “we’d like to know who’s accused Andrew and Tristan of what.” The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other alleged victims in the UK between 2012 and 2015.



Their lawyer said in a statement on Saturday that he believed the arrests were “greenlighted by a low-level functionary” at the Justice Department without input from leadership. The Justice Department told The Associated Press that the arrests were approved by leadership of its Criminal Division. Loading The new allegations are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the Tates that has spanned the US, Britain and Romania. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing. Their social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny has made them among the world’s most polarising internet personalities.



The dual US and British citizens moved to Romania in 2016. They were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. Related Article Crime What to know about the Tates, the misogynist influencers facing rape, sex trafficking and child porn charges Last year, they were allowed to leave Romania and flew to Florida. The former professional kickboxers have millions of followers on social media and are vocal supporters of President Donald Trump. Andrew Tate, 39, first became known a decade ago when he was a contestant on the UK reality television show Big Brother. The self-described misogynist was booted from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman.



He has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms for violating hate speech guidelines, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram. Related Article Updated

Crime Manosphere influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate arrested in Miami He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women. The Tate brothers have consistently denied allegations of abuse and human trafficking, claiming their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes. AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: LynnMall terrorist was 'soft-hearted', 'misunderstood' - relative
World.content:
A soft-hearted and caring person, fun-loving and adventurous - this is how the family of a man who stabbed shoppers in a West Auckland supermarket remember him.

Ahamed Samsudeen was shot dead by police, ending his rampage that saw shoppers stabbed in a Woolworths in LynnMall.

A coronial inquest into his death is underway, part of which will look at his path to violent extremism, his attitude towards women and the time leading up to the attack.

The coroner has been given a glimpse into who Ahamed Aathil Mohamed Samsudeen was before the attack, through evidence given by someone close to him. Samsudeen's family are no longer taking part in the inquest, but their interests are being represented by stand-by counsel. The person giving evidence cannot be named, but can be identified as a relative.

They told the court said Samsudeen grew up a happy child, always playful, funny and enthusiastic.

While living in Sri Lanka, Samsudeen was kidnapped and tortured "which wounded him physically [and] psychologically".

His father had refused to let members of the Tamil Tigers (LTTE) hide weapons at his school in the years before Samsudeen was born in 1989.

By the time Samsudeen was 15 the Karuna paramilitary group had abducted his father, trying to get some documents and recordings about secret meetings with government ministers.

Samsudeen was also at home with his mother during a burglary while his father was overseas.

The relative wondered if those traumatic events came back to him in his isolation in New Zealand.

When Samsudeen moved here, the relative said he enjoyed his studies.

"He loved the culture and people in New Zealand."

Samsudeen was very empathetic toward Syrian refugees, the relative said, going so far as to letting a refugee stay in his apartment when he had nowhere else to go.

"Aathil never wanted to worry us over anything," the relative said.

The relative said Samsudeen fractured his spine while moving a microwave from his apartment to a mosque, leaving him bedridden.

"He was also online a lot during this time of recovery as he was unable to move anywhere. This period is what has exposed him too much to graphic material online," the relative said.

"Even when he experienced back pain, he insisted that he could and would take care of himself. Aathil is a loving person and he is very much strong minded."

The NZ Security Intelligence Service (SIS) had been alerted to Samsudeen after finding an account on social media in March 2016 under the name Aathill Al-Ceyloni Al-Moori.

The account had posted photographs and videos of graphic violence against Muslims on its public page, along with comments supporting violent extremism and ISIL (Islamic State, also known as ISIS) terrorist attacks overseas. It was later linked to Samsudeen.

In their statement, the relative said he would "always" argue with people on Facebook, and would especially defend people affected by the Syrian civil war.

"He didn't think that he was doing anything wrong. He thought he was helping Muslims who were suffering in other countries."

Ahamed Samsudeen coming out of the New Lynn train station, on the day of the attack on September 3, 2021. Supplied

Authorities first arrested Samsudeen in 2017 at Auckland Airport, with the SIS believing he was travelling to Syria to join ISIL fighters.

The relative said when he was first arrested, Samsudeen argued he did not create any content and was only sharing what was already online.

"We thought the entire thing would be a misunderstanding and would be cleared up soon."

The relative said they would speak with Samsudeen while he was in prison, playing him Tamil and Bollywood songs for him through the phone.

"It is heartbreaking for me to think of how much stress he was under, and that this is why he would like to listen to songs through the phone so that he could relieve his worry and his loneliness," they said.

"I again had no idea about his suffering in those two years. He would always joke, poke fun at me but never reveal the reality of his own situation."

The relative believed Corrections did not want to release Samsudeen as they "couldn't prove their allegations at the time".

While back in the community, Samsudeen had told his father he felt like he was being followed. Samsudeen had been under surveillance at the time of the attack on 3 September, 2021.

The relative spoke about Samsudeen's growing distrust in the system, saying that over time it seemed he had lost trust in everyone.

Provoked?

Turning to the day of the attack, they believed something was done to provoke Samsudeen - the relative could not believe Samsudeen perpetrated the attack.

"It was not that he was short-tempered. He was drained of energy. He had

deteriorated completely and had no energy to execute a plan like this."

Samsudeen's life took a turn as a result of the way he was treated, they said.

"He was misunderstood, and his humanity was never known or appreciated."

The relative said Samsudeen was now defined by his final moments.

"We are devastated that he did not have our support or full understanding of his situation and that he suffered throughout these legal processes, and then also died without any family or close support present."

Their final request was to know the location where Samsudeen was buried.

World.title: Auckland planning chair says proposed changes will remove density around local centres
World.content:
[author:erin_johnson]

The chair of Auckland Council's planning committee Richard Hills says proposed changes to new intensification rules will remove density around local centres and focus it near frequent transport services.

On Tuesday, councillors will decide whether to make changes to the proposed Plan Change 120 (PC120) before it goes out to public consultation for a second time.

Auckland Council is required by central government to enable development capacity for 1.4 million dwellings in the city.

In June, councillors agreed to send two versions of PC120 to local boards and iwi authorities for feedback - Plan A and Plan B, which provided for 1.4-1.6 million dwellings and 1.5-1.7 million dwellings respectively.

The feedback from local boards was largely that "about a third wanted A, about a third wanted B, and about a third wanted a mix of both or didn't say", Hills said.

The big change most local boards wanted was to remove density around local centres, "those are smaller centres in their communities, not the town centres, not the metro centres".

"There were other local boards who asked for things that can't be changed, so a change to a walkable catchment or a change to a town centre that's required under the law to stay."

The chair of Auckland Council's planning committee Richard Hills. Alexia Russell

The proposed changes to go before councillors on Tuesday were a blend of Plan A and Plan B, and focus housing density where infrastructure was already in place, he said.

"...we're largely landing in the place where we're doing all the legal requirements, but adding density, so that's six-storey developments around frequent transport corridors - the really, really busy bus routes, mostly heading into the city."

Building heights would also lift to 10- to 15- stories around most train stations on all lines within 10km of the city centre, not just specific Western line stations specified in law, Hills said.

The exception is Meadowbank train station, where it's proposed to reduce building heights to a maximum of six stories due to its valley location and poor access.

Other proposed amendments include reducing building height limits on the southern end of Takapuna Metropolitan Centre from 15 to six stories, and extending the walkable catchments around Akoranga and Smales Farm bus stations so they join up.

It is also proposed to further reducing the development potential for properties at risk of natural hazards, based on updated data, Hills said.

A law change in April, has enabled the council make changes to the overall plan, or withdraw parts of it.

Hills said removing local centres from the proposed intensification plan would leave just 15 percent of urban Auckland impacted by the plan change.

The plan to intensify in areas with existing infrastructure was in contrast to what's been happening with fast track consenting where 1000- to 2000-home developments have been given the go-ahead in areas with no infrastructure, he said.

"I think for most Aucklanders I hear, we should only be putting housing where there is good transport, water, community infrastructure like libraries and that's what the plan shows.

"It remains to be seen what councillors and iwi representatives will make of the proposed changes tomorrow," Hills said.

North Shore councillor John Gillon has proposed a separate amendment, largely based on Plan A.

World.title: First stage of drought declared for parts of Vanuatu
World.content:
Vanuatu's weather service has declared a meteorological drought for some northern parts of the country.

This applies to Torba province, and parts of Sanma, Penama and Malampa provinces.

El Nino has arrived the Pacific islands Pacific Waves Download MP3 3m

The Vanuatu Meteorology and Hydro-meteorological Services (VMHS) said a meteorological drought is the first stage of drought, and happens when rainfall has been significantly below the long-term average for an extended period.

The areas have recorded significantly below-average rainfall over the past three months.

Vanuatu's weather service has declared a meteorological drought for some northern parts of the country. This applies to Torba Province, and parts of Sanma, Penama and Malampa Provinces. Vanuatu Meteorology and Hydro-meteorological Services

It said it serves as an early warning that, if dry conditions continue, more serious impacts, such as agricultural drought, may develop.

El Niño has been declared, and it often leads to dry conditions in the Pacific.

VMHS emphasised that occasional rainfall events can still happen during El Niño.

"However, these rainfall events may not provide enough water to eliminate the accumulated rainfall deficit or bring an end to the meteorological drought. Several weeks or months of near-or above-average rainfall are often required before drought conditions improve," it said.

"With El Niño expected to continue over the coming months, there remains an increased likelihood of below-normal rainfall across other parts of Vanuatu.

"Communities, government agencies, and stakeholders are encouraged to prepare early and make efficient use of available water resources."

People are advised to conserve water and monitor household rainwater storage.

Farmers should consider water-saving practices and monitor crops and livestock closely.

Other countries in the region are also on El Niño alert.

PNG Prime Minister James Marape said the government was taking early action to ensure that communities, particularly those in drought-prone and water-scarce locations, are prepared.

Tonga's National Disaster Risk Management Committee met last month to strengthen preparedness and planning.

World.title: Phone-sized defibrillator launched to make life-saving treatment more accessible
World.content:
Hato Hone St John launches phone-sized defibrillator Morning Report Download MP3 4m

A new defibrillator - the same size as a mobile phone - has been launched by Hato Hone St John which says it will make life-saving treatment more accessible.

The 'LifeBeat Mini' is as powerful as a full-sized defibrillator, but weighs less than 700 grams, and can fit into a glove box, handbag or first aid kit.

Last year, almost 2500 Kiwis were treated for cardiac arrests, but only 6 percent received defibrillation from a bystander before an ambulance arrived.

St John's Simon Barnett told Morning Report the technology was the same as a standard size defibrillator and delivered the same energy of 150 joules.

"It's safe, it's easy and it saves lives."

Barnett said people who received defibrillation in the community were two and a half times more likely to survive a cardiac arrest.

"It's a significant statistic to consider and that's why we want to see more defibrillators in the community."

The mini defibrillator - priced at $2919 - was designed for people on the go, Barnett said.

The defibrillator is the same length as a phone - just a bit thicker. Supplied

This included people outdoors, in motorhomes or on boats.

"If portability is the go, then we would recommend the mini."

Barnett said there was more recognition of what a cardiac arrest was these days and an understanding that the community played a crucial role in helping St John save lives.

While 72 percent of cardiac arrests happened at home, Barnett said the small defibrillator's mobility was one of its benefits.

There were also a lot of people still training in CPR which also made a big difference in saving lives.

World.title: Fiji's police minister clarifies 'misleading' NZ$3 billion drug statement
World.content:
Fiji's Police Minister Ioane Naivalurua walked back his assertion in parliament last week that more than NZ$3billion (FJ$4 billion) worth of illicit drugs reached the nation's shores in the past three years.

"[The drugs] were circulated within local communities by external and internal actors, with over 2400 drug-related cases recorded last year alone," Naivalurua said during a Budget debate last Tuesday.

"Few issues concern our people more today than the growing threat of illicit drugs and transnational organised crime. Drugs destroy lives, destabilise families, undermine communities and threaten the security of our nation," he told parliament.

"The government continues to make the fight against illicit drugs and organised crime one of its highest priorities," he said.

Fiji's police minister says the government has made the fight against illicit drugs and organised crime one of its highest priorities. Supplied/ Fiji Police

The Fijian government had allocated FJ$1.6m in the budget to strengthen Fiji's counter narcotics capability.

"This investment will support the continued establishment of the Counter Narcotics Bureau, the recruitment of specialised personnel and the development of the Counter Narcotics Bill, needed to provide the bureau with a strong legal foundation," Naivalurua said.

"This is a direct investment in enforcement, prevention and the security of our people."

However, the police minister told RNZ Pacific that his 14 July statement was "misleading", and clarified his parliamentary statement.

"The statement that the FJ$4 billion worth of drugs was in circulation in Fiji is misleading, as it was intercepted by police and law enforcement partners, local, regional and international. The harm it would have caused if law enforcement had not acted, would have been far more devastating, " Naivalurua said in a written response to our questions.

"The seizures over the years in white and green drugs are reflective of collaborative efforts which are consistently being reviewed and strengthened through various security arrangements, such as the recent formalisation of the Vuvale treaty," he added.

The treaty signed earlier this month commits Australia and Fiji to work together in tackling regional challenges, including climate change, transnational organised crime and illicit drug networks.

It was signed alongside the Ocean of Peace Alliance, or Veitacini Treaty, a military alliance that has a mutual defence clause.

Naivalarua told RNZ Pacific that transnational crimes were global and required a global response. Facebook / Fiji Police Force

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka's coalition government is treating the escalating drug crisis as a top national security priority, warning previously the issue threatens the indigenous way of life.

Intravenous drug use, particularly through highly dangerous practices like needle sharing, is also the main driver behind Fiji's rapid rise in HIV infections.

Health Minister Atonio Lalabalavu said the government had been proactive about trying to get the HIV crisis under control, unlike the previous administration under Frank Bainimarama.

A Fijian high chief Ratu Tevita Mara, who is co-deputy chair of the Great Council of Chiefs (GCC), warned the coalition government last month that time was nearly up for it to deal with the country's drug crisis.

"The window to act on Fiji's drug crisis is closing," the former military general said, in yet another salvo fired at the government, as the general election nears.

Ratu Tevita, the son of Fiji's first prime minister and president Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara, said Fiji could be breeding a new generation of drug dealers and it was time the National Security Council acted urgently.

He is the traditional head of the Lau Province, and made the comments after more than 60 parcels containing "white substances" washed up in Lau, and Kadavu and Munia Islands.

"I am issuing a direct warning: if the government continues to neglect our communities in the face of this crisis, the day will come when our own youth realise the true worth of these finds. Through that gross negligence, we will have bred an entirely new generation of drug dealers," Ratu Tevita said.

"The drug crisis is above all, a national security issue and the National Security Council needs to meet urgently and agree on an immediate response. Our national security structures and systems have been tested severely and found wanting," he said.

Both the Fiji Police Force and the Republic of Fiji Military Forces (RFMF) declined to respond to questions posed by RNZ Pacific at the time.

However, Naivalarua told RNZ Pacific that transnational crimes were global and required a global response.

"Considering our challenges as small island nation fighting a global threat, we will need the support of our regional and global partners in this effort, and we are appreciative of our law enforcement partners such as Australia, New Zealand, United States and others that have stepped in to assist," he said.

"Australia and New Zealand's commitment through the announcement of the International Joint Investigations Team (IJIT) comprising of Australian and New Zealand law enforcement agencies and the Colombian National Police to help stop illicit drug shipments coming to the region, is a major step towards stopping the trafficking of illicit commodities through our waters.

Concerns by traditional leaders, including Ratu Tevita were being taken "on board", he said.

Naivalarua said Fiji was working with its donor partners in building a safer and more resilient maritime community under the Solesolevaki ni Veitaqomaki initiative as crime prevention is a shared responsibility between the vanua, communities and government.

Community participation was critical, he added.

"People are our greatest asset and resource in this fight, and by enlisting their help where they work with law enforcement in the reporting of suspicious activities or crimes, we will surely make an impact that will benefit our communities and future generations."

Modernising policing

The police minister told parliament that the policy direction on the national coordination of transnational serious and organised crime and illicit drug enforcement in Fiji was issued two months ago and subsequently endorsed by cabinet in June.

"The intention of this policy is to provide clear direction for a strong and coordinated national response to detect, disrupt, dismantle, neutralise and curb illicit drug networks," he said.

The joint efforts would be manned by the National Joint Enforcement Centre (NJEC) where personnel work to share intelligence and coordinate operations.

"I also acknowledge the role of the military in supporting ongoing joint operations with the police, under this collaboration illicit drug cases in the first quarter of 2026 dropped by 30 percent, with overall crime rates dropping by 18 percent," he said.

The budget would support the implementation of the new police bill, which is before the standing committee on justice, law and human rights.

World.title: 'People just need certainty': Auckland councillors to vote on controversial housing density plan
World.content:
Richard Hills discusses Plan Change 120 Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Auckland councillors are voting today on how much housing intensification the city should have - and where it should go - after getting feedback from local boards and mana whenua.

Councillors will vote on the controversial Plan Change 120, which is needed to meet the government's minimum requirement to plan for 1.4 million new homes in New Zealand's largest city.

Two scenarios were put out for feedback to local boards and mana whenua - Scenario A, which just met the bare essentials of the government's requirement, and Scenario B which allowed for more intensification in areas in walking distance of transport.

Policy, Planning and Development Committee chairman Richard Hills said after consulting the community, council staff have put together a new proposal which is a compromise between the two.

Policy, Planning and Development Committee chairman Richard Hills. Alexia Russell

"So a lot of areas who were freaked out or maybe didn't like the density - most of those areas are not getting that and I think, for most Aucklanders, I hear [from], we should only be putting housing where there is good transport, water and infrastructure, like libraries."

The new proposal keeps six-storey zoning for all areas that are within walking distance of rapid transit and town centres, moving up to 10-15 storeys for some areas within a 10 kilometre radius of the city centre.

"We're largely landing in the place where we're doing all the legal requirements but adding density to that six-storey development around frequent transport corridors, the really busy bus routes heading into the city."

Character Coalition chairwoman Sally Hughes said special character areas, such as those in Mt Eden and Kingsland, are still at risk from the changes.

"We're really disappointed that the special character areas which are all inside that 10km will not receive the relief from the intensification that was in Plan Change 120."

Hughes said if the council votes for the changes on Tuesday, Character Coalition will keep fighting against it at the Independent Hearings Panel.

But campaign manager for advocacy group Greater Auckland, Connor Sharp, said it's a good compromise.

"While we would like it to go further, it's a decent enough compromise. It keeps a lot of the intensification within the isthmus where we really need more housing, so in that aspect, it's really, really good."

Another part of the proposed changes is not requiring intensification around local centres - which are groups of shops smaller than metropolitan centres.

But Sharp said many of those areas in central Auckland are already covered by other zoning requirements.

"It would still be covered by things like the frequent transport network, so you're still going to get up-zoning, whereas a place on the outskirts, like Franklin, which may not be suited to good transport connections, would be downsized."

Councillor Mike Lee. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Councillor Mike Lee has proposed an amendment asking to pause Plan Change 120 completely, until the Unitary Plan is reviewed later this year.

But Hills said the city needed certainty.

"That is often the case with these things - delay seems easier than making a decision - but I think delaying just puts us at risk.

"We've spent five years in this washing machine. I think people just need certainty, people absolutely need clarity about where they can and cannot build in their community."

World.title: Finance Minister Nicola Willis had little option but to protect local cement supply
World.content:
Analysis - It's hard to imagine Finance Minister Nicola Willis was particularly thrilled about handing over $60 million to one of New Zealand's major listed companies, Fletcher Building, so its subsidiary Golden Bay Cement could keep manufacturing cement at its plant near Whangārei.

But in the end, a subsidy of some kind looks like a practical decision she probably had little choice but to make.

Golden Bay Cement is New Zealand's only cement manufacturing facility, supplying roughly 60 percent of the cement used here.

Closing the plant and moving to an import-only facility from 2030, as Fletcher Building had signalled might need to happen if it did not get help, would surely not be in the interests of the country.

New Zealand has a lot of infrastructure to build in coming years - would we really want to rely only on imported cement, in a world where supply chains are disrupted and protectionism is on the rise?

The best Willis could do was ensure there were plenty of safeguards around this deal, so taxpayers' money is as well spent as possible.

And there are some, it seems.

Fletcher Building has committed to investing at least $150m of its own money in the plant through to at least 2040, covering operations, decarbonisation and resilience, with claw-back provisions if it does not deliver.

The decarbonisation part is important, as the cost of being part of the Emissions Trading Scheme is a key factor in Golden Bay Cement's struggles and inability to compete with foreign competitors.

Cement imports do not face the same ETS charges.

Willis says she did consider changing ETS settings to help Golden Bay Cement, but in the end decided doing so might undermine the wider integrity of the scheme and cost the government more.

A specific one-off grant was deemed the best option.

Supplied / Fletcher Building

The decision to keep the cement flowing in Northland is not yet drawing much criticism, with even ACT, the party of the free market, saying it supports keeping New Zealand's only cement manufacturer operating.

A ''necessary evil" was how ACT leader David Seymour described it.

ACT's issue, however, is with the ETS and its impact on Golden Bay Cement's ability to compete.

It claims this is evidence that New Zealand's climate change settings are not working for the country because they are loading emissions costs onto businesses.

The Employers and Manufacturers Association is strongly welcoming the move.

It sees it as a practical step. One that is also an important signal that New Zealand is more focused on resilience and looking after sectors critical to its economic future.

Perhaps that is not surprising, as just this month it issued an election policy document encouraging the government to offer financial incentives to firms critical to the economy.

The idea was even backed by the leading union E tū.

The government has been at pains to stress this is a one-off case.

Some in the forestry and mill industry, of course, may feel a little aggrieved. They too have faced multiple closures in recent years due to rising costs.

However, the government would likely argue that wood simply doesn't have the same supply chain weakness as cement, where New Zealand has just one manufacturer.

All of this does suggest something has shifted a little in New Zealand's political and economic landscape when it comes to government involvement in backing core industries.

More broadly, there seems to be a deeper recognition that New Zealand must now be smarter about its self-reliance in a world of oil shocks and Trump tariffs.

Industries such as steel, cement or fertiliser suddenly look a lot more important.

The real challenge here, of course, is making sure the right sectors and industries get help, and that the government does not simply hand out money to companies that should be lifting their own productivity.

World.title: Chris Hipkins urges National to not delay on sexual consent law change
World.content:
Weekly interview with opposition leader, Chris Hipkins Morning Report Download MP3 8m

Chris Hipkins is urging the government to get on with changes aimed at clarifying the law around sexual consent, rather than making it a campaign issue.

National has promised to make the law clear that there must be consent before sex every time, rather than assuming it has been given, but only after this year's election.

But Labour already has a bill doing much the same already drafted. It was developed by a cross-party group of MPs, and would define consent as something "communicated through words or actions", not silence or inaction, and that a person cannot reasonably believe consent has been given unless they have taken reasonable steps to establish it.

Speaking to Morning Report on Tuesday, the Labour leader said National declined to back the bill, led by Labour justice spokesperson Camilla Belich.

"The National Party decided not to support the bill - all the other parties in Parliament have all indicated they'll support - so that they could go off and delay progress so that they have something to campaign on," he said.

"They could progress the issue right now and a bill could be entered into Parliament right now and progress could be made on it."

Hipkins said Labour would back National's changes, if they were put forward. The Greens likewise, co-leader Marama Davidson saying on Monday it could happen right away.

National justice spokesperson and present Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith on Monday said National was "focused" but already had an "extremely" busy agenda.

"'I've got many changes in relation to retail crime and a whole bunch of things that we've been doing, and we're indicating that if we're re-elected, we'll be changing the law in this space.

"I'm glad that Labour are supportive of it, and I'm surprised they didn't do it when they were in government."

World.title: Ex-league star Dureau dies at 39 after long cancer battle
World.content:
Former Newcastle NRL halfback Scott Dureau, who became a Super League star with the Catalans Dragons, has died after a battle with cancer. He was 39.

The Dragons confirmed Dureau's death last night, amid reports he had died of brain cancer.

"A former iconic player of the club, he had been courageously battling the illness for several years," the Dragons' statement said.

"Beyond the exceptional player that he was, Scott was a man cherished by all those who had the privilege of knowing him.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"His talent and numerous achievements on the field, but above all his humility and kindness, will forever be etched in our memories.

"In these painful moments, president Bernard Guasch and the entire club extend their most sincere condolences to his wife Libby, his two daughters Imogen and Everly, his family, and all his loved ones."

Dureau played 42 games over four seasons with Newcastle before teaming with French club the Catalans Dragons for four years, chalking up 97 appearances.

He was named in the British Super League's "Dream Team" in 2011 and 2012 and won the Albert Goldthorpe Medal, the competition's equivalent of the NRL's Dally M medal, in the second of those seasons.

After his retirement in 2015, Dureau took up a coaching role with the Knights.

He had been battling cancer for more than decade, having retired from playing after a tumour was removed from behind an eye.

AAP

World.title: 'I love my name': Swans star on having the best name in the AFLW
World.content:
Sydney Swans' star youngster Zippy Fish was not surprised her name garnered some attention last season.

"Growing up, everyone was like, 'Is that actually your name?' Like, 'Yeah, it's my name,'" Fish laughed, talking to ABC Sport ahead of the upcoming season.

"I thought it would be quite a big feature [coming into AFLW].

"I love my name. Well, my full name is actually Zipporah, but I actually kind of forget that myself sometimes, because everyone just calls me Zippy … Very grateful for my name."

The attention Fish attracted after being drafted was immediate. She announced herself on the AFLW stage in her first game against Richmond last year, equalling the all-time AFLW record for most disposals in a debut match, with 26 touches.

Zippy Fish became known for her run off halfback and blistering speed. (Getty: Darrian Traynor)

Her blistering speed and ability to launch off halfback made her an instant fan favourite.

This was then cemented by her easy-going nature.

In her first post-match boundary interview with Fox, she said: "I don't really get nervous for anything really, I just went out and did my thing."

Over the course of her first season at the Swans, a new moniker developed. She started to be called "Zippy Ya Ya".

"That nickname came from [fellow Swans AFLW player] Imogen Brown, and it was so random, how it got out of here [the club]," Fish said.

"She does this thing, she just puts 'Ya Ya' at the end of everyone's name. And it just stuck on my name."

Halfway through the season, fans made this into a shirt.

Zippy Fish with the fan-made "Zippy Ya Ya Fan Club" shirt. (ABC: Marnie Vinall)

Her teammate Jasmine Grierson bought the shirt from League Tees. The team had a fines wheel last season and if someone spun the wheel and landed on it, they had to wear the shirt for the day.

Fish said she never landed on it.

While her move to the Swans is one she says she is deeply grateful for — it's hard to catch Fish without a giant smile plastered on her face — she does admit there are times she gets homesick.

The now-20-year-old is from Newman, a small country town in the Pilbara region of Western Australia, approximately 13 hours north-east of Perth.

When drafted to Sydney, she had to move across the width of the country as a teenager.

"It was definitely tough. I'm a big family person, and I love my family, and obviously my boyfriend's back there, so it sucks. But I think it's made me grow as a person," Fish said.

Zippy Fish won the Rising Star in 2025 after a sensational debut season. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

She was drafted from the East Fremantle Sharks at pick number five after running in the WAFL as a teenager with Molly O'Hehir, now at the Melbourne Demons, and Claudia Wright, now at the Brisbane Lions.

You can often hear draftees say how coming into AFLW is a bit of a surprise because you go from playing against girls to playing against women. But Fish said the Western Australian league prepared them well.

"I'd always been around footy and I watched a lot of W, so kind of knew what I was going into," Fish said.

What can we expect from her this season?

"Same as last year, pretty much, I reckon," she said.

"Just a little bit of run off halfback, maybe try and get forward and kick some more goals. And you'll probably just see me smiling out on the field, having a ball."

Fish will have a chance to become even more of a household name as she represents Australia in the upcoming Australia vs Ireland AFLW representative game in August.

She will be one of just two Swans players donning the green and gold, alongside fellow fan-favourite Chloe Molloy.

World.title: Tribunal upholds three-match ban for Crows forward Darcy Fogarty
World.content:
The Crows have failed in their challenge to Darcy Fogarty's three-match striking ban at the AFL Tribunal, the panel finding Fogarty had time to decide to swing his arm at Sydney's Harry Cunningham.

Fogarty was charged after his high hit on Sydney's Harry Cunningham in the second quarter of Adelaide's game with the Swans at the SCG.

Cunningham jumped to try to get the ball deep inside Sydney's defensive 50, and Fogarty came in and caught the Swans player high.

Cunningham was ruled out of the game with concussion and will miss this week's match against cross-town rivals GWS.

The hit was assessed as careless conduct, severe impact and high contact.

The Crows argued that Fogarty's actions did not constitute a strike, and that even if they did it should be high, not severe impact.

AFL counsel, Andrew Woods KC, said the actions were careless and a breach of the duty of care. He said it was no surprise the incident resulted in a concussion.

The contact "was flush, it was direct, and it was on a player whose eyes were on the ball, so he was vulnerable in that moment".

"Cunningham goes to ground, he is visibly severely impacted," Woods said.

"He remains on the ground and requires the help of support staff to get up and exit the field."

After deliberating for less than 20 minutes, the panel returned and chair Jeff Gleeson said they were "comfortably satisfied" that Fogarty had indeed committed the offence of striking.

"Fogarty had time to consider how he would tackle Cunningham in those circumstances. He chose to do so by swinging his right arm forcibly in the direction of Cunningham's upper body and head," Gleeson said.

Fogarty will now miss Crows matches against Collingwood, Essendon and Richmond.

Look back at proceedings in our live blog.

World.title: Electric Tiwi football final sees back-to-back victory for Imalu Tigers
World.content:
Just minutes into the men's Tiwi Islands football grand final, black-and-yellow-clad supporters jumped the sideline fence and started storming the field prematurely, caught up in the excitement of their first goal.

The Imalu Tigers had not yet won the flag, but their devoted supporters never gave them a reason to doubt their hopes of securing back-to-back premiership glory.

Some Tigers fans were so passionate, they ran onto the field each time their team scored. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

For the thousands of people living on the Tiwi Islands, Aussie Rules is much more than a friendly sport. It's a religion, and it all culminates on grand final day.

And for the many visitors attending the grand final game at Wurrumiyanga Oval on Bathurst Island, about 80 kilometres north of Darwin, it is a once-in-a-lifetime experience.

Tapalinga Super Stars players and supporters hug after their win in the women's grand final match. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Each year, hundreds of tourists charter planes and catch ferries across to the Tiwi Islands to watch some of Australia's most promising upcoming AFL players battle it out in front of their home crowds.

This year, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was one of them, becoming the first Australian leader to attend the game while in office.

The Tigers' opponents, the Ranku Eagles, also had plenty of supporters. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Victory for Imalu Tigers, Tapalinga Super Stars

Despite the opposing team, the Ranku Eagles, having the home-ground advantage, Melville Island's Imalu Tigers had the real upper hand, with droves of loyal supporters dominating the fence lines.

With reigning premiers Imalu only having lost a single game this season, it was always going to be a David-and-Goliath battle.

The men's grand final game was close early on before the Tigers pulled away. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

At half-time, it appeared the Eagles stood a chance, with the Tigers only narrowly in front by 12 points.

But in the third quarter, Imalu doubled their lead and soon became unstoppable.

For the second time in as many years, the Tigers took home the premiership cup, claiming victory in a thrilling 11.9 (75) to 7.8 (50) win against Ranku.

The winning Tigers team lifts the cup. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

One young Tigers fan told the ABC he hopes to be playing alongside his male relatives next season.

"It's the sport we grew up with and we just love playing it," he said.

"We love to beat people in it. It can get a bit rough, but yeah, we love it."

The Imalu Tigers had a dominant season in the lead-up to the final. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

In the women's division, it was a tight contest until the end between the Tapalinga Super Stars and the Jikilarruwu.

It was tit-for-tat for much of the first half of the game between the two sides, before Tapalinga created some distance in the third quarter, leaving Jikilarruwu trailing by 10 points.

As the final siren sounded, cheers were met with tears as the Super Stars won the game, defeating Jikilarruwu Thunder & Lightning 8.9 (57) to 4.8 (32).

Player with the Tapalinga Super Stars pose with the premiership cup. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Huge day of art trade

Grand final day is the largest social event on the Tiwi Islands' social calendar, attracting hundreds of tourists to the community from around the country.

With art centres open amid the influx of visitors, for the islands' artists, the event also doubles as their biggest day of trade and an opportunity to pour money back into the local economy.

Artist Romolo Kantilla said it was also an important time to share their culture.

Romolo Kantilla says the grand final is an opportunity for Tiwi Islands people to share their culture through art. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"It's a very special day for Tiwi people, it's a big day and we get everyone from the mainland and it's a good time to come see the art," he said.

"The art is based on creation stories, totem and country.

"Art is always part of us Tiwi people."

World.title: Breakthrough win for Bernard Tomic after lean tennis times
World.content:
Bernard Tomic is back in the winner's circle with the Australian veteran cracking his first Challenger Tour title in eight years.

Reaching the final of the Lincoln Challenger tournament in Nebraska, the 33-year-old showed some grit to save a championship point before downing Estonian Mark Lajal 4-6, 7-6 (4), 7-6 (3).

With a world ranking of 206, down from a career-high of number 17 back in 2016, Tomic started as the underdog against 23-year-old Lajal, who is ranked world number 159.

The crafty Queenslander nailed his service games, on target with 72 per cent of first serves as well as nine aces to cause headaches for his rival.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Tomic also had a three-set battle to book his place in the final, downing American wildcard Spencer Johnson 6-7 (5), 6-3, 6-2.

It was his fourth Challenger Tour title, with the last coming in Mallorca in Spain in 2018.

A quarter-finalist at Wimbledon back in 2011 and former junior champion, Tomic recently lost in the second round of qualifying, falling to fellow Australian Chris O'Connell 6-4, 6-4.

On the main ATP Tour, his most recent singles title was at the ATP 250 event in Chengdu in 2018.

AAP

World.title: Spain's World Cup win a reminder collective spirit trumps solo stars
World.content:
You could see it in the Spanish players as they floated euphorically, each kissing the top of the trophy.

You could feel it from the fans in the stands as they straddled that blurry line between overwhelmed and overjoyed.

And you could hear it rumble through Spain, as a nation united through something which in reality should not mean this much but means more than almost anything else.

Nick Hornby summed it up best in his classic football-themed memoir Fever Pitch.

"I fell in love with football as I was later to fall in love with women: suddenly, inexplicably, uncritically, giving no thought to the pain or disruption it would bring with it."

Argentina felt its force too, the scenes of Lionel Messi in tears, fans distraught, Leandro Paredes losing control and lashing out.

Lionel Messi was crushed after the defeat. (Getty Images: Michael Regan)

In that moment they thought may a love like this never find me.

World Cup football can twist and torment, ripping out your heart and stamping on it till you feel like it can never be repaired.

It can also make you fall head over heels and erase all the hurt you ever felt before.

La Roja ruthless in victory

Spain captain Rodri takes in the magnitude of the achievement. (Getty Images: Alex Pantling )

Spain coach Luis de la Fuente spoke about it in his own terms before the semi-final against France, drawing on inspiration from Julius Caesar, and the idea of having to suffer to achieve great things.

And this was a game that was a struggle for all, it lacked the overall quality and excitement you might expect from a final.

Argentina was stubborn and produced heroic defending in the box, but again questionable roughhousing tactics, eventually resulting in Enzo Fernández's send off.

The reigning champions showed little initiative to create much of anything until the final minutes of extra time as their dream dissipated in the warm New Jersey air.

Spain, having only conceded one goal all tournament, and with 20 shots to two in the decider, might not have produced its flashiest performance, but it was its most important.

This is what La Roja has done throughout the past six weeks, control the ball effortlessly, win it back almost immediately, build pressure through well-organised and committed structures, and wait till late to put it all to bed.

Ferran Torres celebrates the goal that proved to be the decider in the World Cup final between Argentina and Spain. (Getty Images)

The Spaniards were particularly effective in shutting out Messi, who saw little of the ball and was quickly dispossessed or forced into errors when he did have it.

Turns out he can be stopped; it just takes the most exceptional defensive team of this tournament to do it.

The European Champions are now World Champions for the second time, unbeaten for 38 straight matches, a magnificent footballing dynasty growing with every game, becoming the first country to simultaneously hold the men's and women's World Cups.

"I'm so proud of this generation of footballers who have grown up with this philosophy, remained true to it, made it even better and set an example as a team and a family," Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said.

"They're excellent, world-class footballers with exceptional talent. I'm very moved. Looking back and thinking about them, we've won everything, absolutely everything, with this generation of players."

Spain's collective triumph

Celebrations in Madrid will continue long after tonight. (Getty Images: Chris McGrath)

Argentina is a team built around one player, the likes of whom we have never seen before.

Spain is built around a collective approach, filled with exceptional players, but all who work in harmony, allowing each other to shine in different moments.

Like Mikel Merino with his repeated winners off the bench, or Rodri holding the side together as the linchpin in midfield, or Ferran Torres with his vital assists, and today's match-winning strike.

"I think in the end the goal came from 47 million people, not just those of us that are here," Torres said.

"Today destiny was written, it was made for us to win. We're far from our people today but we tried to be as close as possible to them.

"A huge relief [to score]. I've been criticised throughout the whole tournament but as I said before, destiny was written."

It says so much that Lamine Yamal, 19, seen by most as Messi's heir, did not play much of an influential role in this final, or at any stage during the tournament.

Lamine Yamal did not quite have the breakout tournament some predicted. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

He was not a passenger, but was certainly not a conductor, and that can only breed even further confidence, and strike further fear into other nations, as he goes from boy to man.

This World Cup started slowly for Spain, a scoreless draw with the tournament's best underdog story, Cabo Verde.

But as the superstars like Messi, Kylian Mbappé, Erling Haaland, Harry Kane, and Jude Bellingham took all the headlines and dominated social media algorithms, Spain was the quiet, conscientious achiever.

That all changed with the terrifyingly efficient dismantling of France in the semifinals, and now a completely deserved win in the final.

"This generation of players is an example for Spanish sport, for the Spanish youth," de la Fuente said.

"Together we are much stronger, and that is why we don't forget anyone."

A team forged through fire, built on discipline and togetherness, now enjoying its love story.

World.title: Tears streaming down his face, Messi leaves the World Cup stage a legend
World.content:
Lionel Messi had so desperately hoped his World Cup would end differently.

Tears running down his cheeks, a silver medal around his neck, his teammates in various states of depression, strewn around him like the detritus of some cataclysmic event as Spain roared amid garish golden confetti and an explosion of colour and joy.

Arguably the greatest player to ever grace a pitch was distraught.

It's impossible to know exactly what was going through his mind.

A decade earlier, on the same Metlife Stadium pitch where he was currently sobbing, Messi had tearfully decided to retire from international football after losing the Copa América final against enormous underdogs Chile.

The pain of that defeat was simply too much to bear for Messi, saddled with the expectation of a nation desperate to anoint him as Maradona's heir.

The world was the beneficiary as Messi reversed that decision.

Fans around the world have rejoiced at Messi's success. (Getty Images: Wang HE)

So too were Argentina, who claimed the 2021 Copa América title, the 2022 Finalissima and, most tellingly, the 2022 World Cup under Messi's leadership, cementing his legacy among his fellow countrymen for all time.

But once again in the New Jersey sunshine, Messi's tears were the defining feature for a generation of football fans.

Was this another tearful goodbye to the international stage?

Messi is 39 years old.

With 19-year-olds Lamine Yamal and Pau Cubarsí on the other side of the divide and winning for Spain, the next generation is not just arriving to force him out but has already arrived.

To play another World Cup in four years may be beyond even his mystic powers, even despite his impressive ability to adapt to the constraints his age has imposed on him.

The next generation, personified by Lamine Yamal, is snapping at Messi's aging heels. (Getty Images: PA Images/Bradley Collyer)

At this World Cup, Messi has walked for roughly half the time he was on the pitch, strolling and stalking for about 5 kilometres per game.

And yet, inarguably, no one player has had a greater role in his team's success than Messi has for Argentina.

His goals, eight of them, and his four assists dragged the defending champions through the group stage and the knockout rounds.

His ability to bend a game to his will, no matter the situation, made him seem nothing short of inevitable.

Despite all the walking, whenever Argentina threatened, the little magician was there in the heart of the action, conjuring and scheming and dragging his team home just when they needed him to.

His very presence seemed to inspire his teammates to feats beyond their capabilities, a totemic figure to rally around, his energy imbuing those around him with positivity and confidence and class.

Lionel Messi came close to lifting the World Cup for the second time. (Getty Images: FIFA/Tullio Puglia)

Against England in the semifinal, his two assists powered the Albiceleste to a famous victory in stoppage time.

Against Egypt, as his team faced elimination at 2-0 down, he provided the cross for the first and delivered the shot for its equaliser.

Against Spain in the final? It just didn't happen.

The fact that his tears only came after he had been given his silver medal was almost illustrative: No matter how late it got, Messi perhaps still had hope that he might somehow manage to influence the game in his favour.

He'd done it before, after all.

Only when Donald Trump laid the heavy silver slice of defeat around his neck did he realise there would be no more magic, that no amount of sorcery from his phenomenal feet could change history now.

Against Spain, the little master managed just 55 touches, none of which came in the Spain penalty area.

Lionel Messi was unable to stamp his authority on the contest. (Getty Images: FIFA/Maja Hitij)

He was stifled as effectively as if Spain wrapped him in a blanket.

And his Argentina teammates simply couldn't back up their superstar when it mattered most.

Messi could not deliver the magical moment that his nation demanded.

It was telling that Argentina offered so little other than niggly fouls and angry words as opposed to the free-flowing football Spain occasionally managed when the mood took them.

Let's not beat around the bush: Argentina were woeful in this final.

Argentina didn't have a single shot on goal in the first 90 minutes of the game, the first time any team has failed to do so in a World Cup final.

Their first attempt on goal did not come until the 26th minute of extra time.

Lionel Messi had Argentina's first shot of the game, in the second half of extra time. (Getty Images: FIFA/Maja Hitij)

Their 25 total fouls resulted in seven yellow cards, one of which was a second that saw Enzo Fernández up-end Pau Cubarsí, making him the sixth player ever to be dismissed in a World Cup final.

Argentina's nefarious skulduggery was finally, belatedly, penalised by a referee brave enough not to stand for it.

Coach Lionel Scaloni said afterwards that his team "showed that we know how to lose" in his post-match press conference, but nothing could be further from the truth.

The Argentines thoroughly disgraced themselves after the game's conclusion, Leandro Paredes lashing out and sparking a minor brawl that ended with him shown a red card after the final whistle.

Fractious barely covers it.

If this is to be his international swan song, the landscape post-Messi may as well be post-apocalyptic, so absent of joy and light does it appear to hold.

Claudio Tapia, the president of the Argentina Football Association, knows how important Messi is to the team. (Getty Images: Andrew Harnik)

It was not Messi's fault that he could not have the impact on the game he might have hoped for.

Spain were able to successfully nullify a far better team than Argentina in the semifinal with their Rodri-led midfield dominance suffocating their opponents' creativity.

Messi simply didn't have the space.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

He was closed down as ominously and relentlessly as the ticking of the clock that will one day herald the end of his stellar career.

Messi couldn't muster the magic to help Argentina become the third men's team to win back-to-back World Cups.

It is not the finale that Messi might have envisaged.

But if this is to be his tearful sign off, fans will still look back at having been blessed by one of football's greatest of all time.

World.title: The 13 photos that summed up the chaos of the 2026 World Cup final
World.content:
It was a tournament where the football was magical, the off-field antics were questionable, and ultimately, Spain left the United States as the champions of the world.

A day after the utter chaos of the third-placed playoff between France and England, where 10 goals were scored, Argentina and Spain played things a little more conservatively — right up until the game exploded into action.

Here are the 13 photos that tell the story of the 2026 FIFA World Cup final.

1. The Fresh Prince of Barcelona

Teenage superstar Lamine Yamal arrives at the stadium looking like the coolest dude on earth. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

While much of the tournament had been focused on the more established superstar names like Lionel Messi, Erling Haaland and Kylian Mbappé, teenager Lamine Yamal had floated under the radar for the World Cup passers-by.

Coming to the final having never lost a match where he had started for Spain, expectations were high on the 19-year-old as he came into the stadium. Would he be the hero Spain needed to overcome the perceived might of Argentina?

Whatever the pressure, he arrived looking like the coolest dude on the planet; calm, collected and rocking a style straight out of The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air.

2. Smoke and mirrors

Mark Carney greets Donald Trump ahead of the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

All eyes turned to the skies before kick-off as US President Donald Trump made his usual subtle entrance into the arena, coming in low and fast in the Marine One helicopter.

Once settled in prime position in a corporate box on the wings, Trump was afforded the questionable chance to give the trophy a little pat as FIFA boss Gianni Infantino brought the iconic gold statue to Trump's seat.

Before that, though, there was the potentially awkward meeting between Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, just a couple of days after Trump accused Canada of being "filthy" and "polluted" over its wildfire smoke that had blanketed New York in the lead-up to the tournament.

All-in-all, things seemed reasonably diplomatic, given Mother Nature had done her job to send the smoke packing just in time for the game.

3. America makes a double Buff

American announcer Bruce Buffer turns the World Cup into a blood sport briefly with his iconic introduction. (Getty Images: Sebastian Widmann)

In the most American moment of this entire game, event organisers decided that what this little old soccer match needed was a double Buffer.

Bruce and Michael Buffer, to be exact, the legendary ring announcers from every blood sport imaginable.

Flipping from one brother to the next, the pair excitedly announced that the game was "ready to rumble", in scenes not far off that time that soccer came to Springfield in The Simpsons.

4. The GOAT meets the rising star

Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal share a laugh together early in the match. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Looking a little less cool than when he arrived, but still the picture of confidence, Yamal made a beeline for Lionel Messi before the match to wish arguably the greatest player in history some luck.

It was a full-circle moment for the pair, who originally met on a photo shoot in 2007 when Yamal's parents won a UNICEF raffle to have Yamal photographed for a calendar with the then rising star Messi.

This time around, Messi's hair was a little shorter and his face a little more wearied, while Yamal was a little less nude.

5. The World Cup's Mariah Carey

Shakira performs during the half-time show, a spectacle one England footballing legend would go on to call "crap". (Getty Images: Lars Baron)

Shakira was rolled out for the half-time show, with the Colombian star fast becoming to the World Cup what Mariah Carey is to Christmas.

She's just always there.

While her performance was fantastic, the rest of it — from Justin Bieber to Madonna to BTS — left a little bit to be desired.

So much so that English footballing champion Wayne Rooney didn't hold back with what he thought.

"I thought it was crap," he said on the BBC coverage.

6. The spectacular red card

Enzo Fernandez fouls Spain's Pau Cubarsi, leading to the Argentinian's second yellow card and a send-off. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

As soon as we all saw it happen on the TV, we knew that the photos were going to be spectacular.

And veteran Getty photographer Al Bello didn't let us down.

Rising Spanish star Pau Cubarsí was sent flying by Argentina's Enzo Fernández, but it was made all the more spectacular by Cubarsí really leaning into the flip.

Had Fernández not already had a yellow, it's unlikely he would have been sent off at all, but the red card made it all the more dramatic as the scores stood at 0-0 heading into the death.

7. Hydration break goes to a new level

Spain's Dani Olmo takes the hydration break to the extreme as he utilises the sprinklers to cool down. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

Two things have been major talking points during this tournament: it's been bloody hot and the hydration breaks have been bloody irritating.

So it was fun to see the two come together in the final regular-time break of the tournament, as the Spanish players took advantage of the sprinklers to cool off.

Was it the trick that won them the World Cup? Who's to say. But almost certainly yes.

8. Free kick wipes a goal

Nico Williams reacts after his goal was marked off for a foul that was immediately obvious on the replays afterwards. (Getty Images: Carl Recine)

In a moment of brilliance, Nico Williams looked to have won it for Spain when he slotted a goal past the keeper to make it 1-0 late.

But the referee called it back. There was a free kick somewhere in the mess of bodies in the box.

In live action it wasn't immediately clear where the free kick was. On replay, it still wasn't totally clear.

But on the fifth or sixth watch: yeah, no idea.

Williams was furious, and rightfully so.

9. Deadlock ends in headlock

Nico Williams gives Ferran Torres a little chokehold celebration after Torres scored the winning goal. (Getty Images: Nick Potts)

Go back to the very first photo at the top of this story and you can experience the majesty of the Ferran Torres goal that broke the game open.

Hair blowing in the breeze, his teammates running in behind him, the fans screaming and cheering in ecstasy.

And then Williams decided to choke Torres for some reason.

Angry that he wasn't the hero after his goal was wiped? An in-joke that we don't know about?

Who knows. But it made for an odd scene in an incredible moment.

10. Tears of a legend

Lionel Messi slumps to the ground after the final whistle, in what will likely be the football legend's last World Cup game. (Getty Images: Michael Regan)

Small in stature but grand in legacy, Messi cut a forlorn figure after the final whistle.

His tiny body huddled in the middle of the massive stadium was enough to make anyone feel sorry for the attacking superstar.

His place as the greatest player the game has ever seen would have been secured had he managed to drag his teammates to victory, but even Messi couldn't get his countrymen through the incredible defensive wall that Spain had built.

11. Infantino chases after Trump

Rodri prepares to lift trophy as Gianni Infantino attempts to move Donald Trump out of frame. (Getty Images: Dan Mullan)

Trump had made headlines this time last year when he joined Chelsea on stage for the celebrations in the Club World Cup final, despite the apparent confusion of the players.

This time there was surely no way that Trump would be caught right in the middle of the pack as the Spanish players lifted the most coveted trophy in world sport, right?

Well, kind of. This time Trump wandered right across stage as Infantino pivoted left, leaving the FIFA boss to scramble after the US president, with the pair awkwardly caught in the team celebration photos.

On the broadcast, you could hear someone say "they'll crop him out" in an unexpected, but funny, hot mic moment.

12. Utter heartache for Argentina

Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez shows his dejection as the ceremony for the winners gets into full swing. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

Goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez had been immense through the World Cup.

But as Spain lifted the trophy, the Aston Villa keeper let the emotions flow, caught by the camera as he sat on the sidelines thinking about what might have been.

It was a reminder of what this thing, this silly, epic, immense mess of a game, means to the people who play it.

13. The love of a mum

Lamine Yamal's mum races out onto the field to celebrate the victory with her son. (Getty Images: John Todd)

In the end, all we really want is the hug of a mum who's proud of you.

And that's what Yamal got as his mum, Sheila, ran onto the ground to give her son a big old cuddle.

Having given birth at just 16 years old as an immigrant from Equatorial Guinea, Sheila's story is the one that really captures the essence of the World Cup.

Not the championship rings or corporate boxes. Not the powerful men in powerful suits making powerful political moves.

A mum with a dream for her son to shine on the world stage.

This was the moment that really mattered.
